(1867-1892) Draft of the Rule entrusted to Fr. Tornatore — Journey to Rome and presentation of the Rule — Condemnation of the Rule and banishment of Fr. Tornatore — Draft of a new plan for the Constitutions — Further attempts — Constitutions compiled by Fr. Tornatore and approved by Cardinal Vannicelli; autographical manuscript of Fr. Tornatore presented to the Sacred Congregation; corrections and definitive approval.

Draft of the Rule entrusted to Fr. Tornatore ~ The idea of Pius IX who wanted the Rule of the Institute without delay, encouraged Mother Gattorno to pray intensely for the necessary enlightenment. But, however hard she prayed, her mind remained arid.

“I prayed frequently”, she writes, “but I never felt anything”. (M. 2, p. 61). Rosa’s frank confession gives us the key to the whole somewhat tormented story of the Rule of the Daughters of St. Anne; it was not to be the direct work of the Foundress who was the depository of their charism; its compilation was to be entrusted to Fr. Tornatore, at first by the Mother herself, and later (in 1876), by Cardinal Berardi. The work was written along the fundamental lines that Rosa had received from the Lord on that February night in 1864; its journey was long and really arduous, with various interventions by the ecclesiastical authority, which, through the animadversiones, was in the process of perfecting the Constitutions themselves.

Therefore the Mother, at first in anguish about the Rule to be written, at last came to the decision which seemed to her the wisest because it had developed in prayer. Once again in her intimate and extremely intense relationship with her Good, she had an extraordinary intervention which she herself recounts in her Memorie: “One evening, while I was alone in chapel, St. Anne and Fr. Bernardo, whom I recognized because Mr. Tornatore had given me his portrait, appeared to me […]. Fr. Bernardo said these words: ‘Tell Mr. Tornatore that he should write the Rule you desire’”.1

With a certain inner confidence, Rosa therefore turned to the Father who, generously accepting her invitation, immediately set to work and finished it in a few months; the manuscript was entitled: “Words of the glorious St. Anne, Mother of Mary Immaculate, in presenting the Rule to her daughters”. So the Foundress presented a copy to the Bishop of Piacenza and to Cardinal Consolini in early 1868.

Bishop Ranza expressed his positive opinion about the new Rule in a letter in which he said that it was dictated by an excellent spirit and would help the Daughters of St. Anne to progress in perfection; but he left it open to those modifications which experience would eventually suggest. On the other hand, Cardinal Consolini merely acknowledged receipt of the manuscript without expressing any judgment.2

Undoubtedly encouraged by the favorable opinion expressed by the Bishop of Piacenza, Mother Rosa also saw fit to send a copy of it for approval to Cardinal Quaglia, then Prefect of the Sacred Congregation of Bishops and Regulars. She accompanied the Rule with really enthusiastic comments: indeed, she maintained that it had been “written by a divine hand”.3

However, at the same time she felt the need for supreme approval, that of the Vicar of Christ, which is why, enclosing the letter from Bishop Ranza of Piacenza, she sent the Holy Father a petition, hoping to obtain the desired approval.4 The petition is dated 17 July 1868.

In the meantime she immediately had a certain number of lithographic copies of that manuscript made to be distributed to the religious as an experiment, and at the end of the year (2 December 1868), she gave it to the printers. The said rule is commonly known in the Institute as “the 1869 Rule”.

Pleased at last to have a guide for her Institute’s religious life, Mother Rosa considered that the Rule was really inspired and corresponded to the new institution’s aim.

In the letters written in this period, the Mother repeatedly calls for the observance of the said Rule and reasserts its importance. Particularly significant is a letter addressed to Sr. Anna Vincenza Rapallino in which she says: “… daughter [concerning] that holy little book which our Fr. Tornatore presented to us after having written it under dictation from heaven, we wretched creatures give it such little regard; reflect, daughter, that these are God’s words and if we want to sanctify ourselves we should make it our job to put them into practice […]; This is what will make us deserve a most beautiful crown of glory…”.5 Again, in a talk she gave in Sampierdarena on 25 February 1871, she insisted on the importance of the Rule, which she described as having “come from the hand of the Lord”.6

In the meantime, Fr. Tornatore, with the Bishop’s consent, was diligently frequenting the Mother House in Piacenza to dedicate himself with the Mother to directing the Institute and to the formation of the novices and sisters; his recommendations came into everything, and it was known that the Mother let herself be guided by him in many matters.

The Father’s presence was agreeable to Rosa in those first steps of the new foundation; she felt the need for enlightened support in the serious work of the formation of the young girls who entered it.

The growing number of institutions in the different places encountered different conditions; they had to be adapted experimentally until a reliable way of proceeding was reached. Fr. Tornatore was now devoting a great effort to formation with conferences, personal counselling and concrete directives for fulfilling the daily duties.7

Mother Rosa therefore considered his collaboration and authoritative presence as superior and director indispensable. However, in that period Fr. Tornatore was also professor at the Collegio Alberoni, where he spent most of the day.

Towards the end of 1870, Mother Rosa knew that this was to be the Father’s last year of teaching, and feared to lose his help should he be sent elsewhere: so she wrote to Cardinal Patrizi in Rome and then to the Superior General of the Priests of the Mission asking that Fr. G.B. Tornatore be permitted to devote himself full time to the care of the Daughters of St. Anne, and that he be released from obedience to the local superior and subject to that of the General alone.8

This somewhat audacious request had been agreed with Bishop Ranza and was accompanied by a recommendation from him. To obtain the desired favor, the Mother presented Tornatore as Director of the Institute and, in her deep humility, even suggested that the Bishop call him “Founder”, to show the need for his work and to induce the General not to transfer him from Piacenza; she was so little concerned with her own honor, and so much concerned with the good of her daughters.9 Her wish was not totally granted; but in the following years, Tornatore stayed on in Piacenza and devoted himself largely to the care of the sisters.

Journey to Rome and presentation of the Rule ~ Towards the end of 1870, Mother Rosa had arranged to present the Rule to the Holy See once again, since she had received no answer to her first request of 17 July 1868.

Totally unaware of the harsh reality that lay in store, she asked Cardinal Consolini his advice about going to Rome; but the Cardinal, in view of the grievous events hostile to the Pontifical States and to the Holy See, suggested that she wait: “In Rome”, he wrote, “you would find only afflictions of spirit, without any of those consolations which you need. Let us say a lot of prayers”.10

The journey was therefore postponed to the spring of the following year. Mother Gattorno asked the help of Fr. Agostino Donadio, Superior of the Minims at the Friary of San Francesco di Paola in Rome, to find somewhere for her to stay. It was arranged that she stay with an excellent family, living in Count Vimercati’s house at San Pietro in Vincoli (St. Peter in Chains), opposite the Friary of the Minims.11

On 27 May 1871, Mother Gattorno left Piacenza accompanied by her secretary, Sr. Anna Vincenza Rapallina, by her daughter Carlotta (whom she could not leave for long periods) and by Fr. Tornatore who, far from suspecting that a judgment against him would have been made in Rome, hoped to be a great help to her in achieving the desired purpose.

Indeed, she had made forceful petitions to the General Visitor to obtain permission for the Father for that journey, with the aim of “having the Institute of St. Anne enrolled among the Church’s children to give it the advantages and stability of which it had so great a need”.12

Having arrived in Florence after a journey that went well for the others but was as usual exhausting for the Mother, they continued on to Rome by a very slow train: thus they traveled all night and reached the eternal city on the morning of 28 May.

After spending a few days visiting Prelates and other important people, on 4 June, according to what Sr. Anna Vincenza says in her Memorie, she was admitted to an audience by the Supreme Pontiff. At the feet of Pius IX, she presented a copy of the Rule to him, which she saw he was glad to accept: “He said he would read it, and continued to encourage me”, the Mother writes in her Memorie (M.2, p. 66).

She stayed in Rome for another month and had the grace of obtaining as Protector of the Institute, Cardinal Vanicelli, Archbishop of Ferrara, who took all the new Congregation’s concerns very much to heart. So the Mother returned to Piacenza happy and full of hope.

The Holy Father had in fact already presented the little book of the Rule to the Sacred Congregation of Bishops and Regulars to be examined;13 thus the Mother, suspecting nothing, was awaiting its approval from one day to the next. Writing to Mgr. Mariano Wanstienkist on 15 July 1871, she said: “I commend myself to you for our business of the Rule, and am anxiously expecting a few words that will comfort me”.14

Condemnation of the Rule and banishment of Fr. Tornatore ~ Instead, the matter took a completely different turn. The little book, according to the consultors, was completely alien to the canonical norms and uses for the constitutions of religious orders: The Rule compiled by Fr. Tornatore presented a discourse in the form of a dialogue through an inspired relationship, as though it were a continuous heavenly revelation that gradually pointed out the way.15 Moreover nothing was established with regard to the governance of the Institute.

Already on 1 August 1871, Fr. Manfredini, in a letter to Fr. Tornatore, told him that negative things were being said about the Rule since it was too strict and was written in the form of a dialogue.16

The vote of Fr. Raimondi Bianchi, the consultor, was decidedly unfavorable to its approval and the booklets of the Rule: “Words of the glorious St. Anne, Mother of Mary Immaculate, in presenting the Rule to her daughters”, and “Applications of the common Rule for the nursing sisters” were sent to the Holy Office on 26 August 1871.

Mother Rosa was informed of this on 16 November by Fr. Manfredini, who added that the consultor was contrary to their approval not because of the content, but because of the form, and suggested several ways for it to be re-written.17

At the end of its examination, the Holy Office condemned the Rule with a letter of 20 January 1872 addressed by Assessore Nina to Archbishop Vitelleschi,18 who informed the Bishops of the Dioceses in which the Daughters of St. Anne were working.

After about a month, on 19 February 11872, Mother Rosa received from Mgr. Mariano Wanstienkist, the secretary of Cardinal Vanicelli, who was the Protector of the Daughters of St. Anne, a letter by which she was thunderstruck.

He ordered the withdrawal and burning of the copies of the Rule that had been distributed to the Bishops and sisters, as well as of all the existing copies of it in the houses. Mother Rosa was also enjoined to expel Mr. Tornatore from the Institute and he was prohibited from approaching the Daughters of St. Anne in the future for any reason whatsoever, and from hearing their confessions.19

There are profuse expressions of paternal solidarity and sharing in this letter, together with a heartfelt invitation to hope: “…You should not despair of the result at all”, he said, “because if the Supreme Authority of the Church cannot accept the form and substance of the Rule presented and prohibits those who had a part in it from being included, this does not mean that an Institute which has already provided and can provide great spiritual and temporal comforts to others should not exist. So be brave, because it is fitting that you put the beautiful qualities that adorn you to the test…”.20

At any rate, it is obvious that in reading that page the Mother must have felt deep bewilderment; but this extremely harsh blow showed the metal of her great soul.

The unexpected negative judgment regarding the Rule which she maintained had been “written by a divine hand”, and which corresponded perfectly to the inspiration she had received, together with the banning of Fr. Tornatore, were a cause of deep distress. In fact, she writes to Mgr. Wanstienkist in anguished tones: “I was not so much upset at hearing what the Sacred Congregation had prescribed with regard to the Rule, as to read that the man who was the true founder has been banned from it. I can assure you that he is everything to our Institute, and if good works have been done, it was he alone who did everything”.21

The Mother’s disappointment about her failure to obtain approval for the Rule, which she continued to maintain corresponded with the inspiration she had received, was real and profound; but to change one’s mind in front of those to whom a Rule has been commended as a lofty norm of spirituality is the greatest sacrifice that can be requested; one’s whole spirit must be sacrificed, not only one’s feelings. It seems to us that the grace of God alone can provide such strength, and only faith can mark its passage. In spite of all, Rosa Gattorno undertook the burning with heroic promptness.

The following morning with the arrival of Mgr Wanstienkist’s letter,22 when Fr. G.B. Tornatore came to the Mother House, he was informed of the order received from Rome and immediately returned to San Lazzaro. She gathered up all the copies of the Rule that were in the house and immediately wrote to the bishops and to her sisters in the other houses to send to her in Piacenza all the copies of it in their possession; the sisters of Ferrara were to deliver the copies to the Vicar General of that city in accordance with Cardinal Vannicelli’s orders. Thus she had promptly obeyed but the cost was so violent that Rosa was smitten with fever and convulsions. That very morning, although she could barely hold her pen, she wrote a long letter to Mgr. Mariano Wanstienkist, in which she told him that the orders had been obeyed and asked his permission to go to Rome.

“God’s will is done”, she said, “over our heads; and I, miserable creature that I am, my head bowed to the ground, adore all his measures and submit to the Church’s wishes”.23 That same morning she communicated the message to the Bishop of Piacenza, telling him all she had already done.

Draft of a new plan for the Constitutions ~ Rosa then wished to return to Rome, also on the advice of Fr. Tornatore. She therefore set out on the morning of 24 February. It took her three days, because her weakness obliged her to stop in Bologna, Ancona and Foligno. She reached Rome on the evening of the 27th at 6.00 p.m. She summarizes the difficulties of that journey in one exclamation: “Oh, what a lot of troubles!”. She stayed in Rome for a fortnight. At first she was given a cold welcome, indeed, an ironic one. “… I was mocked by all the members of the Sacred Congregation of Bishops and Regulars because it had been [written] in the form of a dialogue […]; one of them asked me jokingly if I always spoke to St. Anne. How ashamed I and my secretary, Sr. Anna Vincenza felt! I had not the courage to present myself anywhere” (M. 2, pp. 65-66).

A little later, she was given a kindlier and more encouraging reception because “the presence of the Mother, her words of humility, her obedience and submission changed the perspective of it all”.24 With fatherly kindness, the new secretary of the Sacred Congregation of Bishops and Regulars, Mgr. Vitelleschi, showed that he understood Mother Gattorno’s deep anguish, and at the same time suggested the way to repair everything.

“You have had a good beating”, he said, but immediately added that it was the Pope’s desire that the Institute should continue and expand, and that she should think of keeping its spirit pure and lively.

At the audience she had with Pius IX immediately afterwards, she was very much comforted. “The words of Pius IX”, she said later, “gave me life”. The Supreme Pontiff in fact, showed that he knew that Fr. Tornatore’s presence in the Mother House had caused her suffering and suggested to her “to put that priest aside”. Rosa was surprised that this was known to the Holy Father since she had never spoken of her hardships to anyone (cf. M. 2, pp. 70-71).25

This leads one to think that there was someone hostile to Mother Gattorno and Fr. Tornatore in Piacenza, as Fr. Manfredini had hinted in a letter to Tornatore.26

The Pope ordered the Mother to compile the Rule herself, recommending her, “keep your spirit firm” (M. 2, p. 70).

The Sacred Congregation made Cardinal Vannicelli, Pro-Datary and Archbishop of Ferrara, responsible for helping her draft the plan for the Constitutions, suggesting that she model them on others already in existence, and avail herself, during his absence from Ferrara, of the collaboration of his Vicar, Mgr. Luigi Giordani.

Consequently the Mother left Rome on 10 March 1872 and arrived in Ferrara on the 11th, where she was festively welcomed by the superior, Sr. Anna Adelaide Pezzoni.

In accordance with Mgr. Giordani’s advice, she arranged to do a visitation in the six houses of the Institute before starting to compile the Rule and to base it on her observations. This was also Mgr Vitelleschi’s idea. It was an excellent decision, both because of the information it would provide about the Work’s needs, and because of the consolation it would give her.

In visiting the houses, the Mother gave talks to urge the sisters to observance and to encourage them. Her words to the Community of Ferrara are particularly touching: “Sisters, you are the seed of our Institute; on you, on the first ones, depends the success of the others…”.27

She also said, “…Our Institute is born from hardship and sorrows, but its foundation is all the stronger for that. It was born in a tossing ship battered by the waves on all sides, but it will be kept afloat by the Lord who, having tested it again and again, will steer it to the port of salvation. Let us say to Jesus: yes, bear us on the wings of your Providence, to take us later to the glory of blessed Paradise”.28

“In the midst of so many tribulations”, she then wrote to Mgr. Vitelleschi, “one consolation upholds me and gives me the strength to overcome every adversity: that in the tour of the six houses that I made, I can assure you that in each of them I found an observance and union which left nothing to be desired. I bless God for his Work and constantly confirm that I spoil everything and am truly good for nothing”.29

With such words, the humble Servant of the Lord described all the precious work which she had done during that visitation. Indeed she found great docility in all her sisters, but this was the triumph of her wonderful motherliness and the effect of the boundless trust in her of them all.

In Ferrara, precisely during those days, the aid which Countess Trotti of Bologna had formerly donated regularly for the community’s keep came to an end; although Rosa was being fired at from many sides, she was not distressed; indeed she encouraged everyone and ordered the superior to take into the house two poor, abandoned girls, bewildered and exposed to vice; by opening her loving arms wide, she would be given a larger share of Providence.

She urged the religious to progress in perfection and left them all deeply comforted.

In Piacenza she found some disturbances caused by the change of superior in the dependent house in Via della Morte; peace was fully restored by the Mother’s presence and affability, and life recovered its pace of work and religious fervor.

In Genoa she found the community very poor, but equally strong in spirit; her daughters were working hard with the sick, and she saw that they were so besieged by requests for assistance that she summoned another two sisters from Piacenza to help them.

“Here too”, her secretary, Sr. Anna Vincenza Rapallino writes in her diary, “during the recreations she stayed to talk and to answer their questions, comforting them by her own example and words”.30 However she was given a cold reception by Archbishop Magnasco; perhaps the rumor of what had happened with regard to the Rule had made him suspicious and ill disposed, or perhaps it was because Mother Rosa had previously refused the Rule he had drafted since it did not correspond with the inspiration she had received from God (see chap. VI).

The fact was that when he received the Mother on 23 March, he kept her standing and addressed only a few dry words to her; finally he denied her permission to have the community chapel blessed.

“Patience”, writes the Mother, “I immediately made an offering to my eternal Father and full of resignation and peace, I held tight to Jesus”.31

In a letter addressed to Archbishop Vitelleschi, Secretary of the Congregation of Bishops and Regulars, Archbishop Magnasco himself used rather unkind and resentful tones, confirming the fact explained above. Indeed he said: “…however good the Fouundress may be, and known to me previously, she does not seem to me to be as simple and ingenuous as could be desired”.32

“Then with regard to the new foundations, perhaps wrongly, a certain autonomy is apparent in the small communities, and a closer dependence on the Ordinary is to be desired”.33

It is well known that the Mother was a very humble person, but this did not make her ill-equipped; the accusation that she lacked openness seems to us truly inappropriate, as does that of her lack of submission to the ecclesiastical authority, to whom the Mother always showed deep filial devotion. This is confirmed by a letter from Bishop Ranza of Piacenza, in which he affirms: “…The Daughters of St. Anne directed by prudent and zealous Ecclesiastics, have a spirit of docility and obedience to the authorities of the Church…”.34

On the other hand she was very comforted in Sampierdarena where she could take part in a First Communion celebration in her house. Her presence in the community of Nizza Monferrato where she made agreements for assistance in the hospital and for the opening of a school for the girls of wealthy families was also providential. However, above all, she left the sisters well fortified by spiritual advice and encouragement.

She returned to Ferrara at last, with a fever, exactly one month after visiting the houses. She therefore set to work compiling the Rule, drawing inspiration from the observance which she found exemplary. After only seven days she completed the draft of the Constitutions.

The result was a work that corresponded to the reality and was very similar to the recently condemned Rule written by Fr. Tornatore; in fact the sisters, whose observance had inspired it, were living according to this same Rule written by Fr. Tornatore.

However, although she was the depository of the charism, she was not called to codify it; this was also the case of other foundresses at that time. Cardinal Vannicelli who had arrived in Ferrara, immediately set about correcting the manuscript; he discussed it with the Mother and at a certain point also wanted to consult the Prior of the Agostinians of Ferrara; but she feared that he might not be faithful to the Institute’s spirit and this was borne out by the events.

“Thereupon [the Mother] had to suffer a great deal”, Sr. Anna Vincenza Rapallina recounts, “since the Cardinal tried to base our Rule on other Constitutions, but she spoke with such emphasis about St. Anne’s work [which was] the work and the will of God, saying that she was prepared, rather than that this should happen [to] remove her veil instantly, and hang it on the picture of St. Anne, leaving God’s Work in [her hands]; and she did and spoke so much that the sacred ministers, that is, the Church, were convinced and concluded that the Work of St. Anne should not be joined to any other congregation”.35

Further attempts ~ With a letter to the Sacred Congregation of 14 June 1872, Cardinal Vannicelli sent the draft of the Constitutions and the “Voto” of Mgr. Giordani, but although they also praised the upright spirit that motivated the Foundress and the tireless charitable work to which the new Institute was dedicated, they themselves pointed out the need for further changes.36

In the meantime, Rosa had retired to Piacenza, and hoped that everything would shortly be successfully defined, but she spent months without receiving a reply.

Then new troubles and anxieties began for the Foundress, in anguish about the uncertain future of God’s Work.

The reverberations in her heart, tortured and oppressed by doubt, can also be seen in some of her letters written in this period. She felt the need to give her Daughters’ an established and reliable Rule; since vocations were increasing and the opening of new houses was pressing, the Mother realized how difficult it was to guide them all with her words alone, especially as she did not have the guarantee of supreme approval.

At last, on 1 December in that same year 1872, she was warned that the draft sent needed to be totally rewritten. The Sacred Congregation, having examined the manuscript of the Rule, had not deemed it opportune to approve it for a series of reasons; it also suggested changing the Institute’s name.37

Mgr. Wanstienkist, in giving this news, also mentioned a talk with Mgr. De Luca concerning the work to be done. “I found”, he wrote, “that Fr. Bianchi and Mgr. Vitelleschi were producing thousands of reasons for having to change it all; and to come to a conclusion I was told that it would be possible to take the Rule of the Dorotheans as a norm for the education of the little girls, a Rule that is very beautiful and already approved; and for the part concerning assistance to the sick and the management of hospitals, the Rule of the Franciscan sisters known as the Stigmatines and who depend upon the Minors Observants could serve as a model. With these two guides it should be possible to put together the Rule of the Daughters of St. Anne, making the modifications deemed necessary. And to work out this Rule the holy and learned Jesuit, Fr Fava, whom I know, would be very suitable”.38

The task was indeed entrusted to Fr. Leonard Fava (16 December 1872), and Mgr. Wanstienkist himself gave the news to Mother Gattorno a few days later: “I have obtained”, he said, “that the most worthy Fr. Fava, S.J., take charge of putting this Rule in order, and he will do it without looking at others that belong to different Institutes: he will take the spirit of the one that is yours, shown to the Bishops and Regulars, and not approved.”39

Fr. Fava was well known at the time and esteemed for his spiritual culture and for the sensitive positions he had held in his Order; he spent the last part of his life giving advice to many who turned to him, in the office of spiritual director at the Collegio Romano. However he was unable to start the task immediately because he was busy promoting liturgical and pastoral initiatives in the Church of S. Ignazio.

Thus he could only tackle the rewriting of the draft of the Constitutions at the end of January 1873. The Mother obviously followed all this arduous business with indescribable apprehension; she was distraught by the first opinions, which even wanted to model the spirit of the Daughters of St. Anne on that of other Institutes which had emerged in those years (see the “Voto” of Fr. Bianchi). So she hastened to ward off that blow and succeeded. As in Ferrara, so in Rome her right reasons were taken into consideration; she wanted to have respected God’s plan which had also been corroborated by the Pope, and the Constitutions had to be modelled on that alone.40

She left Piacenza in January 1873 and arrived in Rome in February, having had to stop in Foligno; and she had another disappointment seeing that Fr. Fava had not yet been able to set to work. After some hesitations, pressing him to have the Rule at last compiled and approved, she succeeded in getting Cardinal Vannicelli to have the manuscript returned to her (4 April 1873); the following day she presented other Constitutions to the Congregation’s secretary, Archbishop Vitelleschi, so that he could bring the long and thorny matter to conclusion through the work of one or more consultors. Of course, the Mother, with her desires, overlooked the delays of the Roman Curia in matters of such importance and did not see how difficult the process was. The painful and complicated affair had not yet reached its epilogue. There were other vain attempts, not the last of which was that of Fr. Riamondo Bianchi who, at Archbishop Vitelleschi’s suggestion and after the Mother’s heartfelt insistence, drafted a new plan for the Constitutions, every now and then questioning the Foundress herself on various points. But this time it was she who refused the Rule as it did not correspond to the Institute’s spirit. No one had clearer knowledge than herself of the founding experience of the charism that she would have to pass on to her Daughters.41

Constitutions compiled by Fr. Tornatore and approved by Cardinal Vanicelli; autographical manuscript of Fr. Tornatore presented to the Sacred Congregation; corrections and definitive approval ~ In 1874, the Constitutions were at last drafted by Fr. Tornatore, officially reinstated at the Institute. The text, which lacked the part concerning governance, was approved ad experimentum by Cardinal Vannicelli; in the meantime, the booklet “Special instructions for the confessors of the Daughters of St. Anne” was printed, so that, in fulfilling their duty, it might help the religious to progress in their own spirit42.

Two years later, in 1876, by order of Cardinal Berardi, Tornatore himself presented in an autograph manuscript a new text of the Constitutions, substantially similar to that of 1874 and completed also in the part concerning government; this at last obtained the Decree of Praise for the Institute.

This last text too underwent successive modifications; in 1885 it was approved ad experimentum for ten years, and it was definitively approved, as we shall see, on 26 July 1892.

It could well be said that the Rules, at last approved, were a precious jewel given to the Institute; they were also the fruit of so many humiliations, so many anxieties, so many prayers of Mother Gattorno. Great, therefore, was the joy that flooded her soul when she received the Constitutions: she accepted them from the maternal authority of the Church, presented them with enthusiastic words to her Daughters and recommended their observance with every care.

But she did more than give verbal recommendations; she saw life in those Rules. Therefore, as a true Mother, she offered herself to God as a victim, so that this life might be full in all her Daughters and might never fail. One cannot read without deep emotion what she wrote in her Memoirs: “The irons I keep under my knees when I pray, the meagre food I take, and so poorly, the irons I wear on my arms and legs, [the wounds] they have made in me, all this I offer you, so that you may grant me that your Institute may never fail in the observance of the Holy Rules until the end of the world” (M. 1.1, p. 134).

(1872-1877) Formation in the communities — Foundation in Foligno — Foundation of the first house in Rome: Tor de’ Specchi and other schools: Parrochietta and Via delle Fornaci — Rapid spread of the Institute — First house in Sicily: Agrigento — Foundation in Naples — Prophetic words in Marcianise.

Formation in the communities ~ while she waited for the definitive approval of the new rule, Mother Rosa judged it prudent to restrain somewhat the impetus she had given to the Institute so far. She felt that 1872 should be a year of reflection and conversion. She therefore reduced the number of postulants accepted for many months; she accepted no new houses and even canceled all the celebrations for the Feast of St. Anne. She took the initiative for this last measure as a voluntary and important mortification for the whole Institute; to prevent the decision from being wrongly interpreted, she gave a talk to the community of the Mother House on the eve of the feast, ending with these words: “I have yet to tell you that you should not be upset that we are not celebrating the Feast of St. Anne this year. It does not mean anything: our Institute is going at full tilt. There will only be two Masses, because I believe that in this way we will honor the Holy Mother”.1

Mgr. Wanstienkist, the Cardinal Protector’s secretary, immediately wrote to Mother Rosa that such austerity was uncalled for.

“With regard to not celebrating the Holy Mother in any house this year, let me say that I do not like it, and that you might have done at least what was done in previous years; but I have no strong feelings about it; therefore take it as though I had said nothing”.2

Perhaps the Prelate did not know of all the Mother’s other intentions in that voluntary renunciation of the Feast. It was intended to give the religious a deep shock, so that their tenacious commitment to making themselves more pleasing to the Lord might obtain the great graces the Institute then needed, regarding both the approval of the Rule and the future they would have to face.

We have several notes of the talks which Mother Gattorno gave that year to her daughters and to the nurses in particular. They are forceful and specific reprimands for weaknesses and omissions, noted day after day: in self control, patience and prudence in dealing with the sick, the spirit of poverty and obedience, diligence in working and dignified conduct when out in the streets, exemplary patience also in their own illnesses, and various other points of this kind. The discourse ended with a certain solemnity: “The Daughter of St. Anne, as our Holy Father Pius IX told me, must be an apostle who preaches the faith to believers with her good deeds and her good example, to constantly increase their fervor; and to those who are not believers, to attract them to devotion or at least to make them Christians”.3

This solicitude attracted God’s blessings. Their spirits refreshed and refined, excellent religious were prepared during those months for the many works that God was to require of the Institute.

On 11 August Mgr. Mariano Wanstienkist wrote happily to the Mother: “Mgr. Vitelleschi finds that there are no difficulties to prevent you from opening other houses, with the permission of the Bishops Ordinaries, if you have the staff and the means: so you can continue to receive postulants”.4

The Mother immediately set to work: although the Rule had not yet acquired definitive approval, his invitation meant that she could continue along the general lines already tested. Requests for entry to the Institute soon multiplied; as for the houses, the most numerous requests were for schools for the children of the common people. Thus at the beginning of 1873, in barely three months, the Institute accepted six new foundations: a hospital in Ovada, a school in Foligno and three schools and a house for serving women in Rome.5

Foundation in Foligno ~ The new dawn of the Institute was to be in Foligno, where the Daughters of St. Anne had several friends because of the hospitality they had offered in Piacenza. Through the generosity of the Grampini sisters they were given a house at 12, Via Bellestracci; Duchess Agnese di Sora Piombino, in addition to charitable donations, was generous with her favors and used her powerful influence on behalf of the new religious.

Mother Gattorno arrived in Foligno on 15 January 1873; the six religious who were to live in the house arrived on the 20th; their superior was Sr. Anna Carmelina Carretta. Their arrival in Foligno fully corresponded to the local needs: free assistance to the sick and a school. But the Massonic sect, which had some fanatic members in Foligno, could not tolerate the arrival of a new community of sisters.

The Daughters of St. Anne lived for a month in a country house on the outskirts of the town, since the house they had been given was still occupied by tenants; towards the end of February they opened their new house in Via Bellestracci. The Mother, who in the meantime had gone to Rome to deal with the matter of the Rule, then returned to stay in Foligno to make arrangements at the beginning of the foundation; she was therefore involved in the serious events that marked it.

First of all the local authorities denied her permission to open a school, although the documents presented were in order; this did not put Mother Rosa off and she arranged to open the school despite the unfair prohibition by turning to higher authorities.

On the night of 12 March a strong earthquake tremor was felt: the sisters too were terrified but it did no damage to their house. The following day, however, the Mother was very worried and kept saying that something sinister was about to happen; the next night she wanted to keep a lady friend to stay and sleep in the house, so that she could act as their guide should they have to leave it. At about one o’clock in the morning, a woman’s voice shouted from the neighboring house, “Fire! Fire! Sisters, fire! They are setting you alight!”.

They all bounded out of their beds and half-dressed rushed down stairs to the door. In fact, the outside of the front door was burning. Mother Rosa who was the first, unbolted the door in a flash saying: “Come on, daughters, follow me!”. She gathered up her clothes and leaped over the flames that were flaring up on the threshold. The others followed suit, and they all found themselves in the street.

The fire had been started with criminal intentions. Petrol had been smeared all over the door to a man’s height, and cloths, also soaked in the inflammable liquid, had been stuffed into the cracks between the shutters and the door-jambs as well as on the threshold. The sisters put out the fire with water and the sand left there for the building work; thus after a few hours they were able to return to the house, but they were not quite at ease. In fact, out of the window they saw two men passing who, one after another, stopped a while at their front door.

The following morning, the police who came to see what had happened found a note pinned to the door which said: “This brothel of sisters protected by the Duke of Sora Piombino and the Cavaliere Morotti must go. Goodbye for the moment”. This confirmed the rumor the police had heard, that the crime was the work of the anti-clerical party. It was nonetheless impossible to identify who was to blame for this widely documented criminal episode, despite meticulous investigations.6

Other threatening acts were used to intimidate Mother Rosa and her sisters, but in the end they were left in peace to do their charitable work.

Foundation of the first house in Rome: Tor de’ Specchi and other schools: Parrochietta and Via delle Fornaci ~ Her frequent visits and stays in Rome for the laborious business of the rule prompted the Mother to want a house in the heart of Christendom. Providence met her need, unexpectedly as always.

Several ladies of the Roman nobility who were endeavoring to defend faith and morality, begged her to take on the direction of a school at Tor de’ Specchi, where there was a plan to adapt some premises in the house of the Oblates for precisely this purpose. Rosa was glad to accept, and immediately informed the Bishops of Piacenza and Genoa as though it were an especially important event. She put her secretary, Sr. Anna Vincenza Rapallino, in charge of supervising the work and left her in Rome with her daughter Carlotta.

In the meantime, she returned to Foligno as has been said. Sr. Rapallino was a good substitute for the Mother with the ladies who were their benefactors, but she felt less able than her to undertake new foundations.

“You do everything at full tilt”, she wrote, “the schools [are] already starting in the new house. Do not worry, I will do everything you write”.7

In fact, perhaps because of Sr. Anna Vincenza’s lovely ways, the Daughters of St. Anne seemed so suited to the work that in those days it was also decided to entrust them with the house of Parrocchietta, opened on the initiative of Pius IX.

So it was that on 1 April the house of Tor de’ Specchi was inaugurated and it was shortly followed by another popular school in Parrocchietta; a third was then opened on the Via delle Fornaci.

These districts in the Roman suburbs were famous for the derelict state in which they had been left; no means of communication then linked them to the city; the sparse homesteads were run down and the people, so marginalized, had become particularly uncouth.

The Circolo Romano di Santa Monica provided charitable care for those neglected souls; its members visited them from time to time, giving them money; they were also concerned to provide religious assistance.

In all these cases, in addition to schools, Mother Rosa arranged free nursing for the sick. For each of the two houses in the Fornaci and in Parrocchietta, she was given a grant of 50 lire a month by the Alms Office of the Holy See; this made the two small and wretched communities, which she considered in a certain sense paid for by the Pope, very dear to her. She recommended the superiors not to complain of the poverty in which they lived, the effort required or anything else, and enjoyed being informed of everything. “Do believe, my dear Mother”, the superior of Parrocchietta wrote to her, “that Mgr. Negrotto has not heard a word of complaint pass our lips. That Monsignor should say that he would like us to go to Rome for these two winter months, is because here it is always raining, and the wind is strong enough to deafen anyone who is not deaf”.

They always used to tell Monsignor that they were fine and that they did not need anything, but they did not even possess an umbrella to shelter from the rain on their way to Mass; and the only clock in the house did not strike the hours regularly.

“As for us”, the poor superior concluded, “it is as though we were in the midst of the sea; everywhere lets in water and drafts, and we always have to paddle through water”.8

However, as we know, this was the style of all Mother Gattorno’s foundations: they had to face all the discomforts of poverty in order to relieve the misery of others.

During that period she had an audience with Pius IX who was very pleased to hear that she had opened various houses in Rome. Mother Rosa found indescribable consolation in the Pope’s welcome; once, with fatherly kindness, he even gave her two large pears which she jealously preserved in alcohol.

In April that year (1873), Mother repeated her thanks to Pius IX and explained the state of the Institute to him in this letter:

“Most Holy Father,

Please allow the lowliest of your servants to address a word of thanks to you for all the kindness you have extended to her. Your Holiness’ idea of entrusting two schools to us [which] are supported by you, fills me with joy and brings me dumbstruck before Your Holiness. The poverty of my words and the thought that we are supported by you often takes my breath away. Your Holiness, I have too much to say to you! May my God convey it to you, by granting you all those graces that you, our Sovereign Pontiff, desire, [which] are prayed for by all of us Catholics and in particular by this flock of two hundred women religious and a thousand poor little girls saved from danger. Our prayers have no other aim than yourself, Your Holiness, and the triumph of Holy Church”.9

Rapid spread of the Institute ~ As can be deduced from the figures recorded by the Mother, the Institute of the Daughters of St. Anne, at that time not even seven years old, was growing rapidly.

In leaving Rome, Mother Rosa felt a powerful impulse in her heart to do all she could to guarantee the future of God’s Work. That year she opened another two houses: the hospital in Cortemaggiore and the school for girls in Pennabilli.

The following year, after obtaining approval of the Rule from the Cardinal Protector, she also saw a large flow of postulants to the novitiate in Piacenza; this was God’s most reliable and visible blessing to the Institute, since her generous resolution to give herself to Gospel perfection in works of charity with the Daughters of St. Anne could only come from him.

From that time, the foundation of new houses became an almost ordinary event in the course of the year. A large part of Italy came into contact with Rosa Gattorno’s work, and appreciated its simple life style, its charity to the sick and the very modest conditions requested in the foundation agreements. Some people observed that this discretion explained the rapid growth of the Institute in so natural a way, but on the contrary, its growth revealed the hand of Providence which was supporting those who placed such boundless trust in it.

It would take too long to follow in detail this spreading of charity that was extending throughout the Italian peninsula through Mother Rosa’s tireless work; but we cannot omit to mention the Institute’s marvellous expansion in the south of Italy from that period.

First house in Sicily: Agrigento ~ The first house in Sicily was at Agrigento. On 24 September 1876, the Granata Institute was handed over to the Daughters of St. Anne. It was a beautiful, even sumptuous new building that had just been completed to house the orphanage and the day schools for girls.

The Fidecommissaria Administration, wishing to entrust the work to a religious congregation, sought advice from “a prelate of proven wisdom, resident in Rome, who immediately pointed to the Order of the Daughters of St. Anne, very recently founded, as one which had provided many lovely proofs of itself”.10

The new house was inaugurated in the following September, and it was the first seed of the Institute’s vigorous vine that spread throughout Sicily.

Indeed, from that time, Bishops and civil administrators vied with one another in inviting these religious to take on schools, hospitals and colleges. Archbishop Michelangelo Celesia of Palermo summoned them to his diocese in 1878; after a preliminary experiment in Termini Imerese, he wrote with satisfaction to the Mother General and thanked her for the excellent choice of the people she had sent.11

Other foundations naturally followed in rapid succession in that generous island which, although it was requesting the charity of the Daughters of St. Anne, gave them of its best: donations, attestations of warm gratitude, and what was most precious, lovely vocations.

Indeed, before Rosa Gattorno’s death, Sicily already had 60 houses of her Institute, 10 in Palermo alone. The vicissitudes of the mortal epidemics and especially the various invasions of the cholera, made the humble and heroic charity of the Daughters of St. Anne shine.

This flourishing life was nevertheless due to the Mother General who did not spare herself the most exhausting journeys to make frequent visits to the houses in Sicily and kept an eye on everything. Whenever she visited the island, she roused deep admiration with her great virtue, consisting of sweetness and diligence, boundless faith and inexhaustible kindness to neighbor and especially to the sick and the young.

Mother Rosa attracted all sorts of people with her fascination; many aristocratic ladies of the Sicilian nobility made friends with her, eager to draw from her conversation the lofty religious sentiments with which her heart was overflowing.

One of these was the Princess Emilia Settimo di Fitalia who, already a close friend of Sr. Anna del Salvatore Orsi, after her death became a spiritual daughter of Rosa Gattorno and a great benefactress of the Institute.

In the last decade of her life, Mother Rosa saw a flower of Palermo’s aristocracy enter her institute: Duchess Maria Teresa Patti di Sorrentino. The young noblewoman had met the Foundress for the first time on her visit to Palermo (probably in January 1885); “…the meeting with this really extraordinary woman inspired by God”, as was testified many years later, “exercised such a fascination on this young girl that she became involved and irresistibly attracted to follow her”.12

A niece of the Princess di Fitalia, she had planned the foundation of an institute under the guidance of Cardinal Guarino, Archbishop of Messina, who was her spiritual director.13

Her meeting with the Foundress changed her plans and oriented her to a new work, but one that would be linked with Mother Gattorno’s Institute.

In fact, an undated Rule called “Constitutions of the Daughters of St. Anne Perpetual Adorers”14 by an unknown author, and which provides for its Novitiate House in Palermo, seems to be connected with Anna Maria Patti di Sorrentino. An attentive reading of the above-mentioned Constitutions reveals that certain elements are in affinity with those of the Institute, especially with regard to St. Anne’s inspiring presence. There is no doubt that the Foundress took the new project into consideration and sent her observations on it to Maria Teresa through Emilia di Fitalia.15

Maria Teresa Sorrentino accepted these points, as we can grasp from Mother Rosa’s letter of 8 May 1891;16 however the project came to nothing; the young girl entered the Institute on 8 March 1892 and was clothed as a Daughter of St. Anne on 17 April that same year. It is thus possible to conclude that the Mother, with deep respect, had guided her and helped this final decision to mature.

Sr. Anna Maria Teresa worked intensely with Mother Rosa as soon as she entered the Institute in offices which required great tact and from 1895 she was beside her as General Assistant, also continuing as superior of the community at the Educational Institute in Palermo.17

The Mother, pleased about the triumph of grace, nevertheless avoided any feelings of satisfaction at her achievement. Indeed, in a letter addressed to Maria Teresa, she said humbly: “What a sorrow it is to me to see myself unable to help you in your spiritual needs! Patience! I am always afraid of being in the way of your true good. Forgive me, and you may be assured that I have a very, very deep affection for you”.18

Foundation in Naples ~ just as the reputation the Daughters of St. Anne acquired in Rome gave rise to requests for them in Sicily, so the knowledge and veneration which the Foundress enjoyed with Fr. Agostino Donadio was the guideline that led her to Naples. Here, Fr. Casals, Provincial of the Minims, wanted to be able to do something for the many sick and abandoned poor. Discussing this with Fr. Donadio, he mentioned Rosa Gattorno and her Institute; in short, everything was arranged for a house of nurses to be opened.

Mother Rosa, passing through Rome, had the idea of presenting the community of the seven sisters she had taken to Naples to Pius IX. The Pontiff, welcoming the religious with his large smile exclaimed: “Here are the Daughters of St. Anne, my ragamuffins!”. He spoke to them kindly and ended with some advice: “Be apostles and be alert, for the devil is not asleep; call frequently on St Michael Archangel to defend and assist you, and with his help you will do great good”.19

They arrived in Naples on 4 April 1877 and at the start stayed in rented premises in the palace of Princess Sannicandro Sanfelice. As usual, they immediately found themselves in the arms of poverty: seven sisters with only four beds, so that in order to rest, every evening they had to resort to some sort of arrangement and make do as best they could.

However, soon Providence proved most generous. To start the new community, Mother Gattorno left her secretary, Sr. Anna Benedetta Carrega of the Genoese family of the Marquises Carrega, who had been a member of the Institute for three years. This excellent religious, who was later to succeed the Foundress, was the good angel of the Neapolitan foundation; she instantly inspired a wave of sympathy for the Daughters of St. Anne, so that they were crowned with favors.

“Beloved Mother”, she wrote to the Mother General on 16 May, “I am dumbfounded and beside myself to see the Lord’s Providence raining down on all sides. Today 530 lire have landed in our cash box, and such a quantity of furniture that, to tell the truth, we don’t even know where to put it!”.20

However Providence was preparing that abundance for the imminent development of the foundation. Indeed, the growth of the community and the work requested soon obliged them to move house.

Among the noble ladies who favored the Institute, Princess Granito Pignatelli di Belmonte should be remembered. After she had met Mother Rosa, she pondered every way to help her Work. One day she presented her young son Gennaro to her,21 among his other gifts, he had a taste for art and was very adept with a paint brush. She therefore asked him to paint a picture of St. Anne for the sisters’ chapel.22

That occasion was the beginning of providential events in the Institute’s history, since if the picture of Prince Gennaro could recall the affection of his family, he himself, becoming a priest a few years later, had a valuable spiritual relationship with Mother Gattorno. She gradually entrusted to him the work that the Lord was so miraculously bringing about in her, and frequently turned to him for advice.

Called by God to the lofty office of Prince of the Church, Cardinal Gennaro Granito Pignatelli di Belmonte was one of the most important witnesses of the history and greatness of Mother Rosa.23 He was also the beloved Protector of the Daughters of St. Anne for many years.

The house in Naples was a most fruitful seed. Very soon the Foundress had to establish other communities in and outside the city; then in the province and in the southern regions, from the Abruzzi to Calabria, she opened many houses within a few years, some of them of great importance.

Prophetic words at Marcianise ~ In these foundations, which the Mother always made in person, wishing to see how her religious were settled, the impression she left on all who saw her was very deep, because of the virtue that shone through her appearance and the wisdom of her words. This is a testimony found at every step in the informative Processes. Sometimes, even in the presence of priests, although she was very sparing of words, expressions came from her lips that drew people to God. So it was at Marcianise, where in 1884 a number of people and several priests had gathered to discuss the opening of that house, and all appeared very worried about the lack of means; when everyone had fallen silent, the Mother said, pointing to the floor: “The time will come when these stones will become bread”. All understood that it was necessary to entrust the future to Providence with greater faith; those who heard her did not forget these words, which were later completely fulfilled.

But the fragrance of God that Mother Rosa left behind as she passed through the towns and cities of Italy will have to be dealt with at length later. Here it is enough to consider the prodigious and rapid spread of an extremely poor Institute, wholly devoted to charity.

When Mother Gattorno left this earth in 1900, she had founded no fewer than 318 houses in Italy; in America, as we shall see, 43; in Africa, 7. In all, then, 368 houses with about 3,500 religious Daughters of St. Anne. For this work 34 years had sufficed, and they were the most difficult years for religious Institutes in Italy.

It must be admitted that here the finger of God is revealed, as Mother Gattorno herself told her Daughters shortly before she died. Yes: a creature, however shrewd and strong, could not have overcome so much opposition and such scarcity of means; still less could she have won the support of so many souls ready to follow in her footsteps in a work so difficult and so full of unknowns.

Here, then, is the finger of God. But the figures quoted also tell how much dedication to grace was needed for a woman to succeed in organizing and sustaining such a mass of works and people in countries so distant and so different, without being discouraged by the obstacles that human wretchedness, alas, knows how to sow in the fields where one works for God. This, then, is once again the victory sung by the heroism of love.
