(1866-1900) In the Mother’s study at Piacenza — Formation through thousands of letters — An extraordinary sense of motherhood — Pedagogical guidance of superiors and sisters — The religious vows — Enlightened governance of the Institute.

In the Mother’s study at Piacenza ~ Let us tiptoe into the little study in the large Mother House of Piacenza in which Mother Gattorno devoted herself to governing for 17 years. The room is imbued with an almost religious atmosphere which still recalls her sweet, irreplaceable presence.

The ingenuous simplicity of the first days of the Institute lingers: a few cane chairs stand against the short walls; there are two little doors, one leading to a larger room, the other to the adjacent chapel of St. Joseph.

In the corner next to the chapel is a small desk with very humble writing implements and a crucifix. On the neighboring walls hang pictures of various sizes: a water-color of the “Mater Gratiae”, and opposite the desk and close to it, a print of St. Francis of Assisi of which the Mother was very fond.

Another picture shows Simeon bearing the Christ Child in his arms: a little inscription tells that this belonged to the Mother when she was still in the world. On the corner wall close to the desk are two autographed portraits of Pius IX: group photographs of sisters with the first orphans, the photo of the first sister who died and the first group of Daughters of St. Anne who left for America in 1878.

Formation through thousands of letters ~ In so many years, this corner full of memories has preserved the austerity and simplicity of their origins, ever dear to the Daughters of St. Anne.

We can see the Mother at that little table. She never sat down at it until after she had prayed at length; she wrote thousands of letters which brought to distant countries her advice, her instructions and her great heart.

Those letters, so uncluttered in style and so rich in feeling, all convey in their calligraphy and syntax the Mother’s concern for good and her spirit in full spate; indeed, sometimes a great effort is required to decipher them, but one always discovers a full, rich vein of supernatural life pouring out to make souls and works fruitful.

She was alone with that demanding effort in the early years; later, assisted by secretaries, she still bore the brunt of a large part of it, stealing time from her sleep and depriving herself of any relief. Every now and then, pen in hand, she would pause and raise her eyes to her crucifix, as though imploring light, strength and peace. This is the attitude in which people came upon her thousands of times and this is why her Daughters are so fond of a portrait which captures her in this attitude. Lay people also noticed this: “I must admit”, says a lawyer, “that at certain times, especially when, confronting serious events, she had to take decisions — for which she consulted me — her face would appear to me as if inspired, as though she were asking for or receiving a supernatural illumination”.1

Thus there is a single line that constantly runs through Mother Gattorno’s long governance and which is the basis of any good governance, that is, the specific observance of the Rule. She had an unequalled devotion and love for this Rule which she had received from the Church as though from God himself, “The Rule”, she said, “is everything, and it must come before everything”. Indeed her conduct corresponded to this norm, to such an extent that it was generally recognized that “throughout the time of her long governance, not only did she direct the Institute well with her words, instructions and measures, but above all with her example.” And many called her the “living Rule”.2

However, the Rule that is always clear for those who are required to obey it, often raises questions for those who must command: complex cases which are the bane of superiors who have a high sense of responsibility. Mother Gattorno, undoubtedly a charismatic and very authoritative person with outstanding gifts of governance, was a fundamental reference point and indisputable guide from the time of the Institute’s foundation. Nonetheless, she was always helped in her work by precious and most affectionate secretaries and later, by assistants who knew how to support her and make their valid contribution to the burdensome and demanding activities involved in governance.

We recall for example, Sr. Anna Vincenza Rapallino who, in addition to her great facility in communicating, exercised sound judgment and discernment in the complex situations of the Institute during its rapid expansion. Its vigorous development was certainly one of the reasons why, in August 1881, the first General Chapter of the Daughters of St. Anne, chaired by Bishop Scalabrini, was celebrated. It was henceforth necessary to form a General Council to assist the Foundress, especially when she had to take important decisions.3

This was also a provision of the Sacred Congregation which had formulated further observations concerning the Constitutions presented in 1876 and 1879 (animadversiones).

The above-mentioned Chapter of 1881, without the slightest idea that it was thereby accomplishing an act of insubordination, unanimously rejected many of the Sacred Congregation’s animadversiones, claiming that they were harmful to the Institute, and in so doing risked incurring serious sanctions.

In March 1882, the new General Council, elected in an exceptional way with votes sent by post to Cardinal Alimonda, Protector of the Institute, made an act of submission to the Holy See, openly condemning the involuntary error. All this was obviously a source of deep sorrow to the Mother.4

So the Foundress was surrounded by a Council composed of four assistants and a secretary to help with the massive correspondence; for she took good care of the continuous communication with the houses.

From that time, the secretary’s office despatched about fifty letters a day, all inspired by the Mother and many still written in her own hand.

This work was not only administrative; it was above all a task of religious formation, especially for the superiors. One of the most delicate points was the acceptance of postulants, which at the beginning depended exclusively on the Mother General. Now Mother Gattorno required the newly entered to show their determination to achieve a high degree of holiness: “Since”, she said, “such is the Lord’s will in removing us from the midst of the world”.5

She therefore became ever more exacting on this point, although at first, perhaps because of the urgent need to respond to the numerous demands of the work, she had been somewhat generous. She wanted to know people well before opening the doors of the Institute to them. The information had to be very detailed, well-documented and fully satisfying. “She did not bother about their birth or dowries, but above all took great pains to verify their morality”.6

As for dowries, it is known from the documents how she insisted, also to the Sacred Congregation for Bishops and Regulars, that the obligation to fix any sum for the dowry not be imposed upon the Institute, so that poor vocations would not have their access to religious life barred (cf. Documents of the 1881 Chapter).

An extraordinary sense of motherhood ~ The love with which she nurtured and supported vocations was truly wonderful: when she knew of someone who was faltering or being tempted in her loyalties, she wrote to her personally to encourage her to open her heart. If this did not work, she would summon her, regardless of travel costs, to comfort her in person. When at times the rather lengthy encounter did not have the desired result, the Mother would say: “Well let’s go into church to pray. You will answer me later”. This prayer was almost always a definitive conquest, and there are many Daughters of St. Anne who owe their perseverance to the Servant of God, as witnessed by the many letters sent from the different houses.7

The modest family gatherings at the Mother House were intended to foster in the sisters fidelity and heartfelt love for their vocation. To this end, Mother Rosa even employed her gift for singing and, although she was Superior General, was not above taking some small part in these entertainments. All the sisters remember the grace and feeling with which she sang of her emotions and her ardent longing for God.

She brought up the family of St. Anne with this enlightened and tender motherly love, gradually instilling in everyone the ideas, energy and style of life proper to her vocation.

Pedagogical guidance of superiors and sisters ~ She demanded that superiors show the same maternal attitude to the sisters entrusted to their care. A religious house, in fact, cannot be devoid of spiritual miseries; those who enter it do not completely and immediately abandon their belonging to the world, nor do their characters change with the different life. Furthermore, religious life is not the possession of perfection, but its gradual and laborious attainment. Thus whenever a superior would tell Mother Gattorno that she had a difficult sister, did not know how to deal with her and was therefore requesting her transfer, the Mother would reply recommending that she be loving to the religious in question and, teaching the superior how to win her over, she would remind her to think of her own faults to commiserate with those of others, and of how much souls cost Jesus Christ. Since she believed the capacity to govern derives from this attitude, she would answer some superiors who insisted on being relieved of the burden of such sisters: “I have understood; when a superior is unable to commiserate with the faults of her daughters, it means that she is not suited to being superior: I will recall you”.

She meant: “I will remove you from your office”, which threat never failed to be effective.8

The superiors of the houses, and she was a most splendid example to them, had to be as many mothers and had to establish a true mother-daughter relationship with the sisters, winning their affection and trust.9

She herself, as has been said, was very tender in the case of sisters with some family sorrow. If they were far away, she would write them comforting letters in her own hand which some of them called “letters of paradise”; if they lived in the same house, she would take special care of them, keeping them close beside her and not leaving them until she had seen that they were consoled and at peace.

By doing this, Mother Rosa was emphasizing a distinctive trait of superiors in her Institute. It must generally be said that she succeeded in making them what she wished them to be, that is, genuinely motherly and able to form their religious through a patient and constant pedagogical labor impressed with the most exquisite love.

However, patience and charity should not be confused with weakness. Mother Gattorno was far from keeping in her religious houses women who were not suited to this kind of life. She dismissed without dithering those who clung to superficialities or obstinate opinions, or who were intractable regarding the work of formation; indeed, she managed to facilitate dismissals by remitting any expense for the novitiate period, especially when the person was not well-off. This considerably surprised the General Council, given the poverty in which the Institute lived for many years.

Similarly, she was unsparing in her rebukes for shortcomings but wanted them to fit the circumstances. For her part, while she was correcting sisters, she would also give them signs of special benevolence; in this regard it is known that on her table she even kept a box of sweets which she offered every now and then to those she summoned for a rebuke. Her manners were so persuasive that they induced the guilty person to confess her error and to receive, indeed to ask for, her penance for it.

If the tone of her correction was at times both strict and austere, this was to remind the sisters of the importance of the Rule and the sense of responsibility for the Institute required of each.

This rectitude of intention was also apparent in her deep respect for the individual; she was never impulsive in her reprimands, and she almost never gave them in public, biding her time so as to summon the person who had committed the fault to reprimand her kindly and in private.10

In one of the first houses she founded she put a superior with an excellent spirit, but who was still young and inexperienced. This superior was having various doubts about how to treat a sister who was excessively critical of her and somewhat disrespectful. Mother Rosa sent her this valuable advice: “Listen, my daughter, this is a sure method in order to be effective. You must listen to everything, and then reply only: Very well, I will think about it. Then you should force yourself to examine everything calmly and attentively, commending yourself to God the Father who will provide you with the necessary enlightenment in such a state, keeping in mind what the sister told you; what you see as good and judicious to be put into practice, you will firmly command [it] again, and you will manage to firmly [adhere to it]; the rest you should set aside and attach no importance to it”.11

It also happened that the same superior had had to give a public reprimand to her community for a notable shortcoming, but she had overdone it. Hearing of this, the Mother wrote to her immediately: “Come, for pity’s sake, treat your daughters with more motherly love, without embittering them. Come on, take them calmly and tell them that for the love of God they should quell their bitter feelings […]. Commiserate! […]. Correct your daughters and tell them to be good; bear in mind that they are poor creatures who work for St. Anne, Mother of Mary Immaculate. My daughter, honors are bad for your heart; see, see whether it is true that they are the scourge of our souls!”12

To another superior who was excessively worried about the way her house was going, she gave this wise advice: “You always write to me all worked-up and full of ill feeling: I recommend gentleness to you, because this is the true characteristic of a Daughter of St. Anne, Mother of Mary Immaculate. If we must imitate the Mother this is how we have to be […]. Come on, courage, patience, resignation to God’s will: like this we will set a good example. Superiors are the shadow of the other religious: they all run behind and move as the shadow teaches them to walk. Do you see an irritable mother, always shouting and always sad-looking? All her children then imitate her and in that family no more order prevails; on the one side, they are shrieking, on the other screaming; lastly the devil sleeps on their roofs since he has no more work to do, for little by little they end by greatly offending the Lord. Patience, docility and resignation are the qualities God wants in a superior. If [you] are sorry, run to church and cry with Jesus, weep, and then having dried your tears, there you are back at work, everything to everyone and full of a gentle balm so as to produce it in others”.13

Thus she wanted the soul of government to consist in the most sensitive love, even in such a thankless aspect as the correction of faults.

Supremely respectful of consciences and full of trust in the effectiveness of the sacraments, she foresaw the sisters’ sorrows and remedied them. Noticing that some sister was not receiving Holy Communion, she would summon her and privately, without investigating the reason, ask whether she would like to go to a different confessor than the usual one; at times she would even make the sisters go out, tactfully giving them the opportunity to confess freely. Since the Church had issued the Decree Quemadmodum, she only had to continue in this regard in her practical judgment; but she was severe in preventing the sisters from abusing that freedom by belittling the dignity of the sacrament, taking the petty problems of the house to confession or spreading the internal goings-on of the community.14

The religious vows ~ This fundamental concept of governance in the context of religious life, since it implies the sublime effort of forming souls in accordance with the Gospel, gives rise to the norms for putting into practice poverty, chastity and obedience, which are the substantial points of perfection in the religious state and are professed with vows.

With regard to poverty, as regards the criteria which directed Mother Rosa in governing, it is right to recall her rare talent for administration of which she had already given convincing proof in her family. Hence shone out with an even purer light not only her ability to remain immune from any contagion of greed or attachment to earthly possessions, but even more, her supremely evangelical approach to temporal affairs.

Having founded the Institute as a work of charity, she did not want this charity to be easy but an effort, and therefore to be a service to the poor, not only with the sacrifice of the person herself, but also with the humiliating and exhausting quest for the necessary means for its keep. Consequently, according to the custom common to many congregations at that time, she allowed several sisters go out to beg for alms; and she preceded them with her example, going personally to hold out her hand or by writing humble letters.

Later abolishing alms-begging by sisters, the needs of the Institute were covered in various other ways, not the least of which was to request them from benefactors for the love of God.

This uncertainty of human means was always particularly pleasing to Rosa Gattorno as an incentive to trusting in God and serving him humbly; thus we see it frequently mentioned in her letters.

She tried to ease the efforts of the alms-collectors, which often abounded in harsh humiliations, reminding them to think of their similarity with Christ who was poor and showed his solidarity with the poor. She treated the sick sisters with the greatest possible attention and tenderness to alleviate their sufferings and to ensure they lacked nothing they needed. On the other hand, those who were sent to found new houses had to live a really radical spirit of poverty with total trust in God.

Thus in 1886, when she sent a group of 13 sisters to Bolivia led by Sr. Anna Camilla Valentini, she gave them tickets for the journey as far as Mollendo in Peru but only two hundred lire in reserve, since she had no available cash at the time. The journey from the port of Mollendo to Sucre in Bolivia, the sisters’ destination, then took two months on horseback, without counting other needs. Those two hundred lire, as Sr. Valentini observed to the Mother General, would not be sufficient even for tips on such a long journey; but the Mother replied: “I realize, but if you have faith, I assure you that you will lack nothing”.

With this viaticum she sent the missionaries off to Bolivia. During the journey they humbly asked for help and from time to time found the necessary and even comfortable supplies from wealthy and powerful people; they had various adventures but all arrived safely at their destination.15

However, Mother Rosa wanted their trust in God to be accompanied by a genuine practice of religious poverty. In visiting the houses, she personally inspected the wardrobes to check that everything was in conformity with religious poverty and that there was nothing superfluous or unusual; everything had to be absolutely simple and ordinary.16

Some thought that the decor of the reception rooms in the Generalate in Rome was in contradiction to this spirit of poverty. The rooms were built and furnished at the time by Mother Gattorno; she wanted them to have a distinguished air suitable for receiving prelates, and especially the Cardinal Protector, with the proper respect. But the furniture was presented to her as a gift, and when she saw it she complained that it was more elegant than she had expected.17

Moreover, it was easy to see that on this point of poverty Mother Gattorno set an example for her daughters. She herself and her room mirrored Gospel simplicity. In her room, she only wanted a small writing table and on her bed, a simple straw pallet with a cover; she did not use sheets and rested wrapped in a black shawl.

Her clothes had no age limit nor did she ever think to renew them; they were secretly mended or changed by the secretaries.

However, as for the other sisters, she wanted the superiors to give them all they needed. Poverty was not to be wretchedness that stemmed from excessive parsimony; so if it sometimes happened that some superior was being too stingy in the maintenance of her sisters in order to send contributions to the Generalate, she received severe rebukes from the Mother and was also the object of strict measures. The Mother, in fact, knew that to teach true poverty of heart, a simple community life was advantageous; but superfluity which softens would have been as harmful as scarcity which saddens the soul and saps strength. True privations had to be the result of personal choice regulated by a healthy balance and never the effect of strictness in the governance of a house. These were the instructions that she gave the superiors in person or in writing.

Thus in following the poor Christ it was easier to experience the fascination of the supernatural; Mother Rosa knew this very well, just as she knew that chastity is indispensable to love and that infidelity contaminates it. For her, common prudence was not enough if it could not count on real emotional and spiritual maturity. She was consequently opposed to any form of friendship which was exclusive or which limited interior freedom and openness to everyone. She herself had experienced love as such as an absolute, pure and total; she knew that the one infinite love, the eternal divine and human reality of divine love, can also be resplendent in perfect human love.

Accordingly she was painstaking in training the sisters to have a correct and clear relationship with lay people and especially with the administrative and health-care staff of the hospitals or institutes where they worked. She did not tolerate shadows or doubts on this point. It is asserted in the testimonies of the processes that she even summoned to Rome from America one sister who had shown signs of not being properly correct. She then gave her a cold and detached welcome, which, knowing her natural amiability, was a severe and tacit reprimand.18

But these two strongholds of religious life, poverty and chastity, require an ever vigilant spirit, absorbed in meditation in the presence of the Absolute, totally intent on understanding his will; thus the proper atmosphere of a religious house is recollection.

In her Institute, Mother Gattorno wanted special attention to be paid to silence, which was only enlivened from hour to hour by a brief community praise to the Immaculate Virgin and to St. Anne, her Mother. To recall the importance of silence, she did not only require moderation of the voice in all circumstances when speaking was necessary, even at recreation, but established a period of silence during the day in addition to that commonly observed by other Institutes from evening to morning.

How much the Mother suffered to see silence ignored! In one community which failed on this point, she did away with recreation for a week, imposing as a penance for those days that the sisters spoke only when necessary and in a low voice.19

During the recreations, while with her motherly kindness she was the focus and comfort of all, she lent a most attentive ear to the subject of the conversations of others and to the most spontaneous words; if she heard anything tending to be frivolous or superficial she would be deeply vexed and did not fail to make it publicly known. Thus once when she heard some sisters discussing the restoration of the body and the quality of food, she gave a lecture to the community in such tones that it remained famous; its draft with copious annotations made by the secretary, Sr. Anna Vincenza Rapallino, is still preserved.

Enlightened governance of the Institute ~ These norms of government affected the external life of the Institute, but Mother Gattorno devoted her best energies to the interior formation of the sisters in true charity to God and neighbor; without this encouragement she knew that any appearance of piety would have been useless.

Hence those clear concepts of obedience, which are a practical compendium of all self-giving to God, and that need for participation in community life with the aim of carrying out a specific mission, not as a school of discipline but of love.

Mother Rosa dedicated to this interior formation not only her living words but her epistolary relationship with the superiors and sisters. Her massive correspondence, as has already been mentioned, is a praiseworthy attestation of her formative work as Mother General of her Institute. She kept the correspondence with the houses in America for herself; regardless of her business or ailments, she wrote all those letters in her own hand so that by writing personally, her distant daughters would be recompensed for not being able to hear her voice. The dominant note of that multiplicity of letters was the exhortation to love God sincerely.20

In the Mother House then, or wherever she might be, she wished her office to be open to anyone who wanted to talk to her and received everyone kindly, as though she had nothing else to do. The secretaries, who knew the quantity of work she had pending, often tried to limit the sisters’ access to the Mother and, especially, to prevent from seeing her some importunate or insistent sister whom they presumed would always have the same trifles to tell her; but when the Mother realized this she would reprimand them seriously for preventing the good which she held to be a specific part of her role.21

A religious tells that for the Chapter of 1888, 200 (sic for 180) superiors had assembled in the Generalate for the election of the provincials; for a fortnight she tirelessly received them in audiences which sometimes lasted until late in the evening, since each one wanted the advice and enlightened instructions which they knew that the Mother they all loved so dearly could give them.22

This diligent work of religious formation, always in harmony with the pedagogy of grace which can adapt to individuals and to whatever they happen to be going through at that moment, was also her main purpose in visitations to the houses.

She visited them scrupulously every year, except in the last months of her life, when her strength failed her.

She made exhausting journeys through Italy in conditions of health which were at the least precarious, so that she often arrived drained of strength and in a piteous state. Yet she normally traveled third class, without any comforts, using the time for work except, of course, the periods she devoted to prayer. Only with the persistent insistence of her Daughters did she at last become used to traveling second class.

She was never able to visit personally the distant houses in America and Africa, but arranged for them not to miss an annual visitation, charging the provincials with this task or sending suitable visitors from Italy. As for herself, she frequently visited houses without giving them warning, as she felt the need to see things in their normal state. She knew that such concern to visit the houses was pleasing to God because she felt guided by a superior light to go to one place rather than another; and it happened that in following these impulses she found her presence needed precisely at that moment. Likewise she often found that having been dissuaded from going somewhere, she later heard that had she gone there she would have been in great danger.

For example, the Mother told Cardinal Belmonte that at the point of setting out for a town in Sicily where the Institute had a house, she had changed her mind because of a strong inspiration that came to her; she later discovered that a plot to harm her was being hatched in that place.23

Therefore led by the Spirit and in absolute docility to his directives, Mother Rosa did not spare herself in order to see regularly and from close at hand as much of the Institute’s life as possible. She was interested in everything, even details, and kept records of it all in a notebook. She gave a suitable talk to each community, pointing out faults to be corrected and measures to improve the service of God and making suggestions for the effective teaching of the children and adolescents assisted in the colleges and orphanages.

She kept notes of these conferences and the names of the houses to which she had given them for future reference. In this way we know that meditation, mutual love, dynamism in striving for perfection, discernment in the important choices of life, were her habitual topics in those talks, so that on every visit she soothed discontent, rejuvenated minds and filled hearts with enthusiasm, leaving them with a spirit of hard-working charity and a high esteem of their vocation.

In this way all the religious came to know their Mother and could not but feel for her deep esteem, immense affection and boundless trust. Her motherly presence, marked by an intense tenderness, betrayed her familiarity with heaven and exhaled a mysterious sense of greatness, unanimously attested by all who knew or approached her. Her intimacy with God gave a unique value to her teaching and direction, while they were reinforced by events that had something of the miraculous about them. Think, for example, of her cognition of distant things and her penetration of hearts. She herself says in her Memorie: “…I was left full of knowledge, full of clear light, I could read in their hearts: there were moments in which I could see everything that was going on in their hearts” (M. 1.2, p. 7).

Various episodes document these extraordinary gifts. The Mother succeeded inexplicably in seeing in her distant sisters states of mind that were negative or that threatened their fidelity to their vocation, and immediately sought to remedy them. It is told, for example, that the superior of a house in Rome, Sr. Anna Fabiana Orsi, had made up her mind to ask to be exonerated from her office because of problems which she had kept to herself. One day Mother Gattorno arrived at the house in a carriage; without even getting out, she had her called and said to her: “We must stay in the place where God has put us. I too would willingly leave mine, but it is right that I stay in it, because such is God’s will”. And she left at once, leaving the superior with a different outlook24.

It was clear, then, that God was assisting the Mother in directing the Institute and held her in his hands as a docile instrument for the good of a work that was wholly and solely his. Naturally all this helped the Daughters of St. Anne to esteem their own vocation. All the more so because Mother Rosa supported the authority that came to her also from those extraordinary facts with a rare and sincere humility. Indeed, she did not wish to be called Foundress or General, contenting herself with the title of Mother. And a mother she truly was. God’s Work, which was flourishing so rapidly in so many parts of the world, had been generated by the generous self-immolation of so great a Mother who, forgetful of herself, was intent solely on following the promptings of the Spirit for a work of charity that was indeed great and fruitful in good, but which she wished to be regarded as the least. Who, in fact, could have boasted of a work that was so manifestly the work of God?

Thus, with evangelical art, like the divine Master, Rosa Gattorno shaped souls in religious perfection, stimulating and sustaining them until she saw them reach the goal, the full maturity of Christ; then she rejoiced immensely, as at the greatest gift she could have offered to her Beloved.

This is true spiritual motherhood. The Apostle Paul summed up his gigantic work in those most tender words: “… my little children, for whom I am again in the pain of childbirth until Christ is formed in you” (Gal 4:19). It is the wonderful reality of every authentic apostolate: the slow and laborious forming of Christ in souls, so that not we but he may live in us.

(1878-1887) Negotiations for sending the sisters to Chile and Bolivia — Departure of 16 religious for Bolivia — Death of two sisters — Aniceto Arce and Mother Gattorno — Miraculous cure of Sr. Anna Camilla Valentini — Departure of the third group of missionaries — An adventurous journey — Mother Rosa’s extraordinary presence in the forest of Jujui — The Mother’s epistolary relationship — Foundations in Brazil: Parà, Manaus, Maranhao — Foundations in Peru and Chile.

Negotiations for sending the sisters to Chile and Bolivia ~ The Institute of the Daughters of St. Anne had now existed for ten years. The harshest trials in that decade had clearly outlined what God wanted from the new religious congregation and confirmed the Foundress’ desire to continue on her path. The Institute’s rapid spread in Italy had caught the attention of all who were dedicated to charitable works and gave rise to ideas of its expansion in mission lands.

Archival documents show that Rosa first offered missionary sisters for Chile in 1874.1 However, the negotiations were not followed up.

In September 1876, Fr. Simpliciano della Trinità, a Franciscan who had been in contact with Mother Rosa since 1874, wrote to her from Rome with these words: “The Lord, through our Father St. Francis, is calling the Daughters of St. Anne who are also his daughters, to take the benefits of charity and religious education to South America where the harvest is immense and the ground already prepared. One of our missionaries there who has been sent here to take sisters to that flourishing land, has prepared everything for the journey and has the proper authorizations from the Bishop. Send seven religious, including some who can teach sewing, embroidery and drawing, grammar, arithmetic and geography, as well as a piano teacher if possible, and of course, some who can assume the office of nurse, both in hospital and at home, since there are no kinds of sisters there who do these things: they would be the first”.2

So religious who could do everything were desired, but for so many needs what good would seven sisters be? However Mother Gattorno, in her boundless charity, busied herself with the matter and wrote straight away to the missionary religious, Fr. Vincenzo Rocchi of the Friars Minor, for further explanations. He answered her from the Friary of Aracoeli in early October that the country which needed the sisters was the Republic of Bolivia, and the residence that would be assigned to them was in the city of La Paz. He asked for an appointment with the Mother, but in the meantime warned that the new missionaries, as well as having beautiful intellectual qualities, had to have a sound spiritual formation. “From what I have told you”, he wrote, “you will realize that since this is to be a new foundation in distant lands from which great good will result and which will have a good start and a successful outcome, it is essential to choose people who have been tested in virtue and knowledge, full of a spirit of sacrifice. This is the main thing”.3

This was also obvious, especially to the Mother who saw all the difficulties of the enterprise and was undoubtedly astonished that only seven sisters were requested for a mission that that had no charitable institutions at all. In any case, she awaited the meeting with Fr. Rocchi, who in the meantime had to make several trips in Italy and planned to leave for Bolivia about a month later, that is, in November.

We do not know the reason why, on that occasion, no concrete agreements were reached, but it is certain that neither the Daughters of St. Anne nor any other women religious set sail for Bolivia at that point.

Departure of 16 religious for Bolivia ~ Two years later, in 1878, the same Fr. Vincenzo Rocchi returned to Europe with an official mandate from the municipality of La Paz and the Bolivian Governor to contact charitable institutes to obtain missionary sisters for that country.

Indeed, the need for a religious congregation which would take the hospitals and the education of children in hand was becoming more and more pressing in the city of La Paz, which then had about 80,000 inhabitants. The finance, administration and organization of institutions of the kind were deficient in every respect, despite the municipality’s considerable contributions. An effort had been made to remedy the problematic situation by changing their staff, but the employees’ incompetence and greed had only aggravated the situation.

Therefore, in a municipal report of 1877, one reads of the decision to make every effort to obtain sisters of charity from Europe. “Remuneration”, it was said, “cannot produce all the self-denial that is required to care for and help humanity in its terrible sufferings. Christian charity alone is capable of such a great sacrifice: hence the hope of an immortal reward, the desire for something superior to an earthly prize. Until the unfortunate sick at home are supervised and cared for by sisters of charity, by these missionaries of Providence whom some have called the earth’s angels, service will never improve on the scale we hope for. The municipality must therefore make all the necessary endeavors to ensure that these holy women come to the country”.4

The municipality’s decision immediately found valuable support in the generosity of a noble citizen, Don Benigno Clavijo, who had already made one journey to Europe; he had stayed for some time in Chile and was then living in one of his villas near La Paz. He immediately offered 4,000 bolivars for the traveling expenses of the desired sisters. This was suggested by Fr. Vincenzo Rocchi who knew Clavijo well, which is why the municipality thought it appropriate to charge this religious with completing all the procedures necessary for the sisters to come to Bolivia, since it knew no one who could conclude the matter better.

With the consent of his superiors, the Bishop and the Governor of the Republic, Fr. Rocchi left for Europe again in 1878, in search of a charitable congregation that would accept to go to Bolivia.

He had already suggested the Daughters of St. Anne, but as it was doubtful as to whether he would obtain them, he had been given a free hand in making the choice. Disembarking in France, he addressed various institutes, presenting authoritative documents, but none could meet his needs, given the scarcity of personnel. Down at heart he then went to Spain, but there too he encountered invincible obstacles, especially because of the unknown quantities of a journey which was then extremely difficult and perilous.

Fr. Rocchi then focused on Italy. He arrived in Rome and presented himself to the Marquis of Lorenzana, Bolivia’s representative to the Holy See; with his help he attempted, addressing various institutes, to achieve his intention: but in vain. He was put off with the usual excuses of the scarcity of personnel, the long and difficult journey, the lack of knowledge of the Bolivian region and so forth.

Some people then suggested to the missionary that he try Milan where various new institutes dedicated to charitable work were then flourishing. But in the Lombard capital he met only with failure. He therefore sought refuge in Piacenza, in order to knock at Mother Gattorno’s door.

The long and fruitless quest had not discouraged this generous missionary who was determined not to return to Bolivia without the women religious; however, in that string of refusals he could not but recognize the signs of divine Providence, pointing to the missionary vocation of the Daughters of St. Anne. Rosa Gattorno had already accepted this vocation with deep gratitude to God and an impulse of great generosity. In those two years she had made a real discernment, choosing and preparing suitable candidates; so when Fr. Rocchi presented himself to her requesting missionaries, he had the pleasant surprise of being instantly satisfied. On 19 October 1878, negotiations were signed by both parties: the date is an historic one, for it was the moment when the Institute of the Daughters of St. Anne took flight for distant lands with a missionary impetus that was destined to endure and to increase with time.5

So on that day, a group of 16 religious were destined for Bolivia by Mother Rosa as the firstfruits of other generous souls who were shortly to follow. Sr. Anna Giuseppa Troni, whose ability and religious spirit had been known to the Mother for some time, was designated superior. The others were: Sr. Anna Cunegonda Conti, Sr. Anna Felicita Conti, Sr. Anna Livia Favellini, Sr. Anna Amadio Gregori, Sr. Anna Perpetua Torrielli, Sr. Anna Bonaventura

Mother Gattorno, abandoning her usual constant reluctance to appear, agreed to satisfy a wish of her daughters and posed for a photo, perhaps because they might never see her again and because she wanted to be present to them in the most tangible way. Thus a beautiful portrait of the Mother was obtained; and on that occasion she also wanted a photo of all the sisters who were leaving, to keep their likeness by her. She kept it among her most beloved possessions in her study until she died.

The departure took place a month later. On the morning of 23 November 1878, those generous Daughters of St. Anne sailed from Genoa on the steamship “Esperia”; they took with them to the new world their strong and humble hearts, poor in knowledge but rich in unconditional generosity and trust in God.

It was a long voyage; they arrived at the Port of Mollendo in Peru on 17 January 1879; from there, leaving by rail and crossing part of Lake Titicaca, they at last reached La Paz on the 20th, after traveling continuously for two months.

“Las abnegadas madrecitas de la caridad” (the self-sacrificing little mothers of charity), as the Bolivians graciously called them, were welcomed by the people and representatives of the Republic and of the clergy as angels from heaven; the public press had the most sensitive things to say about such promising beginnings: the receptions and attentions of every kind with which they were welcomed must have been a considerable surprise to those simple hearts who had been trained for a not very gratifying job, but were all the more valuable in the Lord’s eyes for this. Mother Rosa had prepared them for total self-denial with a view to comforting the poor and the suffering; instead, even before they started, they saw themselves fêted as public benefactors.

Death of two sisters ~ However they did not let that festive welcome go to their heads; the harshness of the land to be plowed struck them the day after their arrival. The hospital was in a deplorable state and no suitable lodgings had yet been prepared for the sisters, who for the time being were guests of the Clavijo family. In view of the impelling need, they decided to make the best of humble premises from which sick people had been hastily removed without anyone thinking to properly disinfect them. The consequences were, of course, serious. Two sisters caught the disease and were doomed to die barely a few weeks after their arrival: Sr. Anna Scolastica Barilani and Sr. Anna Modesta Molesti; they had been two beautiful hopes for the mission. Sr. Anna Lucia Faraboli also died that same year.6

The citizens of La Paz were therefore in deep mourning and expressed their condolences at the funeral rites. Who can tell of the grief the Mother must have felt when she received that news? However she did not let herself be discouraged, and started to prepare other missionary sisters for the following year; in fact, another group of Daughters of St. Anne left for Bolivia in 1881 to found a boarding school for little girls in La Paz, the first in the city, and which was later very successful.

This institution opened in a former private school adapted for the purpose. It had been run by the Bolivian Clara Telleria, who became a Daughter of St. Anne and took the name of Anna Rosa out of affection for the Mother, whom she had not yet met. However this sister was so dedicated to that invaluable work that her health was undermined and she soon fell seriously ill. Feeling that her end was near, she asked as a last grace to be able to see the Foundress of the Institute. Her wish was granted, and called to Italy, she died in Piacenza on 2 August 1884 in the Mother House, only six months after her arrival.

The fame of the new charitable Institute spread rapidly throughout Bolivia, giving rise in many cities to the wish to have religious there too, to look after their hospitals and schools. One providential circumstance was shortly to permit this wish to come true in what was then the capital of the Republic, that is, Sucre.

Aniceto Arce and Mother Gattorno ~ Because of unstable political events in the young State, in 1880 the President, Mr. Narciso Campero, had exiled Mr. Aniceto Arce, a well-todo rival, who was later the second President to succeed him. This gentleman, who had a superior intelligence and an iron constitution, took the opportunity to make a study trip to Europe. He stayed in Paris to have a close look at the most modern institutions for social assistance which were then thriving in Europe. He soon realized that in the female educational institutes and especially the hospitals, where there were exclusively lay personnel and administrators, things did not go as well as he wished for his own country: a nation starting out on a process of economic and cultural transformation needed trustworthy persons, motivated by generous dedication which is born from and sustained by the imperious command of the Gospel.

He therefore decided not to go home without bringing back for his people the gift of a religious congregation devoted to education and works of charity. He made several journeys to Spain and Italy to acquire a close knowledge of many institutions; at last, having reached Rome, he turn to Leo XIII for advice. The Pontiff, who already knew of the first expeditions to La Paz of the Daughters of St. Anne, suggested he call on these sisters, who were splendidly proving themselves in both the hospital and educational contexts.

So the distinguished Bolivian went to Piacenza to talk to Mother Gattorno. He wanted a large number of religious endowed with different gifts; above all he wanted them to be healthy so that they could resist his country’s climate and to be perfectly fluent in Spanish in order to teach. The Mother prepared to overcome the most serious difficulties with her great faith and bravely to face the perilous undertakings for the glory of the Lord, she complied with the demands of Mr. Arce and stipulated an agreement with him that was to last for almost ten years.

Miraculous cure of Sr. Anna Camilla Valentini ~ Pulling her self together, she realized that the most problematic aspect of the undertaking was to find a superior to whom she could entrust the new foundation and the direction of the large group of religious. After many prayers, she set her sights on the young superior of the hospital of Borgo San Donnino (today Fidenza), Sr. Anna Camilla Valentini. This young sister who was just 27 had great determination combined with an unusually sweet manner and so had found favor with all the directors of the hospital and gained the respectful affection of the sick; these were excellent qualities for the new Bolivian mission, where a fine tact and determined action were indispensable. The events fully satisfied Mother Rosa’s expectations.

At the first mention of a simple invitation, Sr. Anna Camilla thought it prudent to respond respectfully in the negative, both because of the problems she foresaw in the venture and because of the state of her health which was then rather precarious. However, she soon received the order so went promptly to Piacenza, despite having something wrong with one foot, which was very swollen and threatened to become gangrenous. It was well known among the Daughters of St. Anne that prompt obedience works wonders. Having arrived at the house in Piacenza she had to go to bed and put her painful foot under a cage to take the weight of the bedclothes.

One morning the Mother General came to her room. Smiling and serene she spoke a few words of comfort to her; then as though there were nothing the matter, she asked her to get up to have a photo taken as a souvenir for her family. Despite the sister’s logical protestations, the Mother ordered the nurse to put on her shoes: her astonished eyes met those of the sick woman, whose foot, so swollen it had become shapeless, she squeezed into the usual shoe. She left the house and returned, still on foot and without the slightest difficulty or pain. It is superfluous to describe Sr. Anna Camilla’s amazement and feelings of gratitude; in that instant she acquired boundless trust in the Lord and in her Mother General, who always managed to extract visible and inexplicable miracles from him.7

Departure of the third group of missionaries ~ In the few days that followed, the Foundress instructed the new missionary superior about the work she was entrusting to her. “As regards the language”, she added, “you will do as best you can; I have no sisters who know Spanish, you will learn it in time”.

Towards the end of May 1882, Fr. Louis Fauré of the Society of Jesus, the tutor of Mr. Arce’s two sons, arrived from France to fetch the missionary sisters and take them to Bordeaux from where they were to sail for South America. Therefore, blessed by Mother Rosa, the twelve sisters led by the superior, Sr. Anna Camilla Valentini, set sail on 30 May from Genoa; they continued on to Marseilles, Cette and Bordeaux. Here Mr. Arce had gathered a group of engineers, artisans, cooks, a dozen people in all whom he intended to take to Bolivia at his own expense, to give the workers in his country a better training.

On 5 June, that large group of artisans, craftsmen and missionary sisters left Bordeaux for Buenos

Aires on the steamer called the “Orenoque”. Speeding on their way, the group arrived in Bolivia, this time through Argentina rather than Peru.

An adventurous journey ~ We will refrain from describing the long and adventurous journey of four months, colorfully told by the superior, Sr. Anna Camilla Valentini in a manuscript of her Memorie8.

The grave problems they had between Tucuman and Sucre in crossing the Cordillero of the Andes in carriages on roads that were barely practicable, were so numerous that the poor sisters arrived at their destination utterly exhausted, some in a precarious state of health. The carriages had been guided by expert natives, but this did not suffice to lessen the bumps or avoid them being overturned several times. They usually had to sleep in the open, under improvised tents and rolled up in blankets, while the armed men of the escort watched over them and lit great fires to keep wild beasts at bay.

In addition was the rapid increase in altitude of more than two thousand meters, where the thin air caused some serious discomfort. In these picturesque but uncomfortable journeys the lively spirit of the Daughters of St. Anne was undaunted; well prepared by their most courageous Mother, they saw in them the first-fruits of their sacrifice.

They arrived in Sucre in mid-August. When the hospital had been organized and arrangements made for the boarding school, religious life proceeded at such a rapid and edifying pace that lovely vocations for the new Institute soon flowered in the Bolivian capital; on the Feast of the Immaculate Conception in that year 1882, the first solemn clothing of some novices took place.

All this was not as simple as it might seem. The superior, Sr. Anna Camilla, soon found she had to struggle with the obvious problems which already existed in the hospital because of the lack of organization and precise norms for the sick. But the sisters’ tireless and intelligent work earned them the open sympathy of the whole population and the authorities.

It very soon became evident that there was a demand for the Daughters of St. Anne to open other houses in various Bolivian cities. By the time President Gregorio Pacheco, a friend of Mr. Arce and like him, a good Catholic, was elected in 1884, the Italian sisters had expanded from La Paz to Cochabamba and Oruro and there were prospects of other foundations.

In the meantime, Mother Rosa, following the Holy See’s directions, had had the idea of giving the new houses an organic structure and unity of government by grouping them together in canonical provinces. From March 1882, the houses in Bolivia had been established as a province, but still lacked a provincial superior. Having discussed this matter with her General Council, she chose Sr. Anna Camilla Valentini as the first provincial in America and recalled Sr. Anna Giuseppa Troni to Italy.

The new provincial, who with the other sisters had already learned to ride, made long journeys in the Republic, founding hospitals and colleges in Tarija and Potosì, and putting the other houses in better order, having at her disposal the young local forces who had entered the Institute and others, sent from Rome.

Mother Rosa’s extraordinary presence in the forest of Jujui ~ although she was minutely informed by letter and kept up her own correspondence with her distant sisters, the Mother still felt the need to deal personally with the provincial about the business of the flourishing mission. Since she was more than ever concerned to preserve a good religious spirit, she had a clear idea of all the problems and risks of her daughters in a context so different from that to which they were accustomed and so full of new things. Therefore a year after her appointment as provincial, she ordered Sr. Anna Camilla Valentini to come to Rome to talk to her.

This brave sister, after overcoming Bishop Pucci’s resistance and taking her leave of the Arce family, set out on the journey back over the Cordillera, accompanied by two sisters, a Filipino priest (Fr. Taborga) and two servants given them by Mr. Arce. The whole journey from Sucre to Argentina was on horseback. Among their many adventures, they became lost in a forest while riding down the eastern slope of the Cordillera to Jujui. The sun was already setting and they could not find their way out of the forest; the men were also at a loss, since they were not familiar with the area. Suddenly they saw flames on the distant horizon, which seemed to be a bush fire.

They were all terrified, since they thought they would be trapped by the flames, but as they approached to have a better look, the fire seemed to be surrounded by some shadows; so they staunchly continued in that direction and found themselves in a clearing at the edge of the forest: three children, the oldest of whom must have been nine, were feeding a fire with green and dry branches, which they were collecting here and there. Hearing the sound of the caravan, the little ones burst into cries of joy, exclaiming in their language: “Here they are, here they are!”. They ran to meet the sisters, inviting all the travelers to follow them. So they did, trusting in the innocent manners of the little Indios, who led them to a hut set on a hill outside the woods.

A man and a woman came out, and as soon as they saw the sisters bowed low and greeted them with deep respect. The man explained that the fire on the fringes of the forest had been lit at his orders, precisely to give a signal to the caravan that was expected.

“But how did you know about our arrival? Who told you?” asked the astonished provincial.

“A lady dressed like you”, the Indio replied.

“Dressed like me? Where?”.

“I saw her this morning, here in the forest”.

The Indio continued, telling them how that morning, while he was hunting in the woods, he had seen a woman dressed in black with a black veil and white collar, who, slowly coming towards him, with a sad, pale face, had said: “Good Indio, perhaps this evening my daughters will be lost in the forest. You who are a faithful servant of Jesus Christ, please try to go to their help”. So, at sunset, he had busied himself preparing a fire in the clearing, recommending his small children to keep the flames high during the evening.

“I thought”, he continued, “that if you were to lose your way in the forest, when you saw the signal of the fire, you might be able to see the hut and spend a peaceful night here”.

The Indio’s artless tale deeply moved all the travelers; even the men’s eyes were bright with emotion. That good family had also prepared a copious meal to refresh their guests: cream, sweet corn, potatoes and chicken.

They spent the night in a restorative sleep and the next morning continued on their way to Jujui, accompanied for a stretch by the three lively, merry little ones.

The rest of the journey was quite the opposite of that made by Sr. Anna Camilla on her first journey to Bolivia with Mr. Arce. It should only be mentioned that the “Adria”, the steamer on which they embarked at Buenos Aires, took almost two months to reach Genoa because of constant breakdowns of the propeller.

Mother Gattorno had sent her secretary, Sr. Anna Celsa Speranza, to meet them in Genoa. On 26 July the missionaries finally reached Piacenza; they were met at the station by Mother Rosa herself, who embraced them with emotion.

A solemn reception had been prepared for them at the Piacenza house: the provincial of America and her companions passed between lines of postulants holding lighted candles, almost as if attesting to veneration for those generous missionaries. Then they all went to chapel where they sang a solemn Te Deum of thanksgiving.

This was followed by manifestations of joy and excited enthusiasm: sisters, lay people, priests and prelates competed to see the provincial, Sr. Anna Camilla, back from Bolivia, and wanted to hear thousands of things. Cardinal Alimonda, Protector of the Daughters of St. Anne, expressed the wish to see her; Sr. Anna Camilla visited him two days later and stayed for a week in Turin to give the Cardinal a detailed account of the houses founded in Bolivia and the conditions in which apostolic work had to be done in that Republic. On her return to Piacenza, she had long talks with Mother Rosa and informed her in detail of the progress of the mission Institute. She also told her about the incredible episode in the forest of Jujui: the fire lit, the children keeping it alight, the hospitable welcome of the Indio who had been warned of their coming in advance by the mysterious lady. The Mother, calm as always, listened smiling. At the end she said: “Did you really think that St. Anne had nothing to do with it?”.

Sr. Anna Camilla was astounded at such calm; had the Mother known about it all? At that moment, it flashed to her mind that the lady dressed in black who had appeared to the poor Indio must have been Mother Rosa herself.

The following year, 1886, Sr. Anna Camilla Valentini left Italy again, taking with her a lovely group of fourteen missionaries: they took their former route, down the coast of South America; then through the straits of Magellan, entering the Pacific Ocean, back up the coast of Chile and Peru to Mollendo. This time too, divine Providence watched over the journey of the missionaries who were constantly accompanied by Mother Rosa’s ceaseless prayers and motherly concern. Serious reasons of government, health and age, prevented her from going to the mission lands where her daughters were working; but she endeavored to be present there with her prayers, her authority and her many letters. She took infinite care to form the sisters she was intending to send to the overseas missions,9 closely supervising them in the novitiates of Piacenza and then of Rome. They all had to volunteer to go, since the Institute did not have and still does not have a vow of obedience which includes the mission lands; but the desire to be a missionary must stem from the pure love of souls and consequently from proven detachment from every earthly thing and from a mature understanding of religious life. Therefore, after the novitiate, she tested them further in various houses.

What was Mother’s approach in sending the sisters on mission? Here is an example.

In 1886, for Sr. Anna Camilla Valentini’s second expedition, she wrote to a sister: “I know that you will be averse to going to America; but now would be the right moment, since I have a place destined for you and you would leave with Sr. Anna Camilla. Tell me, are you ready to make this sacrifice to God? Answer me immediately, even by telegram. I add no more in the hope that you will wish to console the Holy Mother”.10

It is useless to add that the sister, Sr. Anna Virginia Gaggi from Cremona, overcame any reluctance, came to Rome and left with Sr. Anna Camilla’s group.

The Mother’s epistolary relationship ~ What can nonetheless be described as authentic heroism is the infinite patience with which Mother Rosa directed her daughters’ work from such a distance and in such scrupulous detail: tenacity and immense effort, not only in the thousands of letters she wrote, especially to the superiors, but in her steady forbearance in tolerating opposition, suspicions of every kind, ingratitude and, what saddened her most, the infidelities of some religious, at times very serious. In such new and different milieus and cultures for the zealous Italian missionaries, with a form of spiritual assistance that was not always suitable, it was inevitable that human weakness should get the upper hand and it was manifested in insubordination, lack of balance or the relaxation of observance. Mother Gattorno’s letters, together with the great evangelical conquest in which her daughters were engaged, reflect the intimate drama of their minds and the shocks that the evil spirit gave to their communities, lost in the vast expanses of Bolivia, Peru and Brazil. But in these innumerable pages, we can interpret Mother Rosa’s soul above all: what love! What motherly sweetness combined with prudence and boundless humility! Wherever she guessed that something was wrong, she would track it down it with such supreme tact that she infallibly succeeded in discovering everything, even after long months of comparisons, calculations, and the most patient investigations. And then she exacted repentance and the determined will for reparation, for she was particularly jealous in guarding God’s honor. However, with the exception of these cases which were indeed rare, the Mother was the animator of every enterprise, the mother who comforted every sorrow, who found for each of her daughters the most fitting words to help them live the true missionary spirit at the foot of the Cross. In those letters, the sisters saw and heard their Mother and were heartened by her example to overcome themselves and all human reluctance.

We have mentioned Sr. Anna Virginia Gaggi, an exuberant and tempestuous creature; she was impetuous and therefore imprecise in her judgments, she would face her objectives squarely, sometimes causing sparks to fly with her energetic decisions. She was a tall, robust woman to whom dithering of a moral order was unknown. After a few years of missionary life, the Mother gave her some trusted tasks, and she was also visitor of a group of houses in Bolivia. However, as she candidly admitted, she lacked balance in her dealings; wherever she felt something had gone awry, it was to be eliminated instantly. Forgetting the teachings and pedagogy of Christ, the greatest educator and teacher, she would be prompted to use only drastic and harsh measures. Since the Mother did not always comply with the sister’s suggestions, dictated by her impulsive and impatient temperament which was not exempt from an ill-concealed jealousy of those who were perhaps more highly esteemed, she received cutting letters from over the ocean; she would have proceeded with punishments, removals and replacements. But Mother Rosa attempted to tame her with her own humility.

“I feel deep pain because of your continuous reprimands”, she wrote, “not for me, because I deserve far worse since I am really wicked, but for the good Lord who, through my lack of knowledge, must have trouble from his brides. Oh sweet Christ Crucified, the sight of you teaches me how to suffer!”.11

Sr. Anna Virginia Gaggi realized at last that she had gone too far: “My dearest and beloved Mother”, she immediately replied, “I am sorry to hear that a letter of mine was a bit too cutting and that it saddened your poor heart…”. And she prostrates herself to ask forgiveness but reaffirms her viewpoint in seven dense pages. She suddenly has a generous impulse: “Since I see it is your will that I go and visit the houses, now and for always I promise you that I will go […], even if I have to put up with having the door slammed in my face by the lady superiors: I will pay no attention to this, but armed with patience, I will go ahead with the hope of doing a little good”.12

However her patience ended even before the letter, so that two pages later, she wrote: “Do you want me to speak to you clearly? Remove the superior or I shall go myself, as I will be happier to stay in a cellar and pass on the crown!”.

With wonderful gentleness and humility, Mother Rosa did not rise to the provocative bate, and wrote to her: “dear daughter, what must I say to you? You tell me to change the superiors and to replace them with good ones; but what should I answer you? Only to pray a lot so that God with his infinite mercy will settle everything […]. With regard to obedience what you say is excellent, and if this lovely virtue were put in practice, religious orders would certainly run like clockwork: ah, let us pray and try to obtain from the Heart of Jesus that they change and become truly holy”.13

“Let us pray and try to obtain from the Heart of Jesus”: the first weapon, perhaps the one the sister had all too often forgotten!

However it should not be thought that Mother Rosa only sought refuge in prayer, falling short of her specific duties.

She provided for the American houses with motherly care and, when necessary, with energetic fortitude which did not stem from impulsive impatience quick to extinguish the little smoking flame, but from undiluted and patient love acquired from union with God. She well knew that before other souls she had to care for and sanctify those of her daughters. So she bore with them and admonished them, making them feel the full suffering of her maternal heart, reminding them of the commitments they had taken on before God and from where they should draw the strength to be faithful to him.

Then when sisters had to be transferred or recalled to Italy, she was unconcerned about the heavy expenses.

She sometimes sent a person from Rome to Bolivia specifically to remedy irregularities in a house.14

The indomitable faith of this marvellous woman imbued them with the courage to face any squalls. “Everything seems truly to have fallen apart, according to this [letter] of yours”, she wrote to a superior, “but I have such faith in God, the Master of his Work of St. Anne, that from the very stones he will bring forth holy Daughters who will give glory and honor to the Institute. The uncultivated fields will flower, and the power of God will overthrow the false altars and build magnificent temples from them, all for his glory”15.

Humility, moreover, was the most effective remedy with which she healed the wounds of others and enlightened their minds. “You ask my forgiveness: I give you not one pardon but a hundred. If the superiors say something, it is for your good and for nothing else […]. I pray a great deal for you. If I were a little better, you would certainly receive great graces […]. Poor daughters, you have the misfortune of having a wretched Mother, equally poor in everything, who is truly to be pitied, since you are so badly supported. I feel for you and am truly grieved, and I pray that God may send you another [Mother] with all the gifts needed to govern this flock well: everything will go better. Goodbye, pray for me”16.

Foundation in Brazil: Pará, Manaus, Maranhão ~ The growth God gave to the Work of the Daughters of St. Anne in distant America is certainly due to the merits of these virtues, to the penances and to the unceasing prayer of Mother Rosa. The Institute prospered not only in Bolivia; in fact, requests had been arriving from Brazil too since 188317. Amid many hardships and persecutions of every kind on the part of the liberal party, a house was founded the following year in Pará; from there the Daughters of St. Anne soon increased in number, doing great good in hospitals for lepers, smallpox and tuberculosis patients and in various educational institutes. Indeed, in 1885 they were called to Manaus; in 1887 they were entrusted with the direction of the hospital of Maranhão.

It should not be thought, however, that ample means were available to these angels of charity, as though the cities that called them provided them with all they needed. Things were often very different. In Maranhão, for example, the Daughters of St. Anne were lodged for two months in two little rooms so cramped and dilapidated that they did not know how to shelter from the rain, and when a storm came they had to put the lamp under a table so that it would not be put out by the water and wind. Mother Rosa, while sending all the help she could, encouraged her daughters with the great principles of religious life. “When houses begin in poverty”, she wrote, “they prosper more and are pleasing to our Mother St. Anne”.

Harsher still were the privations endured by the sisters at the leper colony of Tucunduba, where there was also a psychiatric hospital run by the Daughters of St. Anne.

The great material and moral misery in which those unfortunate people lived was truly repellent; but the exquisite and heroic charity of the young superior, Sr. Anna Ida Paganini, guided the other religious in bringing relief of body and spirit into that desolation. Great things were told of the virtue of Sr. Anna Ida, deeply imbued with the spirit of her great Foundress; she died at only 27, on 27 October 1891, on the ground broken by her generous labors18.

Foundations in Peru and Chile ~ Peru and Chile too asked for and obtained from Mother Gattorno the Daughters of St. Anne for hospitals and schools. Within a few years the houses in South America thus multiplied: in ten years more than sixteen houses were founded; at the Foundress’s death there were already forty-three. As was to be expected, many authentic religious vocations blossomed around these houses among young American women, attracted by the charm of the charity that makes life so rich and precious. Many of them came to the novitiates in Italy; others entered those which the Mother’s wise foresight had opened in their own native lands.

Rosa Gattorno naturally saw the hand of God in all this; that prodigious flowering of vocations, that ability to meet so many requests, that eagerness she saw in her daughters to go and work in unknown countries made her feel that God had opened to her Congregation a horizon far wider than the first plan he had let her glimpse. And she, with humble gratitude, called this “the second vocation of the Daughters of St. Anne”19.
