(1881-1882) Decree of praise and “animadversiones” (1876) — Decree of definitive approval and other “animadversiones” (1879); Text of the Constitutions with Cardinal Alimonda’s comments — The Chapter and the “animadversiones” — The Mother’s journey to Rome and submission to the Holy See — Election of the first General Council.

Decree of praise and “animadversiones” (1876) ~ In Chapter XII we explained the thorny path to the approval of the Constitutions of the Daughters of St. Anne and told how in 1876 the Sacred Congregation accepted the text of the Constitutions compiled by Fr. Tornatore. The Institute acquired the Decree of Praise (8 April 1876)1 almost immediately, and simultaneously, the Sacred Congregation for Bishops and Regulars sent some observations inherent in the modification of these Constitutions. The Sacred Congregation wanted them to correspond more closely to the purposes of the Work and the canonical requirements for such institutions.

In 1878 the text was re-presented, partially modified on the basis of the “adnimadversiones” received; during the examination the consultors asked the Bishops of Genoa and Piacenza for some clarifications about the two court cases against the Mother at the civil court in Genoa.

The Bishops’ answers were flattering.2

Decree of definitive approval and other “animadversiones” (1879); text of the Constitutions with Cardinal Alimonda’s comments ~ In the meantime, other letters of recommendation had been gathered from the dioceses where the Daughters of St. Anne worked and they were presented in early 1879; on 21 April the Institute received the Decree of definitive approval3 which was sent through the Bishop of Piacenza and accompanied by further “animadversiones”.4

Bishop Scalabrini questioned the Foundress about these, and invited her to set down her observations in writing;5 hence making them his own, he sent them to the Secretary of the Congregation for Bishops and Regulars. Inexplicably he obtained no reply.

In 1881, the work of the revision of the Constitutions was assumed by Cardinal Gaetano Alimonda, who had become the Institute’s new Protector on 30 April 1880.6

On 11 March 1881, the text was presented with the comments that Cardinal Alimonda had agreed with the Mother.7

The Chapter and the “animadversiones” ~ The Sacred Congregation informed the Cardinal that it had given orders to the Bishop of Piacenza to convoke the Chapter and to proceed to the election of a General Council.

Cardinal Ferrieri, Prefect of the Congregation for Bishops and Regulars, had in fact written to the Bishop of Piacenza, prescribing various measures: “Then to give the Superior General her General Council”, he said, “whose consent is required by the norms of the Constitutions for the definition of the most important matters concerning the Institute itself, should you judge it appropriate, you will see that a regular General Chapter be convoked, always in accordance with the norms established in the frequently mentioned Constitutions”.8

The General Chapter was convoked for August of that year, 1881.

74 superiors met for it; the superior of the American mission was absent due to the excessive distance. Fr. Tornatore also took part in this first Chapter of the Institute (see undated autographical manuscript, in AFSA A.1.0).

On that occasion, Mother Rosa had had a new large chapel built in the Mother House, since the former one was no longer big enough to accommodate the community.

A spiritual retreat began here, on the evening of 14 August. It lasted a week, and was given by Fr. Manzi, a priest of the Congregation of the Mission and the superior of Collegio Alberoni.

The Mother made her precious contribution in talks given to the superiors on true spiritual renewal; the theme was always based on some point of the Rule, not only so that they would understand it better, but so that by comparing it to their own life, they might grow ever more faithful in their observance of it.

Mother Rosa’s conferences, which moreover were incisive and marked by a very evident practical sense, focused on certain fundamental points of religious and community life, such as the principal role of authority, always viewed as an educational relationship, supremely respectful of personal dignity and basic freedom, even in the context of obedience. It all had to be impressed with the sincerest loyalty, also in fraternal relations, and always imbued with humility and docility. With regard to humility the Mother excelled, precisely because of her interior greatness and her holiness.

Indeed, on the fifth day of the retreat, she thought it would be a good idea to humiliate herself before all the capitulars: she, who declared herself so full of shortcomings, so far from any edification, so difficult to reform, asked so much from those superiors and was perhaps boring and annoying to them. The tone of these words was so sincere that everyone was moved to tears, and it was an excellent introduction to the important things she was about to say. Certain superiors forbade their sisters the freedom to correspond with the Mother General, perhaps for fear of trouble for themselves: a reprehensible meanness of judgment and selfishness, especially since it openly opposed the true rights of the religious sanctioned by the Constitutions, as well as the good of the community.

This was even more serious in a superior when it was accompanied by abuse and a certain impropriety in correspondence with outside persons; and occasionally a letter would end up in the hands of the Mother herself.

Thus a fault came to light which had been noticed more than once, and she sorrowfully urged them to avoid it.

She would have liked to imbue all those superiors with the loftiest sense of responsibility for the important role entrusted to them in protecting and guiding the brides of Christ; what numerous recommendations she made that day about the approach to a maternal correction of their faults, the way to nourish their souls with an abundance of the word of God and with healthy reading, to encourage them constantly in their growth towards perfection, to properly refrain from those harsh threats that embitter people and expose them to the risk of abandoning their vocation!

The Mother therefore insisted that they always show good humor, concealing whatever troubles they might have in their hearts behind a cheerful expression.

She then reminded them to have special regard for the sick, charity for whom must be more exquisite and generous than ever. And as to the food to which the communities were treated, she had recourse to example rather than to words: “You can observe”, she said, “how you are treated during these days of the spiritual exercises: do the same with your communities”.

With regard to the observance of poverty, although the preacher had already addressed this topic at length, she touched on one point which it would be fitting to mention here because it is a valuable testimony against the slanders she had to withstand in her government, even before the Holy See. “Superiors”, she said, “are never free to give presents, and even less can they associate with their sisters in preparing gifts for others, even if they are for the Generalate”. There is no doubt that the Mother was somewhat obviously limiting the superior’s freedom, but it was her right to do so and she did it precisely because she feared the instances of abuse which had already occurred. The Foundress’ meticulous care to shed the proper light on those points of observance most vulnerable to human weakness is truly moving; a religious must try with all her might to maintain herself within the integrity of her vocation and consecration to God; and also to acquire ever clearer transparency in her daily life.

In these instructions, Mother Rosa emerges as a supremely illumined example and guide, steeped in a deep and inventive love which polarized everything and led back to the essential, the Absolute.

That particular retreat ended solemnly with Mass celebrated by Bishop Scalabrini in the new chapel, festively decorated. After the customary thanksgiving, the Bishop presided at the session of the first General Chapter, at which the observations proposed by the Sacred Congregation were voted upon; all the capitulars expressed unanimous opposition to these instructions, perhaps holding that they were unnecessary or were merely recommendations to be discussed: a grave error, that was certainly due to their inexperience and inadequate knowledge of the juridical norms, indispensable if the Institute was to function properly. As for the Mother, her opinion certainly agreed with that of the Chapter, but there is no doubt that she took pains not to influence anyone’s vote. Each one freely followed her own judgment, adhering to the response formulated by the secretary, Sr. Anna Benedetta Carrega, and signing in the Bishop’s presence.

He did not fail to observe that such a decision might threaten or endanger the definitive approval of the Constitutions, but he did not advise them to vote again and no one thought of doing so.

The Mother’s journey to Rome and submission to the Holy See ~ It is easy to foresee the consequences. Cardinal Ferrieri immediately had the Foundress summoned to Rome; she arrived on 30 November that same year: on 3 December she had an audience with the Cardinal, but after waiting for four hours to see him, when she was at last introduced, she was firmly reprimanded for the Chapter’s act of insubordination to the Holy See in refusing the “animadversiones” to the Constitutions.

The poor Mother, who was very far from suspecting that there had been any disobedience in that voting, made her excuses and renewed her unconditional obedience.

What sorrow she felt at the involuntary mistake! She asked Cardinal Alimondo, Protector of the Institute, for help, and the Prelate willingly devoted all his efforts to it, with Mgr. Carlo Laurenzi, auditor of His Holiness Leo XIII.

Election of the first General Council ~With a papal rescript of 11 February 1882, Mother Rosa obtained that the superiors of the house could elect by post four assistants to the Mother General, who would constitute her Council, and the General Secretary. The ballot papers were therefore sent to the Cardinal Protector, who on 4 March9 communicated the names of those elected to the Mother: Sr. Anna Consolata Massimelli, Sr. Anna Santina Solenghi, Sr. Anna Celsa Speranza, Sr. Anna Giacomina Schenardi, and Sr. Anna Benedetta Carrega as secretary.

On 13 March 1882, the Council, with a special dispensation from the Holy See, met in Rome as a Chapter in the presence of Cardinal Alimonda and Mgr Laurenzi; Sr. Anna Giacomina Schenardi was absent for reasons of health. After the opening of the first session, at the Mother’s suggestion the Council retracted the acts issued at the Chapter of the previous August, with the humblest expressions of submission to the Church’s will.10 They then passed to the deliberations.

Three provinces of the Institute were established, each with its own novitiate: the Province of Northern Italy with a novitiate in Piacenza; the Province of Southern Italy with a novitiate in Naples in the new, recently purchased house; the American Province, with a novitiate in La Paz.11 As for the Generalate, it was decided that it should be moved to Rome as soon as possible, since this was also the wish of the Holy See.

Further important innovations were made regarding the conditions of admission to the Institute: widows could only be accepted with the Holy See’s explicit authorization, nor were they permitted to take only temporary vows: after a suitable period, they were obliged to take perpetual vows.12

The vow of poverty was defined according to the discipline in force in the Church; thus the sisters retained the fundamental ownership and ability to dispose of their own patrimony, but renounced the right to administer it. In addition, dowries were to be invested and not to be used in any way: there was no trace of any of this in the former Rule. Norms were also established for the novitiate: from that time, one whole year had to be spent in the house destined for that purpose under the guidance of the novice mistress, given the importance and need of formation.13

A very exact report of the Institute’s property and on the manner of its management was made on the basis of the civil laws. The requests for the opening of new houses were also examined: at least 24 were requested in Italy and 4 in America: a visible sign of the favor the Daughters of St. Anne were encountering.

Cardinal Alimonda presented the acts of the General Council to the Sacred Congregation on 26 April 1882; four months later, Cardinal Ferrieri, in a lengthy reply, expressed satisfaction with what had been done: “The said acts have been the object of a thorough examination at this Sacred Assembly which could not but praise the General Council which, at the Superior General’s proposal, has declared that it accepts with full submission the measures the Sacred Congregation has taken regarding the Institute…”.14

Thus everything seemed to have been smoothed out. In accordance with the points established at the Council and Cardinal Ferrieri’s new proposals, a new edition of the Constitutions was immediately made, since the basic text of 1876 had not yet been printed.15 However, only the part concerning the spiritual life and disciplinary regime of the sisters was published; the section concerning the government of the Institute was not made known

.

After the storm, life flourished once again, purer and brighter than before: God’s blessing was visible in the rapid growth of vocations, houses and the most important offices entrusted to the Institute, in Italy and abroad.

How great the rectitude of those souls had been throughout the course of these events is highlighted by the words with which a diary of the time concludes its narrative: “The Institute of the Daughters of St. Anne put down deeper roots on this occasion, because an expert and wise hand, that of the Church, was able to uproot, tear out and extirpate those seeds which perhaps with time might have prevented the Institute’s development and expansion”.16

Visit to the houses in Southern Italy ~ At the end of 1882, Mother Rosa made her first journey to Sicily where the houses of the Daughters of St. Anne had already grown to about ten since the first foundation in Agrigento, on 24 November 1876.

The beginning of that journey was marked by another sacrifice: having left Piacenza towards the end of November, traveling to Rome via Genoa, the Mother found her own mother dying and so it was expedient for her to stay a few days to comfort her properly. But at the very moment when the sick woman was nearing the end of her earthly life, Mother Rosa received an urgent telegram calling her to Pisa; she did not hesitate to obey the voice of duty rather than that of her heart and left immediately. On the way from the community of sisters to the station, she had to pass under the window of her family home where her mother lay dying; she kept on going, although she felt her heart breaking from the violence she was forced to do to herself. As soon as she arrived in Pisa, she heard by telegraph of the painful death which, by delaying her departure, she might have been able to ease; but she had long sacrificed herself and all her most sacred affections to God; faithful to the evangelical command she did not turn back and two days later, having arranged things in Pisa, she continued on to Rome and Naples.

On that long journey, so affectionately recounted by Sr. Anna Celsa Speranza, she visited the houses in Southern Italy; she sailed for Messina from Reggio Calabria and proceeded from there as though in continuous triumph, the focus of so many demonstrations in her honor by the people and clergy and especially the Bishops. Some cloistered nuns wanted her to visit them, to see at least once the Foundress who had aroused such enthusiasm. When they met her, they had a profound impression that she was someone extraordinary. She admitted many young girls to the novitiate, founded several new houses in response to the authorities’ requests and gave fresh dynamism to the existing ones; above all, she awakened in every community the enthusiasm and joy of following Christ, encouraging all the religious to persevere zealously on the way they had chosen. It was written that the exhausting journey, which lasted for more than three months, was a real mission for the Institute on whose life and works it indeed made a profound mark.1

Building the Generalate and the church ~ In spring 1883, she returned to the peninsula and stopped in Rome to begin the construction of the Generalate. The Holy See had in fact recommended her as soon as possible to overcome the obstacles preventing the building of the house in Rome;2 so before setting out for Sicily, the Foundress had done her best to implement the project. She had shown the plan for it to her brothers Francesco and Federico, and they helped her affectionately, obtaining credit in various banks.

A large site was purchased in Via Merulana on 27 February 1883, on which to build the Generalate and its adjoining church which the Mother wanted also to be open to the public; the foundation stone was to be laid in May. In March, the foundations had already been marked out and work began.3 It was completed in just over two years, and the Foundress herself often inspected its progress; indeed, during her long stays in Rome she visited the building site to follow the work in detail, to ensure that the building would correspond as closely as possible to its purpose and that the proper economy was being used in its construction. On 6 January 1886, it was declared habitable by the Municipality of Rome, and on the 18th of that month, it was solemnly blessed by the Vicar of His Holiness, Cardinal Lucido Maria Parocchi.

The Mother’s illness and her recovery through the intercession of “Maria Mater Gratiae et Misericordiae” ~ However, some extraordinary events highlight the history of the Generalate. The very evening on which Mother Rosa received the promised sum from Count Caracciolo for building the church,4 on returning home and entering her cell, she was viciously assaulted by the devil who, appearing to her in a terrifying form said to her: “You’ve won but you’ll pay for it”. And he immediately inflicted a mysterious illness upon her, which was so serious that the doctors thought she was nearing her end, as though she were affected by peritonitis; the last holy sacraments were even administered to her. Having received the Viaticum, she wanted to be left alone and then had an apparition of Maria Mater Gratiae et Misericordiae: “I fell asleep and suddenly awoke with a jolt. There was Fr. Bernardo’s Maddonina; the Child was holding out a small cup and he wanted to give it to me…” (M. 5.1, p. 100).

The Mother of God implored the Son to cure her; in fact, shortly afterwards, the doctors and the community were astonished to see that every symptom of her illness had vanished. Then the Mother, as an attestation of gratitude, promised to dedicate the church being built in Rome next to the Generalate to Maria Mater Gratiae et Misericordiae and arranged to have her image crowned by the Bishop of Piacenza. Indeed, the following year, 1884, on 1 June the coronation took place in Piacenza with great solemnity. The splendid gold crown was donated by a benefactor of the Institute in gratitude to the Blessed Virgin for curing the Mother. The seminarians of Piacenza, many priests and the Neapolitan Abbot, Luigi Negri, encircled Bishop Scalabrini in the large chapel decorated for the celebration. When the Bishop had blessed the crown, the sisters, singing, formed a procession; Abbot Negri followed, carrying the crown on a cushion. Joining the procession, the Bishop then crowned Mary’s image; he gave a splendid homily and granted an indulgence to whoever recited three Hail Marys in front of it.5

Mother Rosa’s niece, Sr. Anna Francesca Savignone, also took part in the celebration with extreme weariness. With a dispensation for her young age from the Holy See, she had been elected local superior in Piacenza in 1880. Consumptive and almost spent, she died three weeks later, assisted by the Mother; she left behind her a strong fragrance of virtue, because of her especially deep piety, unconditional obedience and simple faith.

While the image of Maria Mater Gratiae et Misericordiae was being crowned in Piacenza, the church that was to be dedicated to her was already being built in Rome.

On 23 May 1883, its foundation stone was solemnly blessed by Cardinal Alimonda, assisted by Fr. Donadio and numerous ecclesiastics and clerics. The essential parts of the building were finished in 1886, and it was consecrated and inaugurated on 1 May 1887.6

Walking from St. Mary Major to St John Lateran down the long, tree-lined avenue, Via Merulana, the Generalate of the Daughters of St. Anne can be seen on the right, just before the crossing with Via Labicana; it is a building which in those times seemed very majestic, while today it stands with unassuming decorum between the larger buildings that surround it: there is no doubt that in comparison with Rome’s other religious institutes, it is one of the more modest generalates. The reception rooms on the first floor have an elegant air about them, because the Mother wanted to be able to receive the prelates she would have to entertain there with due reverence, but the rest of the building bears the hallmark of the beautiful simplicity of religious poverty.

Next door to the house is the church that is open to the public. Together with Our Lady, the Mother wanted the Patrons of the Institute to be honored there: St. Anne, St. Francis of Assisi, St. Michael Archangel and St. Joseph;7 the Sacred Heart and Our Lady of Lourdes, the reproduction of whose grotto was the first in Rome, are also venerated.

The Travertine marble facade dates back to 1927; the internal decorations and other alterations made to the first design are also from this period.8

The wonderful image of Maria Mater Gratiae et Misericordiae which today hangs at the level of the upper tribune, in the Foundress’ time was embedded in the center of a great sunburst above the altar; in 1927 it was placed upon a beautiful marble throne where it remained until 1970. Although the Church is dedicated to Mary it has always been known as the “Church of St. Anne at the Lateran”.

The stained-glass window in the ceiling that lets in a gentle light, creating an atmosphere of recollection and prayer, is evocative and most original. It portrays the triumph of the Cross; at the foot of the Cross is the Institute’s coat of arms. This arrangement is meant to recall the Foundress’ thought: God’s work is born and lives at the foot of the Cross.9

Today the remains of Rosa Gattorno rest in this church, exactly below the fresco of St. Michael Archangel; they are the destination of ceaseless devout pilgrimages of Daughters and the faithful who commend themselves to her maternal intercession, experienced many times. In this Generalate for fourteen years, as formerly in Piacenza for twenty, Mother Rosa was a most faithful slave of her Crucified Love, ever obedient to the Church and to the Pope and entirely devoted to the Lord’s Work, her Institute.

Second journey to Sicily ~ After the Feast of the Immaculate Conception in 1884, the Mother continued her visits to the houses, down the peninsula. With her shaky health, worn out by strict fasting and the rigorous instruments of penance she had belted around her, one can picture the great discomfort she had to bear during those long journeys, often traveling by night on the trains of the time, almost primitive in comparison with our modern ones.

On 4 January 1885, she went to Sicily for the second time, invited by the provincial of Palermo, Sr. Anna del Salvatore Orsi. Having started on the Metaponto line down the Ionian coast, she suffered enormous hardship during the journey, caused by landslides that delayed the train and forced the passengers to walk over muddy ground under the pelting rain. But this did not detain the Mother, who arrived at the orphanage in Crotone so worn out that she was forced to stay in bed for three days. With grave fears for her health, her traveling companions wanted her to return to Rome via Foggia, but she was determined to continue. So she passed through Reggio and Messina on her way to Palermo, a true and tireless missionary going to her institute where she was needed and not allowing herself to be beguiled, even by the courtesies of benefactors who would have liked to alleviate her weariness by slowing her down.

In Sicily she found the number of houses had increased to eighteen, they had almost doubled in two years. She devoted herself with infinite dedication to advising, consoling, organizing and, wherever possible, gathering the superiors of neighboring houses, to impress upon all a new impetus in their vocation and mission. She stayed in Palermo for almost a month, making numerous efforts which were aggravated by fevers and headaches that seemed worse than any of her past ailments.

Her work in the city’s eight houses, receiving the many people who wanted to see her, including Cardinal Celesia twice, the Bishops of Messina and Mazara del Vallo and many other prelates, as well as the demanding matters she had to settle, must have taken a heavy toll on her body, already so worn out, and on her soul, besieged by all kinds of worries.

Yet the Mother was always seen to be affable and serene, peaceful and refreshed in spirit, as though she had no other thought than the comforting prosperity of her Institute in Palermo. It really filled her with joy to see it so loved and assisted; she was even more delighted to see in the sisters a unanimous spirit of simple charity and love of the Rule, together with generous self-denial in the service of the lowly.

On 9 February 1885, she set out for Messina, greeted along the way by groups of Daughters of St. Anne who were waiting for her to pass through the railway stations near their houses, to see her one last time. From Messina to Reggio and Crotone, she stopped at Rossano where she wanted to visit the hospital. She arrived at the station at midnight, but as a secretary tells, a further two hours by carriage were required to get to her destination.

In those lands at the time, brigandage was widespread, which is why the director of the hospital, armed with pistols to defend them in case of attack, was in the carriage that awaited the Mother, traveling with two sisters. The carriage set out in the dark and rainy night while the hearts of the Mother’s timid companions were pounding with fear, as on many other occasions. This woman’s courage was indomitable; to guarantee her presence and comfort to others she was prepared to face any challenge.

The vicissitudes of Mother Rosa’s long pilgrimages every year until the end of her life have thus been briefly outlined; these pilgrimages were certainly not a secondary aspect of her greatness and total self-denial. Indeed it is natural to wonder how a person suffering such physical pain and the mental wounds of every kind of contradiction and offense, could have withstood such formidable efforts and anxieties for more than twenty years. The only answer that comes to mind is in St. Paul’s words: “Love … endure[s] whatever comes” (1 Co 13:7), even disappointments, failures or ingratitude.

Audience with Pope Leo XIII ~ Nevertheless among all these preoccupations there were two that weighed particularly heavily on Mother Gattorno’s heart; the building of the Generalate which had begun in Rome and which was obviously a source of many problems, and the definitive approval of the Constitutions. She therefore stayed on in Rome all spring until after the Easter celebrations of 1885, giving vent to her deep piety by visiting the Scala Santa on Fridays and devoting more time to prayer. She spent Lent with severe fasting, abstaining even from milk products, and Holy Week in almost absolute retirement, preparing herself for a really joyful Easter. It was in fact a great comfort to the Mother to be admitted with three sisters to Holy Mass in the Sistine Chapel and to receive Communion from the Pope.

At that time she also had a private audience with him. Seeing herself welcomed in such a fatherly way, she opened her heart to him with full trust. Pope Leo XIII questioned her at length about the Work of God and expressed his deep satisfaction with what the Daughters of St. Anne were doing, especially when Mother Rosa offered him a booklet then published in Naples, illustrating their heroic charity during the cholera epidemic in 1884. The paternal pleasure of the great Pontiff was crowned with an ample blessing, so that the Foundress left the audience “drunk with consolation” as one of her secretaries wrote.

Her soul thus imbued with light and hope, she presented to the Sacred Congregation for Bishops and Regulars the text of the Constitutions, amended in accordance with the instructions and observations she had received in those years. This time, she flattered herself that she was near her haven, especially as the Secretary of the Sacred Congregation himself had given her the greatest hope. With this trust in her heart she left for Turin on 22 April, eager to take the good news to Cardinal Alimonda. But her beloved dream was once again short-lived; on 30 August 1885, a letter from Cardinal Schiaffino warned her not only that the Constitutions could not yet be definitively approved, but that they would have to be reprinted with the modifications proposed, and kept ad experimentum for another ten years. It is easy to imagine the deep disappointment the Mother must have felt, impatient as she was to see the Rule of the religious life of her Institute at last established by the supreme authority.10

Death of Sr. Anna del Salvatore Orsi ~ Another serious sorrow afflicted the Mother in that summer of 1885; on 7 June in Palermo, Sr. Anna del Salvatore Orsi, superior of the house there and provincial of Sicily since May 1884, suddenly died.

She was a real jewel of the Institute, so lofty was her spirituality, her wisdom in life and government, her genuine amiability to the sisters and her deep humility. Having sacrificed herself entirely to the service of God, Sr. Anna del Salvatore also had a very special predilection for religious poverty, and sought to live it radically. In her long journeys she would always prefer to travel third class on the train; she sometimes even preferred the rail carriage with the animals, a poor woman among the poor. She begged for the poor as well as for her sisters, to such effect that she succeeded in alleviating their poverty and even in putting the house of nurses in Palermo in a flourishing condition, as well as satisfactorily organizing those in Termini Imerese, Trapani, Sciaca, Sambuca, Linguaglossa and Agrigento; in these towns and in other places, her charity shone out so pure that it roused the admiration of all.

Before this splendid afternoon and the glorious evening that followed, Sr. Anna del Salvatore had known the sorrows and shadows with which the forces of evil sometimes fill the souls most precious and dear to God. Under the pressures of incredible and furious persecutions, in 1878 she had had to be removed from the house in Florence where she had been a very active superior, and sent to Appignano with the same role. In the summer of that year, Mother Gattorno summoned her to Piacenza to the usual gathering of superiors for the retreat.

In those very circumstances the superiors, informed by Mother Rosa of the difficult situation of the house in Florence, claimed inexplicably that Sr. Anna del Salvatore was responsible for it, and even asked that she be expelled from the Institute. But the Mother would not be persuaded to take that extreme measure; a little later she sent Sr. Anna del Salvatore to Ferrara as a mistress of discipline. Here she still had to suffer because her reputation had preceded her and because of the humiliations forced upon her; later she also held offices in Rome, Ovada and Sermoneta, until in 1880 she was sent to Sicily to found the first house in Palermo. Slowly, Sr. Anna del Salvatore was rehabilitated in the eyes of the Institute, and she was eventually declared utterly innocent with regard to the calumnies that had been attributed to her; in the Chapter of 1881, she received attestations of high trust from all the capitulars.

However, that suffering had lasted for two long years! She was born on 22 February 1842 in Albareto, Parma, and when she ended her earthly pilgrimage she was only just 43 years old. The fame of holiness that she left among the people and her sisters was so great that just two years after her death, Cardinal Celesia, Archbishop of Palermo, decided to grant the wishes of the lay people and clergy, and ordered that her remains be canonically recognized. This occurred on 4 February 1887 in the presence of Mother Gattorno, then on her third visit to Sicily; many ecclesiastics and a great crowd of people were also present. The Foundress immediately thought of collecting the necessary means and later too, continued to collect funds for the cause of beatification of that daughter of hers, as one can see in her correspondence with the missionary sisters in America.11

Inauguration of the Generalate and Assembly of 1886 ~ Consequently, the mourning for that premature death soon became a cause of joy for the Daughters of St. Anne.12

Shortly after these events, on 5 September another vista was unfolded to the Institute: the missions in Africa. They were called there by the Italian Government. It took more than two years to finalize the agreements, but in the meantime, despite the difficulties, God showed that he wanted to use the work of the Daughters of St. Anne.

When at last the new Generalate was inaugurated in January 1886, Mother Rosa convoked an Assembly in which 64 superiors took part (about half of those in Italy). Fr. Tornatore also attended, as well as the provincial of America, Sr. Anna Camilla Valentini. He gave several conferences with Mother Rosa during the spiritual retreat which customarily preceded every important meeting (cf. Memorie of Mother Celsa Speranza, AFSA, B.3.78).

In a circular for that same year, 1886, signed by the Foundress and by the Father,13 this Assembly is described as a “private Chapter” at which only topics concerning the internal discipline of the Institute were treated.14

It was therefore a labor of formation and interior growth for the individuals and of internal organization for the communities, indispensable elements for the credibility and prophecy of the Institute that was continuously expanding.

Second General Chapter (1888) ~ However, the Second General Chapter was more decisive. It was held in autumn 1888 and chaired by Cardinal Alimonda. At least 180 superiors met in Rome on that occasion; a few superiors resident abroad and the provincial of America were absent because of the distance and difficulty of journeys, which were really adventurous at that time.

On Friday, 5 October, the first session was opened by Cardinal Alimonda. He reminded everyone of her duty to have the most upright intentions in the work about to be done. When the new Council was elected, the Cardinal demonstrated the need to set up a new religious province for Sicily; to this end he asked and obtained the rescript from the Sacred Congregation and proposed the appointment of four provincials. In the election to these important offices, sisters already known reappeared, but there were also new names in the General Council, such as Sr. Anna Giuseppa Troni. On the last day, the Cardinal spoke to the Chapter on regular observance and on the imitation of Christ; he did not fail to remark on the importance of perfect union with Mother General, taking this opportunity to publicly attest to his esteem and affection for her and her Institute. Lastly, he announced that the Pope would receive all the capitulars in audience.

Fr. Tornatore’s expulsion from the Institute ~ A decision taken with all probability on this occasion cannot be omitted since it left a mark on the Institute’s history. Neither in the acts, nor in any other documentation does it seem certain that Fr. Tornatore was present at this Chapter; however his presence can be rationally deduced from the fact that a series of attestations show that the Father had been readmitted, at least officially, to participate in the direction of the Institute as from 1875; furthermore, since 1880, he had also been delegated by the Bishop of Piacenza for visitations of the houses and had been given every faculty required for this office.15 In 1883, the Father had likewise been granted the faculty of hearing the sacramental confessions of any Daughters of St. Anne who wished to make their confession to him him.16

It is also known that Fr. Tornatore normally lived in the Generalate where he carried out offices of direction and formation. However, for some time relations had been deteriorating and difficulties and misunderstandings had occurred, inherent in the government and role in the Institute of the Father himself. This event is also clearly explained in Cardinal Granito di Belmonte’s testimony: “… Mr. Giovanni Battista Tornatore, a priest of the Congregation of the Mission, who had had a large part in the Institute’s foundation, normally lived in the houses of the Institute itself, and often followed the Foundress and the other sisters on their visitation of the houses; he devoted himself with great zeal to the proper functioning of religious life, but was often influenced and shocked by those religious who were reprimanded or punished by the Foundress and frequently stood up for them against the measures taken by the Servant of God. As it is easy to understand, this two-faced attitude was a cause of suffering to the Servant of God who in her usual way, while she did not wish to oppose the ecclesiastic mentioned, in her heart clearly felt and noted the drawbacks it caused in the discipline of the various communities”.17

The Mother’s suffering in this predicament emerges above all in her Memorie. In an obviously hard moment she says: “Fr. Tornatore says I am disobedient because as superior I do not inform him of everything. It has now been fourteen years and more that he has continued to torture and illtreat me horribly. I have always kept silent, but it was the Church which gave me the assistants. So they and the secretary, poor creatures, are always having to witness horrible scenes; they took my defense and this made him even angrier and he said that he absolutely wanted to be recognized as G[eneral]. Yes, my God, let all the titles be his, but let him leave me in peace because I cannot take any more” (M. 9.5, pp. 94-95).

Equally great was the suffering of Fr. Tornatore who, perhaps unaware of his conduct, saw himself gradually alienated from within what he considered his family. Hence his spirited reaction and attempt to clarify his position by speaking of it to various ecclesiastical personalities. In a letter of 8 July 1888, probably addressed to a priest of the Curia of Piacenza, he too vented his feelings: “Tell Monsignor that the Cardinal Protector was at first very surprised that measures were taken against me when the Mother had always had me as her intimate counsellor, and then he added that he considered me virtually co-founder […] what? The Institute originated from me because it was I who had the idea for it; it had its name from me and the Mother was only the instrument for its execution.18 And then they say virtually? And the Mother herself has proclaimed it hundreds and thousands of times both to the outside world and to the sisters. Then the Cardinal says that the name Superior General does not appear in the Rule. First of all, if I am the founder I am therefore superior of the Institute that has been born […]; I do not want to be the Mother’s counsellor: I want it declared whether or not I am the co-founder and superior. Should that ever happen (which I don’t believe), through the wickedness of human things I will not be able to stay at the Institute, my own child, without it being cut in half, like the baby of the two mothers before Solomon, so I would rather withdraw, but in the meantime what I am claiming is justice and fairness”.19

It is clear that the tone of both writings was equally angry and expressed a situation that was becoming worrying and untenable; therefore a decision had to be reached. This is what Cardinal Gennaro Granito di Belmonte writes to the Mother two months before the Chapter: “With regard to the F[ather], I am constantly worried about what could happen at the time of the Chapter. Rumor has it that the secretaries, out of affection for you and with the help of the Father General [Fr. Bernadino da Portogruaro] have accused the Father. Now I say, if the Father has nettled the Cardinal Vicar he, in his own time, must either examine the facts and call the sisters to witness against the Father, or he must bring the Father to the fore, giving him an office in the Chapter to atone for what has now happened: I should not like either of these things”.20

From the letter just cited it appears obvious that perhaps an important part in the clash was played by the persons who lived close to the Mother and who defended her role in the Institute, which was, moreover, irreplaceable. They obviously did not understand that Fr. Tornatore was far from intending to deprive the Mother of authority, indeed, “he exhorted the sisters to obey and to listen to what the Servant of God said to them”.21

The secretaries were therefore trying, also by turning to ecclesiastics, to have the Father’s effective position in the Institute defined.22 The Mother herself writes in her Memorie: “For Fr. Tornatore the problem comes from those sisters who, because of their office, have had to safeguard the functioning and discipline of the Institute which [in their opinion] can no longer continue like this…” (M. 7, p. 82).

It is known that the advice of Cardinal Alimonda who chaired the Chapter, of Fr. Bernardino da Portogruaro (see the letter cited in note 22) and, in a certain sense, of Cardinal Gennaro Granito di Belmonte, had much to do with this decision.

Fr. Tornatore expresses his deep sorrow in his words to Count Caracciolo immediately after his expulsion: “… it is certainly hard for a father to be driven out of his family; and by whom? […]. Let us adore with full resignation whatever God wants or permits in our regard, since everything is for his greatest glory and for our greatest good”.23

Also: “I am at Montecitorio with our missionaries who all love me dearly and have received me with open arms. No longer being with my daughters is of course painful to me; but I am thoroughly resigned to the divine dispositions and can help them with prayer”.24

What happened at the Chapter and how the definitive banishment of the Father from the Institute came about is difficult to say with absolute certainty, since there is no trace of it in the official documents of this period. We know, however, that relations were not definitively interrupted.

Actually, in the following years Fr. Tornatore continued to love and benefit the Institute, maintaining cordial relations with the Mother, as emerges from the letters written until three months before his death. For her part, Mother Rosa was always sensitive to the Father. She visited him several times at the home of the Counts Caracciolo showing him great attention in his illness. The Father died in Piacenza on 31 January 1895, leaving deep regret in many of the Daughters of St. Anne, who loved him like a father and appreciated him as a teacher and guide.25

Papal audience ~ on 7 October 1888, the work of the second session of the Chapter ended and all the participants prepared their souls for the papal audience the following day; in fact, on Monday 8 October, the 180 superiors, led by Mother Rosa, were presented to the Supreme Pontiff Leo XIII by Cardinal Alimonda himself.

The Pope smiled at that large group of religious, as it were opening his fatherly heart to the whole Institute which they represented and about which he had heard so much from the Cardinal Protector. He therefore turned to the Mother General and said to her: “Rosa, what have you done?”; “Nothing, Holy Father”, the Mother answered, slightly embarrassed, not understanding in her great humility to what the Pope was referring. He then stretched out his hand pointing to the multitude of capitulars and added: “You prayed a lot and this is the effect of your prayer. Continue to pray and to observe the Rule”.

Mother Gattorno then mentioned the mission in Africa, saying that the Daughters of St. Anne already had many houses there; Leo XIII discussed this subject with great interest, encouraging them and recommending them not to rush conversions; then he again insisted on the need for prayer and observance of the Rule.26

The Supreme Pontiff’s address which was so fatherly, his great benevolence and lastly the apostolic blessing which he imparted with deep affection, filled them all with such consolation that they were able to draw a true renewal of spirit from it. The Mother did not seem to feel the slightest weariness from the great efforts of those days when she had had to listen one by one to all the superiors; indeed, going straight back to work, in a few weeks she saw to the foundation of nine houses. In addition, preparing in so short a time a large number of religious for the new foundations as well as the many required by the missions meant that fresh energies were constantly flowing to the Daughters of St. Anne and that the Mother, with her unflagging activity, immediately found places for them. The Institute had by now acquired very distinctive features; more than twenty years’ experience had clarified many things, while the apostolic work of the Daughters of St. Anne had developed; they were called to many nations and to various continents. The importance and size of God’s Work now made an impression on public opinion, and its life in the world was clearly defined.

All that was missing was the definitive approval of the Constitutions; for this too, the Foundress’ longing hastened the event, although it still seemed distant.

First intervention of the Holy See ~ Another crucifying moment fits into this climate of hope, proving once again how what is great and beautiful in human life and in a Work of God brings a tribute of suffering, which must in any case be paid. Indeed after an anonymous letter denouncing disorders within the Institute was received by the Holy Father at the end of 1889, the ecclesial authority intervened, although not in an official capacity. The Protector, Cardinal Alimonda, was charged by Pope Leo XIII to appoint a Delegate with specific secret functions as an Apostolic Visitor. Mgr. Beniamino Cavicchioni was the person who received this mandate, and he visited the Generalate to examine the Institute’s general affairs. With the appointment of Cardinal Isidore Verga, Prefect of the Congregation for Bishops and Regulars, as the new Protector, Mgr. Cavicchioni’s office ceased.27

Despite this painful episode, the Institute’s life continued to be intense and was interspersed with great moments of joy and emotion.

Definitive approval of the Constitutions (1892) ~ As has just been mentioned, on 6 July 1891, Cardinal Verga was named the new Protector, replacing Cardinal Alimonda who died in Genoa on 31 May that year. On 10 November, Mother Gattorno confided to him with filial trust her desire to see the Constitutions finally approved. The Cardinal promised his full commitment, asking that in the meantime the amended Rules be submitted and the letters of recommendation of the Bishops be collected. A dawn of hope was rising, and this time a truly promising one.

What is more, the Protector, told by the Assistants that the following year would mark the twenty-fifth anniversary of the Mother’s religious clothing, wished to take almost the overall direction of the celebrations and gave instructions for the anniversary to be prepared solemnly.

All the houses of the Institute vied with one another to show their beloved Foundress their gratitude for the good received in those twenty-five years: a fine exhibition of gifts was like a hymn to her spiritual motherhood, from whose heart the new Institute had sprung.

But the finest gift for that 26 July 1892 was brought by the Cardinal Protector himself. That morning he came to the Generalate to celebrate Holy Mass, bringing with him a precious secret. After the celebration, as he left the chapel for the welcome that the whole community, lined up in the wide corridor, wished to give him, he had Sr. Anna Benedetta Carrega and Sr. Anna Celsa Speranza walk before him, carrying on a silver tray the booklet of the Constitutions with the pontifical decree of definitive approval, dated that very day: 26 July 1892. To the Mother, who was the first to come forward on the threshold of the chapel, he smilingly handed that little volume and that sheet, so precious and so long dreamed of: they could truly be called the seal of a long and troubled history, the reward for so much suffering and for a hard, anguished wait28.

It is easy to imagine the emotion in the hearts of all, and especially in the Mother’s.

“I felt such a strong pang”, she writes in her Memoirs, “that I [could not] understand [anything]; indeed, unable to hold back my tears, I ran off (I still do not know how I managed to get free of the nuns) and, running down the stairs, I made for my room […]; I burst into [great] weeping. How was I to thank my Beloved? I stifled [my sobs] for fear of being heard. What a day! Nothing could distract me from the holy Rules” (M. 12.1, pp. 131-132).

When on 10 November of the previous year she had asked the Cardinal for this great grace, she had ended by exclaiming: “Oh, then indeed I shall die happy!”.

Now her prayer was answered three years before the end of the ten-year period laid down by Cardinal Ferrieri. Yet not everything was accomplished; very hard battles still awaited her in the field of the Lord. For souls destined for great things share the destiny of Christ, the “Son of Man who must suffer many things” (Mk 8:31), and are called to the most complete involvement with him on a journey of cross, death and resurrection.

Mother Rosa had truly been seized by the mystery of the Cross; she lived the most radical belonging to it, and by virtue of this belonging her extraordinary vocation and mission also acquire their meaning.

(1884-1887) Cholera in Naples — Heroic love of the Daughters of St. Anne — Exchange of letters with the daughters — First cholera victim among the sisters — Recognition by the ecclesiastical and civil authorities — Cholera in Liguria and the heroic self-denial of the Daughters of St. Anne — Another victim of love — Cholera in Sicily — Christ’s love made tangible.

Cholera in Naples ~ In Mother Rosa’s Memorie we often find her mentioning signs predicting future events with which her Good was pleased to forewarn his most humble servant; so it was that she learned in advance of the forthcoming death of some sister by the appearance of larger or smaller stars that shone more or less brightly (M. 4.1, pp. 15-16; 75-76; 104-105 and M. 4.2, pp. 20-24; 30; 47-48).

On other occasions, as on 17 May 1872, she knew an epidemic was imminent because of the apparition in her cell of vast, black, strangely pointed marks (M. 3, pp. 29-30). At the same time she was assured that her sisters, although they were heroically helping the poor victims, would be immune to infection.

We also read in the memoirs of Sr. Anna Celsa Speranza, already cited, the reference to disasters inexplicably foreseen by the Mother who spoke of them simply and naturally, identifying them as signs of premonition. This happened for the outbreaks of cholera in Toulon, Marseilles, Paris and Italy.1

These signs were not always accompanied by an intellectual elucidation which showed her the nature of the event announced or the time when it would happen; indeed, occasionally Mother Rosa would be left in fearful uncertainty, abandoning herself to the Lord’s dispositions; every now and then she was granted to understand their meaning clearly, or at least to grasp it from the customary sequence of events.

Whatever the nature of these apparitions, it is certain that in summer 1884, cholera broke out in France and in early autumn many provinces of Italy were already infected. The disease had the most violent forms. “The scourge is advancing so relentlessly that those who are stricken with it immediately become corpses”, Sr. Anna Martina wrote to the Foundress from Naples on 10 September. In fact, the disease killed in just a few hours, leaving the corpses blackened.2

Heroic love of the Daughters of St. Anne ~ Mother Gattorno immediately saw the heroic moment for God’s Work: all the sisters must be ready for the boundless love asked of them in such circumstances, and she had formed them to this end.

Now, remembering what the Institute had done in Piacenza in its early days, she stimulated, guided and supported her Daughters in the gift of themselves to the victims of the epidemic. Since she had to stay where she was in command, in addition to the extraordinary efforts of the day she embarked on special penances and lengthy prayers, keeping close to her religious as they toiled among the sick with her constant letters. She prayed with such faith! “Pray”, Fr. Gennaro di Belmonte wrote to her from Naples, “Naples is at the height of devastation. This disease is the plague rather than the cholera. May God, Mary most holy and St. Anne help this people! Her Daughters are doing feats of charity”.3

The conditions of Naples at the time were truly distressing: about a thousand people a day were succumbing to the disease and the people were in the grip of terror, as it became more and more dangerous with the confusion that prevailed and the lack of measures of hygiene. “Yesterday”, Sr. Anna Martina wrote on 10 September, “I found a poor young girl flung down outside the door by her employers, on the ground with nothing but a little mattress. After equipping myself with the permit, together with a municipal policeman I took the sick girl to the Conocchia Hospital. We must see what sort of a hospital for cholera victims this is: so many are admitted, and so many are discharged dead. Yesterday almost a thousand cases broke out, this is not an exaggeration; and the papers only report about a third of them. The city is in great confusion: [there are] many penitential processions and at this very moment as I write, five have just passed! Men barefoot, women with their hair loose…”.4

Further: “There were two days when we could not take any more: how many we assisted, how many died […]. What a tumult, what confusion! Two evenings ago, at the hospital of la Maddalena there were 250 sick, almost all at death’s door! A wave of such fear followed that the doctors and priests fled; at midnight the Cardinal, with Fr. Belmonte, was called to help in the catastrophe; there were only five sisters of charity!”.5

“There is a scene of great wretchedness” wrote another sister, “concealed corpses are being found in homes, poor little orphans deprived of their fathers and mothers, houses abandoned for fear of the disease; it really wrings one’s heart. Let us hope in God’s mercy that this illness will cease and that many poor sinners will be converted”6

The dreadful scourge took the civil authorities by surprise; they did all they could with generosity and self-denial, but were far from issuing adequate measures for an emergency of this kind. In such desolation, the miraculous power of Christian love was revealed once again, since the humble religious and generous priests were voluntarily and without respite giving themselves to the sick, the orphans, the abandoned, bringing them the comfort of the faith and assistance of every kind. The important figure of Cardinal Sanfelice stood out before everyone. Accompanied by Fr. Gennaro di Belmonte, he tirelessly visited hospitals, pesthouses and homes, administering the sacraments and the comfort of his fatherly kindness and offering every sort of help, while encouraging others to give themselves generously with the same heroic devotion.

The Daughters of St. Anne devoted themselves wholeheartedly to the cholera victims. More than forty were sent to nurse cholera patients at home, and six to the hospital for infectious diseases of San Giovanni in Teduccio. Mother Gattorno asked the Cardinal Archbishop by telegram if other sisters were necessary and was begged to send them. She immediately sent many, and subsequently other groups; and she could always find sisters to send because, motivated by the extraordinary charity of their Mother, the Daughters of St. Anne offered themselves enthusiastically for this heroic task. Under the direction of the superior, Sr. Anna Martina, and their spiritual guide, Fr. di Belmonte, they did an invaluable and diligent job.

“These Daughters of yours”, Fr. di Belmonte wrote, “are no longer women, but angels of charity. The whole Institute is certainly supported by the blessings that these nurses receive […]. Mother, as soon as the cholera is over, you must come and comfort them with a visit”.7

Exchange of letters with the daughters ~ However, the great Mother arrived among her daughters every day with her letters, filled with love and spiritual encouragement, which brought them indescribable comfort and made them appreciate more and more the lofty mission of charity in which they were toiling: “We listened to your letter [read out], ever beloved and comforting to us, your poor Daughters […]. All day long mortuary carts can be seen trundling everywhere […] but we hope St. Anne will protect us”.8

“Reverend Mother, we thank you for the courage”, wrote the superior, Sr. Anna Martina, “thanks be to God and to Mother St. Anne, we are all still well”.

After God, they attributed their courage to their most beloved Mother; because of her prayers, they were sure they would continue to be immune to contagion, but were ready to submit to it, should that be God’s pleasure.9

First cholera victim among the sisters ~ All the sisters were saved from the tremendous peril except for one, Sr. Anna Adele. After spending herself in every kind of effort while the disease raged, at the end of September when the cholera in Naples was dying down, she caught such a violent form of the disease that in a few hours it brought her to her end. In her terrible pain, which she could not hide from those beside her, she gave an example of the strongest virtue and the most generous sacrifice. She replied to the confessor and Fr. di Belmonte who were comforting her: “And is this suffering compared with what Jesus suffered for me?” She died offering up her life to God in expiation for the evil of the world and so that the city might be freed from that terrible scourge.10

Such spiritual heights were bound to honor the Mother who had forged them, since formation in the Institute was wholly focused on acquiring such love. Mother Rosa spoke on the subject with extraordinary eloquence, and what is more, she gave an enthralling example of it.

Not only the nursing sisters, but also the teachers, excellently trained, bravely devoted themselves to nursing the cholera victims. “If you could but see”, wrote Sr. Anna Martina to the Mother in another letter, “how [excellent] the little teachers have become, after the nurses’ example!”.11

Recognition by the ecclesiastical and civil authorities ~ The élan of those sisters’ generous dedication knew no bounds; as well as nursing assistance in the hospitals and pesthouses, when summoned by the ecclesiastical and civil authorities they hastened to visit in their homes those stricken with the disease, and to ascertain which treatment they especially needed; they went promptly wherever they were told, and first of all guaranteed spiritual comfort to the dying. A unique aspect of their charity was the relief they brought to the sorrowful families; they sometimes watched with the sick for entire nights, since at times the relatives, petrified by grief, could not manage to help those poor unfortunates. They cared for new babies, arranging for them to be bottle-fed, while they nursed the new mothers stricken by the disease. Entire families fled, terrified of contagion, leaving in the custody of these religious their homes and their sick, until they recovered or died.

They were not satisfied with giving the needy what had been entrusted to them by public charity; they gave them everything they had. “I had prepared fifty new sheets for the house in Rome”, the superior, Sr. Anna Martina, wrote to the Mother, “now they will be used for the cholera victims. A disposition of God!”.12

All this contrasted with the cruel wickedness of unscrupulous people who preyed on private homes and hospitals for infectious diseases, making the most of the common confusion. In the pesthouse of La Maddalena, a large number of sheets were stolen on a single day. “The newspapers cannot mention this”, wrote the same superior, “or they would cause a revolution. You can’t imagine how necessary it is to be vigilant; now all sorts are thieves […], so one has to deal with magistrates and delegates. Yesterday I had to go about with policemen. Do you know why? People fall ill and their servants discreetly steal everything from their houses. The delegate insisted that the sisters accept the keys of an old Marchioness called Badessa […]. So many hundreds of thousands of francs, and the poor remain without aid! In short, it is a terrible scourge”.13

The pesthouse of La Maddalena ai Cristallini was then entrusted to the Daughters of St. Anne. Sr. Anna Maria Felice, who was put in charge, set to with every ounce of her energy to obtain order and discipline.

“She is like the mistress of the house”, Fr. di Belmonte wrote of her, “and does not miss a thing; she firmly does her duty and does not let the prefect, the mayor, lay people or soldiers get away with anything”.14

Since the sisters were giving proof of indisputable ability and worked tirelessly in all fields, the authorities put the greatest trust in them. The Mayor of Naples gave the superior free rein to send her sisters wherever she thought best; as long as they were Daughters of St. Anne he was not worried about who the individuals were, and was always completely satisfied. At a certain point, novices also had to be sent to meet the impelling need for assistance and set a splendid example of courage and dedication, despite their youth. There were also many acts of heroic fraternal love among the sisters themselves. Seeing their superior extremely oppressed by work and indeed, succumbing to the first symptoms of cholera, a novice, Sr. Anna della Pietà, did a triduum, praying God to cure the superior and to take her instead. On the third day of the triduum, the superior had recovered and was up and about; Sr. Anna della Pietà was smitten by a violent attack of cholera while serving in the pesthouse of La Maddalena. She was given no more than a few hours to live. Everyone was distressed, especially the superior, also because this novice had shown an incredible spirit of dedication in nursing many cholera patients in the city; fortunately the prayers of the good and the doctor’s rapid intervention obtained her cure: after developing a temperature she survived.

Another very young sister who had never seen anyone die, suddenly found herself in the midst of the raging epidemic, burdened by enormous efforts: experiencing the tragedy and harshness of the moment, she saw people die like flies. Yet, she confessed to Mother Rosa that she never lacked strength and attributed this to a true miracle.15

With this courage that blossomed from faith and from the pure joys of love, the Daughters of St. Anne in Naples bore the harsh trials of that massacre. The fame of their incredible devotion was so widespread that their presence was requested in every family troubled by the disease. “The sick at home”, wrote Fr. di Belmonte, “lock themselves in and the door is not opened, either to the mayor or to the police or to priests, but only to the nuns”.16 “Your Daughters”, he said in another letter, “are adored for the way in which they serve the sick…”17 But the praise which was certainly the most authoritative and precious was that of the Most Eminent Cardinal Sanfelice, who wrote to the Mother: “The work of your sisters is truly edifying; they compete in trials of the rare love which inspires them, and have increasingly reconciled that reverence and love they so deserve, among the Neapolitans and in other places. May the Lord bless them!”.18

At so dramatic a time and in circumstances so marked by danger, those sisters truly adopted an attitude as dignified as it was heroic, even if for the most part it was an everyday heroism and not the kind that draws attention or is publicized by the press. The superior appropriately asked Mother Gattorno for instructions and the due faculties: “I beg you in these circumstances to give me every authorization so that I shall not find myself in a muddle, either in my mind or in fulfilling my office”.19 She watched tirelessly over her sisters, although their conduct was far above any praise. “I am in constant admiration”, said Fr. di Belmonte, “indeed, I am edified by the determination with which your sisters work in the field of charity; and the superior, even against my will, never spares herself; she works, surveys and watches over the house and outside it and in all the new houses, always keeping the good of her neighbor and the good conduct of the sisters as her goal. St. Anne is most tangibly among us!”.20

“Your valiant soldiers”, he wrote a few days later, alluding to the sisters, “want to take the whole crown, and so now, ever firmly at their post, they are behaving extremely well and without any guidance because they only manage to see me occasionally at some late hour, and with enormous difficulty. The superior, Martina, is adroit in changing sisters when she sees that they can no longer stay in their post”.21

Indeed, their love of observance was such that it required Fr. di Belmonte’s authority to provide the novices with some relief from their ordinary practices, they arrived so exhausted from nursing the sick. “Poor creatures! In the house they are always few and when they retire, I cannot allow them to be so strictly constrained […]. I take responsibility for suspending the novitiate…”.22 Fr. di Belmonte had to pluck up his courage to make these provisions, given Cardinal Ferrieri’s frequent observations to the foundress about the novitiate.

In the meantime, high praise of the Daughters of St. Anne reached the ears of the Supreme Pontiff Leo XIII from various sides, but especially from the Archbishop of Naples; and the Pope lavished very special blessings upon them. Fr. di Belmonte was then inspired to implore a most extraordinary reward for them; so he wrote to Mother Gattorno: “This morning I asked His Eminence the Cardinal for permission to write to the Holy Father to ask for a reward for my company of nurses. He told me that I could. But I first want your advice too. I will ask the Holy Father to obtain for all these novices the possibility of making their vows, extraordinarily, straight away, so that these good young girls are not required for another ten years to give any further proof of their vocation than that they have already shown during these two months. Then for the others who are already professed, an indulgence, in receiving Communion on the day when the others make their vows. His Eminence will recommend my request and so on the day of the “Te Deum” there will be a lovely celebration for this family”.23

These proposals must certainly have been a great comfort to Mother Rosa’s motherly heart; they attested yet again to the great firmness and self-denial of the spirit and love of her Daughters.

The events had also tested the seriousness of the formation received by the novices and in the houses of the Institute, as well as the efficacy of the Rule as a spiritual guide.

The onslaught of the disease therefore revealed the solid foundations of the Institute of the Daughters of St. Anne. The merit must obviously be attributed to a large extent to the Foundress, although she herself had not personally worked among the cholera victims.

Cholera in Liguria and the heroic self-denial of the Daughters of St. Anne ~ The same generosity was remarked in the religious of Liguria where in those months the cholera broke out and was particularly virulent in Ovada, Sestri Ponente, Sampierdarena and Genoa. The outbreak of the contagion was terrible here, but it killed less people because it spread in more sparsely inhabited areas. Fear, however, threw the citizens into such disarray that in some cases they seemed to lose their common sense. Doctors were even accused of poisoning those stricken with the disease in order to make them die; and this fabrication was so widely believed that in some places, such as Ovada, doctors did not dare to leave their homes for fear of being beaten up.24

The Daughters of St. Anne, summoned by the municipalities, had to redouble their work because the sick wanted to be cared for at home and refused, through prejudice, to be taken to the hospitals for infectious diseases.

Mother Gattorno sent many religious from Piacenza to help in the various places affected: In Genoa they were at the beck and call of the Archiepiscopal Committee and the Red Cross. It must be admitted that the sisters sometimes went singly to the sick, for they were so much in demand. The cases were serious. “We hope that the Lord will not let his hand weigh too heavily on this poor town”, the superior of Sestri wrote to the Mother, “those we have nursed so far have all died; there were even some lightening cases. The newspapers only report half of them, so as not to frighten people”.25 In the dramatic circumstances of Liguria, the Daughters of St. Anne were also distinguishing themselves by their conduct. A local gentleman wrote to Mother Gattorno: “All those who were sworn enemies of the nuns have been forced, on this occasion, to admire them and to praise the acts of heroic self-denial of these sisters, true angels on earth for the poor sick! The whole populace is truly edified”.26

The Mother would have liked them to continue their work in permanent charitable institutions because the cholera left many orphans in a wretched plight, but the circumstances and unwillingness of the local authorities did not permit her to set them up.

Another victim of love ~ Exactly two years later, the Asian disease made another appearance in the South of Italy. In the Naples region it caused widespread bereavements and struck with its usual violence. Just as they had been two years earlier, the Daughters of St. Anne were on the field of pain, hastening from the houses in Naples and from the most distant houses in the peninsula; large groups also arrived from Piacenza and Rome. God was pleased to pluck a heroic flower of charity from precisely among these. A young novice, Sr. Anna Illuminata, one of the group of eight sisters whom the Mother sent to Resina, near Naples, was smitten with the disease while nursing cholera victims on the evening of 2 September 1887, and was rapidly brought to death’s door. She was only 16 years old. A native of the province of Siena, she had spent some time as a postulant in the house of the Daughters of St. Anne in that city; she had then been clothed in Rome and begun her novitiate there.

With the outbreak of cholera in the Neapolitan region, she entreated Mother Gattorno so insistently to be sent to help the stricken, that the Foundress, seeing God’s call in her determination, felt inspired to grant her wish. Therefore Sr. Anna Illuminata left Rome and arrived in Resina on 17 August with her heroic companions. There was no hardship, poverty or risk of contagion that she did not face generously and calmly to help the suffering. Having seen two of her sisters, Sr. Anna Degna and Sr. Anna Sofia, succumb to the disease, she almost envied them. One evening, although somewhat unwell, she took a little refreshment and returned to the sick; but almost immediately she developed the terrible disease: taken back to the house, she rapidly approached her end. Her sufferings were unspeakable, yet she said she was happy to die while doing her duty, hoping that her sacrifice would obtain from the Lord an end to the scourge in Resina once and for all. She died on the morning of 3 September, and a few days later the cholera vanished from Resina.27

Cardinal Sanfelice arrived from Naples immediately and blessed the body, and in the presence of the national authorities, among the general excitement, exalted this young sister, praising the love of Christ who had once again wrought miracles of heroic self-giving.28

The Mother replied to the Mayor of Resina, who had written to her expressing his deep sorrow for what had happened and promising a commemorative stone slab, thanking him humbly and exalting the sacrifice of charity.

“It is beautiful”, she said, “to die on the field of charity and that daughter who departed from life while fulfilling her mission is blessed! She will now be in heaven enjoying the reward for her sacrifice, and up there she will pray for Resina, to which she dedicated one of her last thoughts. She died a martyr to duty, imploring from God the grace to be the last victim of the fatal illness; and may the Lord hear her prayer and preserve this excellent population from worse evil”.29

Cholera in Sicily ~ As for Sicily, which had remained immune from contagion in 1884, in 1887 all its regions were invaded by cholera, while at the same time the disease was raging in Naples.

Messina was the city most harshly struck from the very start; Cardinal Celesia, Archbishop of Palermo, immediately turned to Mother Gattorno to have Daughters of St. Anne at his disposal and, in accordance with the Foundress’ wishes, they generously devoted themselves to caring for the sick and the orphans. Sr. Anna Battistina Bertuzzi, provincial of Palermo, stood out among the other sisters in those terrible days; she was a wise and indefatigable organizer in that mobilization of charity which once again demonstrated the Institute’s high caliber.

“Yesterday evening [12 September] we arrived in Messina”, Sr. Anna Battistina wrote, “What are sorry spectacle! Not a house, not a shop open […]. No food was to be found, and we had eaten nothing since morning. Certain that His Lordship the Archbishop would help us, we went to his house and as soon as we had told him we had nothing to eat, he provided us with bread and other things”.30

So many sick persons were taken to the pesthouse that the sisters had to lift the dead from their beds as soon as they had expired and lay them on the ground to make room for the new patients. How many died before they even reached the hospital! Because of the common people’s superstitious ignorance, the sisters sometimes encountered serious difficulties in their generous service but they never shirked it. In many places, they were slandered and held to be Government spies and poisoners. In Palermo, sent by the mayor himself to look after a man smitten with cholera in Vicolo Giliberti, they saw a group approaching them with evil intentions, whistling and shouting threateningly; to reach the sick man, they had to turn to the police for help. At first he gave them a cordial welcome, but then, goaded on by some superstitious people who accused the nuns of spreading poison, he leaped in fury from his bed and threw himself upon the sisters. It took some doing to extricate them from his furious attacks and usher them to safety.31

God specially protected those wonderful daughters of Rosa Gattorno: no sister in Sicily caught the disease. A chorus of grateful praise was sung by the newspapers in every region, exalting the heroic work of the Daughters of St. Anne. The Mother received moving letters from everywhere, attesting to the splendid work of her religious.

In Messina they were put in charge of the orphanage for the children orphaned and abandoned after the cholera.

Christ’s love made tangible ~ “Blessed be God”, Archbishop Guarino wrote to the Mother. “These Daughters of yours, led by their distinguished superior, are truly the love of Jesus Christ made tangible. Oh, may God preserve and bless them! I see them everywhere, steady, prompt, hardworking, serene. How dear they are! Their virtue must be immense. How is it possible not to love them and bless them in the Lord in the depths of one’s heart? Even the common people, who are not much concerned with God, admire their self-denial and charity, their cheerfulness at work […]. Rejoice in them, Mother, just as I wholeheartedly rejoice, especially since the whole city appreciates and reveres them…”.32

“Rejoice in them, Mother!”. After so many storms, this horizon inflamed with love must have flooded Rosa Gattorno’s heart with joy. The Institute had been born for this purpose and she had deeply suffered for this ideal; out of the blue these epidemics had come to show what masterpieces of grace God had made of her religious and what beneficent strength lived in that Institute of humble and, perhaps to some, all too modest appearance. Mother Gattorno did not have an elegant style for expressing her thoughts; but these facts spoke to the Church and to the world better than any fine literary page. Many understood this, and Cardinal Alimonda wrote these warm words: “I have gloried in being Protector of so highly charitable an Institute; I have also had to become convinced that the Spirit of the Lord truly hovers over the Daughters of St. Anne”33.
