(1886-1900) Request from the Italian Ministry of Foreign Affairs — Departure of the first four religious for Assab — Mission in East Africa — Mother Rosa’s epistolary relationship — The opening of a house in Asmara — Italo-Abyssinian War and nursing in the military hospitals — Dramatic episode in Keren — Service in the hospital of Massawa — Mother Rosa’s last letters — Bishop Chidanè Mariam Cassà: a fruit of the Catholic mission in Eritrea.

Request from the Italian Ministry of Foreign Affairs ~The enthusiasm for the missions in Latin America did not prevent Mother Rosa from extending her gaze to other lands where her humanitarian work would be able to open the door to the proclamation of Christ’s message, with the certainty that the forces of the Institute would increase at the same rate as its generous dedication to the service of God.

She had set up the Generalate in Rome two years before: until 1885, the small Roman houses of the Daughters of St. Anne, which were opened thirteen years earlier, had been enfolded in the silence of their work, the more precious the humbler it was; but the building in the Via Merulana attracted the attention of the civil authorities because of the size of its structures, large by the standards of the time, and because the Institute had developed in a period of secularization and anti-clericalism hostile to religious orders. Furthermore, it is likely that the Mother’s brother, Federico Gattorno, who had many contacts with Government representatives, had often spoken to them of the Daughters of St. Anne, to smooth out difficulties or to obtain some favor or other for their works.

So it was that on 5 September 1885 Mother Rosa received a request from the Italian Ministry of Foreign Affairs for two sisters for the hospital in Assab.1 This was the first time Italy had requested a women’s congregation in its new colony.

Assab, far south on the Danakil coast, had been a modest place during the previous century and only had specific interest as a base for the shipping lines. In fact, on 15 November 1869, a Vincentian missionary, Prof. Giuseppe Sapeto, was able to purchase the small town and bay of the same name for a modest sum from Sultan Raheita, on behalf of the Società Rubattino which had a coal warehouse built there for its ships.

Later the possession was enlarged with new purchases, in 1882 ownership of the territory passed to the Italian Government which declared it a colony of the Kingdom [of Italy].

Several political upheavals stirred up in the Sudan by the Mahdi, repeated acts of violence by the natives against Italian citizens such as the massacre of Giuletti’s expedition (1881) and of Bianchi’s (1883) impelled Italy, in full agreement with the European powers, to occupy Massawa. It established a military landing place there in 1885, declaring its own sovereignty instead of that of Egypt.

Wishing to give a preliminary military and civil order to that first nucleus in colonial territory, the Royal Government therefore also decreed a mission settlement with Italian personnel, distancing the Priests of the Congregation of the Mission who were French, and the Daughters of Charity who had been working there for some time. It therefore turned to the Daughters of St. Anne.

Departure of the first four religious for Assab ~ the negotiations with Mother Rosa lasted from September 1885 to October 1886. The difficulties in coming to an agreement were due to the Mother’s firm insistence on all the guarantees for her daughters’ religious life; in fact the Government had limited its requests to only two sisters and did not want to admit men religious. But the Foundress was determined to establish a community of at least four sisters, and on condition that there would be priests for their spiritual guidance.

These very proper reasons were finally recognized, and it was agreed that the new mission should have a first nucleus of four Daughters of St. Anne and two Capuchin Fathers.

The four religious, led by Sr. Anna del Conforto Stassi, prepared for their departure towards mid-November 1886. The Mother herself presented them at an audience to Leo XIII who blessed them warmly and encouraged them in their arduous mission; they left for Naples, from where they sailed for Massawa on 20 November with the two Capuchin Fathers2. They arrived on 4 December. Here they stayed a week, with the Daughters of Charity; then they continued on the steamship, the “Palestina”, landing at Assab the following day. They were welcomed courteously by the Commandant Luigi De Simoni and Dr. Angelo De Martino, who was in charge of the modest military and civil hospital.

On that remote shore of the Red Sea, the climate is torrid and at that time the area was totally uninhabited; except for a few colonial dwellings and the occasional native hut, there was nothing but a lonely expanse of bare, stony land, with practically no vegetation. The sea flows into a wide bay strewn with small islands; the abundant corals along the coast change its shape constantly, making navigation perilous.

If Italy was attempting to achieve its expansionist dreams on those arid shores, the Daughters of St. Anne were motivated by concern for the kingdom of God, certain that miracles of the Lord’s power and grace would be accomplished.

The spiritual formation received from Mother Rosa and her frequent exhortations only opened up these horizons.

The four religious, since they did not yet have a house of their own, lived together for eight months in a room of the military building for convalescents, adapting themselves to the local customs. The broad bay of Assab with its archipelago extended before their eyes, imbued with a solemn calm beneath the relentless sun; it was furrowed by little native boats; European ships seldom passed, and when they did they sped past on the horizon on the important communication routes bound for India and the Far East.

Therefore without the distraction of travelers or cosmopolitan traders, those sisters worked with admirable dedication and did not scorn even the humblest and most exhausting of tasks to alleviate the wretchedness and suffering of the local people for whom they had come; to cultivate their minds and win their hearts was their one desire, despite the enormous hardship of isolation and the lack of necessities.

“The sufferings and deprivations suffered in that period”, said Sr. Anna del Conforto Stassi, “were unspeakable”.3

The Government entrusted the new elementary schools to them; at first a Capuchin Father helped them with the boys’ classes, but later, ill with malaria, he had to go, leaving the sisters with full responsibility for the boys.

The fascination of love which penetrates souls in mysterious ways soon overcame the natural mistrust of the little black children: the sisters were teachers, nurses and tender mothers to them. They were always unruffled and friendly, giving them clothes or sweets whenever they had them; with smiles and the complicity of forgiveness, they allayed all suspicion.

The children not only went to school, but also at times and on days when they should have been at home, they would run to the sisters and chatter to them for hours, playing and listening. The mothers, obviously, came with their children. These simple and naturally gentle women soon began to confide in the religious and ask their advice, and always left comforted by a kind word and often with some material help.

Cautious and respectful in their apostolate, the Daughters of St. Anne took care to avoid any attitude of prevarication and not to wound the religious sensitivity of the local people who however, soon felt the fascination of their hard work, gratuitous purity and composed and genuine piety. When the sisters were in chapel praying, the children and their mothers found a way in and would wait close to them, in silent wonder, enchanted by the mystery and recollection which raises souls to God. This was the path on which Mother Rosa had formed her sisters, making them true missionaries.4

The first news the Mother received from Africa filled her with joy, because in their first serious hardships her daughters were truly exemplary in their conduct, motivated by the true spirit which is an incentive to total sacrifice for the salvation of souls and knows how to wait with generous forbearance.

Mission in East Africa ~ Very soon she had to send other groups of sisters, because the needs were becoming greater and more pressing.

In fact, the young colony was constantly caught up in war. In January 1887, barely a month after the first sisters’ arrival, attacks against Massawa and the slaughter of De Cristoforis’ troops on the Dogali plateau put paid to all dreams of conquest and gave rise to deep disappointment in Italian hearts; it must also have caused a shiver of fear in the young missionaries of Assab, although they were distant from the scene of the fighting. However, far from being upset, they generously and promptly set about helping the injured and the sick in the hospitals.

There was already a functional civil hospital in Assab to which they contributed their charitable work. The new arrivals from Italy were employed in places closer to Massawa; so it was that the mission of the Daughters of St. Anne in Italian East Africa began to develop, rapidly expanding towards the Eritrean plateaux and with rigorous hard work, following the destiny of the colony until Italian domination was established in Ethiopia. If it always cost them a great effort to sow the seed, they reaped immense joy in harvesting the fruits from the earliest times.

At the end of their first year of work in Assab they were able to baptize many children, and some were soon admitted to Confession and Communion.

They also did so excellently in their school examinations that General Genè, moved by admiration, sent a report to the ministry, full of praise for the Daughters of St. Anne who were the first to bring a breath of Italian culture to the colony.5

After attending a school entertainment the following year, the captain and doctor, De Martino, who was in charge of health-care services in Assab, wrote enthusiastically to the superior: “Well done, and then a thousand times well done for the wonderful display this morning! Keep up the work, doing honor to our religion and to our beloved Italy”, and he added an ostentatious donation for the mission.

“The Daughters of St. Anne” the new civil commissioner of Assab wrote to Mgr. Granito di Belmonte, “are always full of charity for everyone, and they do honor to themselves and to their Institute”.6

As well as these official voices, the words of humble hearts testified warm gratitude to Mother Rosa for the splendid charity of her sisters during particularly sad times. One young Italian lady, Carolina Berti, with her husband in Assab, had suffered the agony of seeing their ten-month old child die. The sisters spontaneously visited her for the last attentions to the tiny dead body and then carried it to their church and the cemetery down a long and very bad road in a howling gale.

“May our good Lord bless you, Reverend Mother and your daughters”, wrote this lady in her terrible grief, “and may it please him to crown your holy and beneficial Institution with his blessings”.7

Their charity was not limited to the hospital and schools. Unfortunately, slavery and the abandonment of infants was also common on the Eritrean coast.

Sr. Anna del Conforto Stassi took in twenty-six children over a short period, some of whom had been redeemed from slavery, and some dumped by a steamer from Massawa. Those sisters certainly had impressed upon their hearts the story of each one of the little creatures, which at times reached the peaks of tragedy and at others was accompanied by happy circumstances. Sr. Anna Pierina Della Valle tells: “On 29 June [1892] an unnatural Abyssinian mother brought to our door a boy of about three years old and a little girl of about six; she left them here and was never seen again. The boy was baptized on the feast of St. Anne, on an occasion when the bishop was visiting, and he gave him the name of Peter…”.8

Sr. Anna Gerarda Canovi wrote a whole volume of these tales; we mention only one. Although it concerns an event that occurred a few years later on the Asmara plateau, it nonetheless shows the character of those adventures: “One day we were all at lunch: I heard the bell ringing loudly, and ran to the door; I was presented with a closed basket, like those used here to carry Abyssinian dishes [as gifts]. On their most important feasts, the sisters also take them as a very special present, so that to refuse one would be an insult. In offering me the basket, the person carrying it said: “This is a present for you”. I ran to the sisters to give them what was supposed to be a gift; I opened it, and seeing [something] moving, I undid a string… How surprised we were! Inside was a baby boy, as long as the palm of a hand! We all burst out laughing! Some kind of dish! I returned to the door to find out who had given us that beautiful present […]. Actually it was lovelier than the special dish, it was a person! I had him baptized and gave him the name of Luigi since that day was the feast of St Aloysius Gonzaga. After fourteen days he died: he is in heaven!”.9

In almost all the houses in Africa, things often ended like this, with Baptism, but they began very differently.

It should not be supposed that the toils of the first missionaries always brought them gratification.

Mother Rosa had prepared them for the Cross of Christ and the joys which are found in it, so in ending her letters to them she always finished by saying: “I embrace you closely in your beloved Crucified Christ”.

And the sufferings that tempered the virtue of those generous Daughters of St. Anne were truly hard to bear.

In Assab, since the Capuchin father who helped them had soon departed, as has been said, they were left without any kind of religious comfort. To those sisters who found their strength in Jesus alone, the pain of being deprived of holy communion for months on end was excruciating;10 and once, when the Bishop of Aden chanced to pass by that house, celebrating St. Anne there, he was amazed that the little girls they had taken in had not been able to go to Confession for eight months because the new missionary had not wished or had not been able to look after them. Indeed, a certain incomprehension of the circumstances and sometimes strange prejudices against the sisters gave rise to dissent rather than to charitable unity of intentions in that country.

Mother Rosa’s epistolary relationship ~ These spiritual hardships, together with the tough material conditions and extreme poverty, must have harshly tried the virtue of those missionaries; but Mother Rosa always gave them support and courage. Her great passion for the Cross was echoed in her letters together with a most tender motherly feeling. Reference has already often been made to the fact that she wrote the letters for her distant daughters herself and frequently. Glancing through the list of those she sent to Africa from the beginning of the mission to the end of her life, it is astonishing; from the letters preserved (since the sisters themselves attest that many were lost)11, we see that she even wrote directly to the superiors five times a month, with the express aim of comforting and encouraging them. When one thinks that she did the same for the missionaries in America and for the many superiors in Italy even during visitations of the houses, one wonders where she found the strength for so much work.

Yet these letters were always clearly thought out, and so full of affection!

“Well done! Your zeal, your efforts, will crown you with precious pearls”.12

“May God keep you for thousands of years for the good of Africa!”.13

“I hear with pleasure that God’s will is the only motive of your action: be steadfast and always with Jesus and for him alone!”.14

“May God bless your work and your efforts and accept them as expiation for my [sins]”.15

Sometimes the deep sorrow of being unable to supply all the necessary candidates for the needs of the mission prompted heartbreaking tones: “My God, what sorrow not to have sisters! […]. I wish I were ten years younger and strong; I would come and be your cobbler! But I am getting on in years and [am] always rather unwell!”.16

However, even more than the desire to console, concern is expressed in these letters for the safety of the religious among the dangers of their apostolate, and from afar she saw and thought about them better than those who were in their midst.

The opening of a house in Asmara — Since the Government of the colony then insisted on other houses being founded in Massawa and on the Asmara plateau, the Mother accepted as soon as she could, although she had to bear the full cost of those new stations. In 1894, the house of Asmara was opened and in 1895, that of Keren and the two in Massawa. However the provisions made by the local person in charge were not sufficiently enlightened, which is why the missionaries’ work was sometimes dispersive and frustrated.

Furthermore, the sisters in the villages lived too far apart and did not have much protection, which was a source of worry to the Mother. “I hear that you are leaving two sisters in each house […]. What will happen? In those lands, my God! If something should occur, what would be the result? Be careful for pity’s sake: be sure you reinforce everything soundly […]. Check that there is no cause for danger: I assure you I am in the greatest distress…”.17

She was alert to these risks and even asked for information from persons who had nothing to do with the Institute. Indeed, a month later, she repeated her warning to the same superior: “Tell me something about your situation. A highly placed person disapproves of our sisters being scattered about here and there: enough, they are saying that there are too few in each house”.18

To satisfy the great need for sisters on the mission, she would often send small groups chosen from the different houses, but mostly she preferred to send the ones who had lived for some time under her supervision in Rome. She wanted them to be robust in mind and body and therefore still young, saying that they would have to grow old on the mission; but she never succumbed to the temptation of removing someone even from her second year in the novitiate. “How troubled I am not to have sisters! It really is a scourge, because the novitiates are full but they are not ready. You know that I cannot take the novices out of them”.19

With the same wise firmness she dampened the unbridled enthusiasm of those on the mission who let themselves be carried away by the over-enjoyable undertakings. The lovely conquests to the faith which crowned the missionaries’ work had encouraged the visitor to accept young African girls in the Institute: it did not seem true to the Mother that it could be possible to pluck such fresh and promising flowers on the African continent in so short a time. Times were not yet ripe for this and everything had to be done with the proper discernment.

For Africa too, she deprived herself of candidates who could have worked most fruitfully in Italy: in 1895 she sent a sister very good at playing the piano, the harp and the organ; she recommended her to the special care of the superior, because she was rather too forthcoming in her dealings with everyone, because of her naïve temperament. And she repeated this advice many times. The good superior, properly guided, behaved in an edifying way and did much good. Two years later she died in Massawa and Mother Rosa, hearing of this, made this sublime comment: “I hear of the death of Sr. Anna Doralice; how consoling it is to give her up to Jesus! He gave her to us and we give her back to him.”20

These words call to mind Jesus’ prayer to the Father: “They were yours and you gave them to me, and they have kept your word […] I kept those you had given me true to your name” (Jn 17:6; 12).

She was not only concerned for the good of her religious but used all the means she knew to be most effective and did not spare anyone reprimands when they deserved them, even her most beloved superiors, although she poured balm upon the open wound. “I do not intend to cause any pain to the Daughters of St. Anne”, she replied on this subject to a superior, “indeed, I try to do all I can to relieve them. Not only do I forgive you, but I fervently desire to relieve you and to assure you of my great affection. Be at peace and do not fear. May God comfort you, may the Holy Mother lavish her graces upon you”.

However, a year later she replaced this superior with a young religious sent from Rome, who in her long years of government gave the Mother all kinds of consolations.

In addition to these obvious difficulties when the mission was beginning to put down roots in Africa, a serious problem was caused by the different nationality of the clergy who had been entrusted with the evangelization of East Africa until then. The French Priests of the Congregation of the Mission and the Daughters of Charity who had occupied the principal areas in the territory for many years did not please the new Government which, however, respected the rights of ecclesiastical jurisdiction; but since in these circumstances the religious spirit was not always superior to natural feeling, every now and then friction and misunderstandings which hindered the zealous quest for the good of souls were unavoidable. The Daughters of St. Anne had much to put up with also because of this, finding themselves in a cross-fire: but they adopted the prudent attitude of the humble, awaiting the hour of God. They therefore remained calm under the Mother’s guidance when in 1892 they were prevented by the Bishop of Massawa from complying with the request to open a house in Asmara made by the Governor of the colony.

In 1894 Leo XIII established the Prefecture Apostolic of Eritrea, entrusting it to the Capuchin, Fr. Michele da Carbonara; after that, the field was free for the expansion of the Daughters of St. Anne.

General Baratieri wrote this letter to the Mother, full of praise, in September that year: “I am always glad when I am granted to render a service to the sisters ‘Daughters of St. Anne’, out of natural sympathy as well as for the good they do in the colony. Therefore I not only willingly welcome them to Asmara, but I have already arranged for the Reverend Fr. Bonomi to prepare temporary lodgings for them and I am prepared to give up a wing of my villa to house the worthy sisters of religion and humanity. Now, thanks to the decisions of His Holiness, I will be able to be more useful to your devout Institution. I gladly take this occasion to express to you the sentiments of my special esteem, Most devotedly, G. Baratieri”.21

Italo-Abyssinian War and nursing in the military hospitals ~ Everything seemed to be going well when the Italo-Abyssinian War suddenly broke out in 1896. It had been talked about vaguely for several weeks. Mother Rosa, despite the first rumors, did not hesitate to send a group of sisters to Africa destined to form the new community in Keren, but her motherly heart was fearful.

“Here we are in great trepidation”, she wrote on 13 January, “because nothing is known about the war. What will happen, my God? It is such a dreadful thing! I would like to be younger or at least stronger, so that I could go and see!”.22

In February, hostilities began and the outcome of that very short conflict is well known.

Three Daughters of St. Anne and two local women from Asmara, sent by the Prefect Apostolic, Fr. Michele da Carbonara, went with a Capuchin Father to the battlefield to aid the wounded; but after a three-day journey, since the defeat had occurred, they had to return to Asmara, dedicating themselves with the others to nursing in the hospital overflowing with wounded men.

Under Fr. Michele’s direction, the sisters of the various houses were wisely employed meeting the urgent needs caused by the war; they suspended the children’s instruction and thus divided themselves between the military hospitals and helping the soldiers and officials on the various battlefields. Recalling the work of those tragic days, at a conference Fr. Michele da Carbonara gave in Naples at the end of 1898, he said: “I said that the Daughters of St. Anne were working side by side with the Capuchins, my confreres. What do these sisters do? What have they done?[…]. When there was a large number of the sick and war-wounded, the sisters stopped teaching the children. I delegated thirty of them to the infirmaries and military hospitals so that they could bring comfort to those unfortunates and thereby to their families. Twenty-five of them cared for the soldiers and officers on the various battlefields and assisted them day and night, materially and morally. When they were no longer needed, they returned to their houses to resume the care of their little orphan girls and the new-born babies entrusted to them…”.

Dramatic episode in Keren — In Keren, where the house had been open for three weeks and had about thirty children in care, some dramatic hours were passed. The Royal Commissioner, having arrived at his post on 1 March, arranged that in the case of danger the sisters should take shelter in the fortress, leaving the children in the enemies’ hands. The superior, Sr. Anna Gerarda Canovi, protested that she would rather die with them and repeated her protest with another two sisters, arousing admiration in the Commissioner and the missionary priest with him. As God pleased, they spent the turbulent night in the din of the retreating vanguards and in the morning they heard that all danger was over.

On the other hand, another small community which had been established a few days earlier in Saganeiti was forced to flee to the fortress of Adi Ugri, where they were given a separate tent and treated with proper regard by the soldiers. When Mother Gattorno heard this news, she was very worried and immediately expressed to the visitor, Sr. Anna Pierina Della Valle, her great distress at her sisters’ serious plight of hardship and danger. “I was not at all happy about the news of our sisters. How can it be that they have moved from Saganeiti to Adi Ugri? Whatever happens I hope for the best: but what will they be able to do in that fortress?” A week later, learning that they had returned to the house, she showed her relief: “It was extremely consoling to me to know that the sisters are no longer in the fortress of Adi Ugri…”.23

In the meantime, she sent out other religious and was always ready to send new ones, even in answer to a telegraphic request, to meet the great needs of that difficult moment. Her correspondence in that period is filled with expressions of human compassion for the wounded and dead, but also a splendid greatness of heart that stemmed from the incalculable gift of love.

Service in the hospital of Massawa ~ In her desire to relieve all the hardships, but with the guarantee that all the sisters would preserve their authentic religious spirit, Mother Rosa accepted full responsibility for the hospital in Massawa towards the end of that year, although she had opened other houses in Africa. “So we promised the Government”, she wrote, “that we would always be ready for all the places it requires”.24

Indeed, since the Italian Government had actually expelled the French Missionaries, the Daughters of St. Anne were to replace those religious.

This impulse of Christian generosity was noted by many in Italy, even lay people, who congratulated Francesco Gattorno for his good fortune in having such a sister. He would have liked the newspapers to report on the humanitarian and evangelizing work of the Daughters of St. Anne, as they had publicized the work of the Capuchins; but the Mother energetically opposed any kind of public praise.25

Having survived that painful episode and when normal life was resumed in Eritrea, the Daughters of St. Anne soon asserted themselves in many effective missionary activities.

Above all they had to care for young people. The Prefect Apostolic had huts built and the existing houses enlarged so that boys and girls in various places could enjoy the benefit of education.

The new visitor, Sr. Anna Gerarda Canovi, who acted as superior for the whole mission, was in full harmony with the Mother’s views, so that in every letter she had only words of praise for her. The Mother had sent her to Africa in November 1895, saying to her: “I was not thinking of you at all: but last night I had a dream and the Holy Spirit told me to send you to Africa. Therefore go, and I assure you that you will be happy and will do many things well, and will bless the hour when I was inspired to send you”.26

Three years later, on 7 November, she wrote to her: “You will die in Africa. Ah, poor souls! How happy are you who have sent so many souls to heaven. What a consolation to me!”. These predictions all came true. Sr. Anna Gerarda Canovi always blessed the Lord for having sent her to the mission and she ended her life there. Indeed, after Mother Rosa’s death, in 1904, she was recalled to Italy for several months but was sent back to Africa where she worked for several more years until she died on 27 April 1911.

Sr. Anna Gerarda always had comforting apostolic news to send the Mother; it is therefore not surprising that the Mother told her in every letter that she was very pleased and felt as it were, soothed by reading it. “Of course”, she replied to her, “people will marvel at your sacrifice among them […], but sacrifice is the only thing that embellishes our souls and makes them great before the Lord. So here are some more Christian souls. How lucky you are in such a lovely mission!”.27

Many of the sisters had their own dramatic story behind them, like, for example, that of Illuminata. One night a group of Abyssinians surrounded the orphanage of the Daughters of St. Anne in Keren making an enormous din. They were looking for a girl who had run away on the eve of her wedding. They roused all the children, but did not find the fugitive; so they left. When silence had fallen, the religious were surprised to see the girl emerging from the boiler in the laundry. Having secretly crept into the house, she had hidden there without their knowledge. She protested that she did not want to hear about marriage. With the help of the Royal Commissioner, she was protected from her relatives and stayed with the sisters. Three months later, she died of a sudden rapid consumption.

Mother Rosa’s last letters ~ The long series of similar episodes which Sr. Anna Gerarda recounts in two large volumes could enliven her correspondence with the Mother, but her heart was consoled above all by the beautiful testimonies which showed the edifying behavior of the missionary sisters.

This was a solace to the Mother, a fruit of the diligent and most attentive care she had given to forging the personalities of these creatures, in accompanying them even from afar, in sustaining them with every proof of unparalleled motherly goodness. We are moved to read: “Just a line, because I [am] quite ill; but I fear that you might be upset to see a different handwriting…”.28

Until the end she wanted to be present through the unmistakable sign of her handwriting to foster good in her daughters, wherever they might be. She heroically continued this effort even on her deathbed.

The words cited were written eight days before she died. The Mother’s last letter to Sr. Anna Gerarda is dated 30 April, and it is the only one she dictated, for she was then no longer able to write herself. It has the tenderness and solemnity of a spiritual testament: “Your lovely letter gave me immense pleasure and I assure you that I only give up my pen with sorrow so that you may have an answer; but I am forced to do so because I am acutely swollen and breathless, and I am reduced to a sorry state. Pray for pity’s sake and have prayers said for me, only a miracle can keep me a little longer among you, beloved daughters. I recommend to you the holy observance of the Rule: the superior must be the beacon of all those she guides to the safe haven […]. If you do not receive a letter from me on Holy Thursday, you are receiving it today, and in it I repeat what I suggested to you in the Heart of beloved Jesus. Attract a lovely number of souls to his beautiful Heart and you will see that in this life and in the next you will be rewarded. Look after the interests of your heavenly Bridegroom, win souls for him! Courage therefore, and holy competition with your beloved sisters to advance in virtues. Give all the community my greetings. Always do good…”.29

The brilliant light of the Mother was still shining with the splendid gleams of faith with which she wanted to brighten the way of salvation for many souls, especially her daughters. Her mind set on lasting things and overwhelmed by the sublime mystery of the Redemption, she still faced the challenge of death so that her self-immolation might be total. Difficulties were shattered before that indomitable faith which knew only the strength of God. Otherwise her courage, her constancy and her freshness amid the whirl of every care could not be explained: “Look after the interests of your heavenly Bridegroom: win souls for him!”. Her last words to a missionary superior expressed the dream of her whole life.

Bishop Chidanè Mariam Cassà: a fruit of the Catholic Mission in Eritrea ~ On 29 April 1935 His Majesty the King of Italy conferred the Gold Medal and the Diploma of Merit on the Daughters of St. Anne “for uncommon services in favor of education in the Italian Colonies”.

But there is a still more flattering testimony to the missionary work begun by Mother Rosa in Africa. Bishop Chidanè-Mariam Cassà, the finest flower of the Catholic Mission in Eritrea, referring to those now distant years, wrote: “Almost fifty per cent of the young people who make up, it may well be said, the new generation of Catholics have passed through the schools of the Daughters of St. Anne. In these schools not only are the first rudiments of knowledge imparted, as one would naturally think; but above all and principally the seeds of religious formation are planted in the souls of the young.

Together with intellectual formation, given through the assiduous and fruitful teaching of the catechism, the virtues too are sown in the tender hearts of the children. I remember very well, from personal experience, the well-suited religion lessons the sisters gave, with a method so adapted to that age that all those truths of our holy religion were indelibly impressed on our souls, so that we remember them to this day […]. And it should be borne in mind that this instruction was not given exclusively to Catholic infants and children, but to all those who […], eager to learn the Italian language, flocked in great numbers to their schools […]. It was above all the Catholic boys who benefited from these schools, many of whom went on from them to those of the Seminary, so that those schools became the seedbed of young Levites, a nursery of holy vocations. And the dear Sisters, the Daughters of St. Anne, may be proud to count many of their former pupils among our priests: they may have the holy pride of having had as their pupil the first native Bishop, the writer of these lines”30.

Mother Rosa and her children ~ St. Paul, writing to the Romans, describes the figure of a disciple of Christ in these words: “through our Lord Jesus Christ, by faith we are judged righteous and at peace with God, since it is by faith and through Jesus that we have entered this state of grace in which we can boast about looking forward to God’s glory. But that is not all we can boast about; we can boast about our sufferings…” (Rm 5:1-3).

Therefore it is not only suffering in itself, but knowing how to accept it as proof of fidelity to Christ which is the hallmark of Christians: then if this lifestyle is unique, both because of the gravity of the tribulation and the spiritual fortitude in bearing it, one has heroism. It seems to us that this heroism truly shines out in Rosa Gattorno.

She knew pain from the day of her marriage, which is generally thought of as the peak of happiness; so all her life was a journey towards Calvary. Here let us pause to consider the sorrowful events in her family life.

We can recompose and, in a certain sense, plumb the depths of this intimate drama in Mother Rosa’s heart through the many letters of her two children which she jealously preserved. From the first of these, written by unsteady childish hands, to the impassioned letters of their more mature years they attest to the demanding efforts and often bitter struggles of a mother highly aware of her mission and more painstaking than ever in her commitments of responsibility.

The serious financial straits in which she had found herself at her husband’s death did not prevent her from wishing to give her children a good boarding-school education; she humbly asked for possible reductions in the fees, she gratefully accepted the help of relatives and friends and with diligent tenderness sought to lighten for her little ones the sacrifice of separation and the difficulty and aridity of life as boarders. For many years she wanted them to be entrusted to people whom she considered suited to training them for the future. Since the Mother was scrupulously strict in never wishing to use even the smallest part of the patrimony of the Institute she founded to meet the needs of her own children, it is easy to understand how she must have lived the intimate conflict created by love and poverty.

Yet, for all this loving, motherly concern, she did not have the corresponding abundance of consolations which parents usually expect; indeed, Rosa had such a large share of sorrows as to be reminiscent of the heroic mother of St. Augustine.

Alessandro’s adolescence ~ Alessandro, the only male child left to her, had a very sensitive temperament which at first was oriented to goodness. He was born on 28 October 1855; when he was nine years old he went to boarding-school where he stayed until he was eighteen, first in Genoa and then in Savona, at Mondovì, and lastly in Novi Ligure. He made gradual progress in his studies and grew up with a good religious formation. He began classical studies rather late and had still not completed them by the time he was eighteen, since we find him at that age in his fourth year of secondary studies.

There was a constant, deep desire for his mother’s presence in this lively boy who, to please her, applied himself to his studies as best he could. At the bottom of his letters, the superiors of the Institute of the Sons of the Immaculate in Genoa and of the high school of the Congregation of the Priests of the Mission in Savona often added various pieces of information: there was never a complaint; indeed there are allusions to the boy’s piety and good conduct, and his school reports confirm this. In fact Alessandro could justifiably sign every letter he wrote to his mother: “your most affectionate and obedient son”.

The reward for this goodness, which was still in evidence when he was fifteen, was his mother’s visits and small presents; he was particularly pleased when he was given some little birds which he enjoyed training in a way of his own. All in all, he was a good boy. But heaven help anyone who said anything disapproving about his mother! One day, a superior unwisely came out with these words: “Your mother takes so long to pay. If she does not have the money to keep you at boarding school why don’t you leave?” That was all it took: the boy wrote secretly to his mother that he did not want to stay in that school precisely and only for this reason: “What do you think? I believe that you will agree with me that the food I eat is so toxic that it poisons my blood. So I again beg you to take me away because I can’t resist any longer, and one day or another, if God doesn’t help me, I will take the matter into my own hands”.1

This was the first time that the boy had realized how poor his mother was; he counted her sacrifices and could no longer accept that she be humiliated for them. After the holidays which he spent in Piacenza staying with Onorata Colli, therefore close to his mother, he agreed to go to another institution but a modest one, as was the episcopal college of Mondovì where most of the students came from peasant families.

For Christmas, upon receiving a parcel of delightful presents from his mother he wrote with surprising sentiments: “Finally I am all yours, O dear mother. I did not write to you sooner because we had a spiritual retreat for three days, during which I prayed the Lord for you and for my sister. I received the parcel in which I found what I had never expected. You sent me marvellous and luxurious things, the coffee machine, oranges that I regret you gave up in order to send to me; so, I say that I too am poor as the Infant Jesus who this morning came to make me a gracious visit and comforted me a lot, and I even prayed to him fervently to take me from this life of torment to his holy city of heavenly joy where my father and my brother are; with time I hope that with his divine help all five of us up there will be united for ever. Tell my sister to pray for me and I am sure that she will do so: I do not even ask you, because I rather think that you do nothing else…”.2

His highly sensitive adolescent heart reverberates with such a lofty resonance, deeply in harmony with his mother’s, but it is impossible not to see at the same time that it was veiled in a deep sadness about life, which did not seem to be at all happy for him.

Alessandro also tried to do his best at his school work and told his mother of his well-founded hope of deserving a silver medal, adding, “thus I hope I shall be able to repay all the sacrifices that you have made for me so far”.3 Indeed, at Easter that year, the third-year high school student had a magnificent school report.

Although at first it seemed that the boy had settled well, he was unable to resist for long; towards the end of that year, feeling deeply hurt because one of his companions had labelled him “the son of a nun”, he asked his mother to send him somewhere else, or better, to let him come back to her.4

Her son’s deep unhappiness must have had repercussions in his mother, but more than anything, she must have been wounded by his lack of sensitivity and understanding of her particular state of life. Alessandro was so good as to feel almost repentant for having told his mother about his unhappiness; shortly afterwards he actually wrote to her: “Do as you see fit: I can look after myself and do not be anxious about me […]. Moreover, if God suffered so much for me it is right that I should have my share of suffering too”.5

The first signs of deep disturbance ~ So the following year he was sent to the boarding-school of San Giorgio in Novi Ligure. But here his character radically changed and his health also declined. He had a clash with some teacher and joined the perilous and absorbing play of loose-living companions. At the age of seventeen he felt adult and autonomous, he no longer frequented his own age group and distanced himself from the healthy principles of his mother’s upbringing.

The Mother immediately realized this change from the style of his letters and the deterioration in his studies. She did not spare herself in visiting him, writing to him, giving him advice and even forbidding him from seeing certain people; but unfortunately his character which was formerly so compliant, was now closed to the calls of goodness.

He spent a year without any visible catastrophes, but without a thought that reflected his former ideals. Mother Rosa was then busier than ever traveling for her foundations and for the approval of the Rule, but she kept up a continuous correspondence with her son.

Nevertheless, although he maintained a deep intimacy with his mother, he obviously felt frustrated in his love for her and no longer managed to understand the deep motivation which spurred her to devote herself to the great works of charity now foreign to his life; which is why there are sometimes sharp words in his letters.6

There are traces of the rebukes and advice she received in this correspondence, as well as of the improprieties or accusations of which she had been made the object; but a letter written in spring 1873, which betrayed the fragility and deep disturbance of the young man who was already beguiled by unhealthy affections and even troubled by suicidal thoughts, must have seriously preoccupied the Mother, although he added: “Something suddenly happened, through the grace of God, who held me back with his hand and I thank him with all my heart”.7

Alessandro was entering his eighteenth year, but the transparency of his childhood and early adolescence was more and more clouded. At the end of the school year 1873, something unfortunate must perhaps have happened to him, because in a letter to his mother he told her that he was in rather a bad way, that he had broken a rib and damaged a lung, so that he had been in bed for a week and was supposed to stay there for forty days; the doctor advised him to return to his family. The same letter also once again revealed his attachment to his mother: “I will calmly take anything anyone says against me, but to hear anyone speak badly of my mother or slander her, breaks my heart”.8

The Mother certainly knew from other sources that many calumnies were being spread about her, but she had probably not imagined that what she was doing for the poor and needy was so unjustly condemned at her son’s school, while the sacrifices she had to face to give him a fully human and Christian education were well-known. Were other parents condemned who had placed their sons in that boarding school or in others like it, in accordance with the custom of the time?

Departure and return from America — Since the young man did not want to pursue his classical studies but wished to become involved in business, she took him away from boarding school and settled him with his relatives in Genoa while she sought reliable information in order to find a way for him to learn business activities, and a job.9 But when it seemed certain that a good position had been found for him, Alessandro, who was now almost twenty-one, decided to leave for America with the help of Fr. Accinelli and his uncle Federico.10

He went to Piacenza to take say goodbye to his mother. That was a truly agonizing moment for Mother Rosa, who was particularly worried by the disintegration of the family and the dangers that her rather frail and insecure son might encounter. “Today”, she wrote in her Memorie, “my son, who is leaving for America, came to say farewell to me. The pain I felt at the thought of not seeing him again gave me deep sorrow; but even more agonizing was the thought that in those countries of such depravation he might be lost. And what if he should unfortunately meet with death, where would he go? Because he would certainly die without the comforts of Holy Church and [not] as a good Christian. As it is certain he would forget my God, then I would lose him for an eternity. Oh, what pain! A creature who belongs to me, not to die in the embrace of my God? Must I think that he will be a thorn in the heart of my Good? Oh, what have I done! I cannot bear such pain! Oh my Love, I would see him suffer a thousand deaths, but as a Christian! I said all this weeping profusely” (M 1.2, p. 81).

But suddenly, her tears stopped flowing as a thought flashed through her mind; then she made that solemn promise which she faithfully kept as we shall see later: “My Love, yes, I promise you that if I have the chance to see him die a Christian, I will not shed a tear, but I will absorb the pain I receive from your most holy hands and [be] happy to be able to deliver him up, so that he will be yours for eternity” (M 1.2, p. 82).

On 5 December 1875 Alessandro sent a greeting to his mother from Cadiz; on 4 February he wrote her a note from Buenos Aires, saying he was pleased to be earning his living with his own efforts.

But far from his homeland and the presence of his loved ones, poor Alessandro felt he was abandoned by everyone and suffered deeply, especially because, it seems, he had to be separated from a cousin of his who had been his companion at work in that foreign city.

But even there the heartfelt words of his mother reached him in his bewilderment, awakening the thought of what was most essential: eternal salvation.

“You see that we are all thinking about you, it is not, as you say, that we have forgotten you. No, no! Ah, my God, if you could see how many prayers this poor mother is saying, you could certainly not have a single thought that would disturb you or which might suggest that I do not think of you. Ah, my dear son, one day you will see that I have thought of you […]. So take care of yourself and realize that everything on this earth comes to an end and we are left with only good and evil; these two things alone we take to eternity: good will obtain for us eternal life, and evil, alas, I cannot even bear to think of it, because it would be a pain that would kill me: will I not see my beloved son any more for an eternity? No, but Our Lady will keep him good for me, and I will enjoy him for ever…”.11

With such letters Alessandro also received material help. But the young man could not stand the distance and solitude; he was unable to set himself up in business on his own, nor did he have the means; so a year later, on 17 December 1876, he was already back in Genoa, unemployed and disgraced.

In spite of this he still felt supported by his mother who did all she could to integrate him in society in a dignified way and give him a serene future. But it was a year of humiliating requests and privations. Mother Rosa rightly left him poor, so as to remove from him a means of disorderly dissipation; instead, she multiplied proofs of her affection, heartfelt appeals and incentives to change his life while she strove to find him a job. Alessandro was grateful for his mother’s love, but also still felt that he was a burden to his relatives and to family friends; so that, falling ill, he begged his mother not to spend money on treatment for him but to let him die instead. “If I was worth something, patience! But instead I am a miserable mortal who does not know how to do anything and am good for nothing. Oh, how much better it would be were merciful God to call me to him, forgiving me my sins! I assure you, O Mother, (be sure not to take my words badly, there!) that I pray him to call me to him and I am praying with all my heart”.12

In this letter, the strange death-wish of the twenty-two-year old boy is repeated; he never expresses joie de vivre or happiness at being alive. He also wanted to die to put an end to the sacrifices his mother was making for him. These sentiments show that a constant presence still dwelled in his heart, the figure of his mother who was always important and irreplaceable for unhappy Alessandro. And she, his mother, hoped and longed to save him at any cost, and was holding out her arms to him to rescue him in his extreme wreck.

The young man showed how sensitive he was by expressing the irritation and despair he felt when facing hardness in someone: “Forgive me, O beloved Mother, if I cause you displeasure by my behavior without meaning to; but I am a son who was publicly accused of having no love for his mother or his relatives. Mother, as I write these words I am crying, because perhaps Accinelli, who said them, does not know how he wounded my heart which is still bleeding and sees itself surrounded by people who must be treated hypocritically […]; I have no one other than you and God in heaven to whom I can confide my troubles on earth”.13

At this point the young man revealed to his mother the mystery of the religious upheaval which for three years had made him so different from what he had been as a student.

“I have also changed a lot with regard to my religious ideas”, he added in the same letter, “and I will tell you how. You must know that since I was a boy, hearing about Federico and then seeing how much he cared and still cares for the family […] I had taken him as my teacher and wanted to follow in his footsteps. However, I now realize that his way is false, as the whole world can see; so, if God allows me, I will leave the path I have been following and try to remedy the evil I have done”.14

Signs of illness ~ It is easy to imagine how Mother Rosa strove to put her son back on the right track, while she was very prompt in treating his physical ailments.

Therefore she paid for him to do the cure at the spa of Savignone and redoubled her insistence that he pull himself together.

In the autumn, on 30 October 1877, she received this comforting news from Alessandro: “Tomorrow or the day after tomorrow, I will go and do my devotions, and I hope that God will hear me”.15

Again, a few days later: “I managed, with your prayers, to tear myself away from vice. I confess that I feel much happier. It is true that it is a constant battle; indeed, I will tell you that temptations have never been so numerous as they are now; but I feel a je ne sais quoi that protects me. I do not ask you to pray, because I am sure that you are praying as much as you can”.16 The love of a holy mother had triumphed once again. However, the harsh combat was not over; Mother Rosa was still to suffer and shed bitter tears to save her son.

Dissipated life and false attribution of paternity ~ Towards the end of that year, because the Mother had busied herself and through her acquaintances, a post was found for Alessandro in Florence at a bank, a branch of the Banca Industriale Subalpina; he lodged and had meals with the Piarist Fathers who also looked after him later, when he moved elsewhere.

In the two years of his stay in Florence, the young man’s dissipated life reached its heights; in addition to giving up his work for no valid reason, he had a relationship with a woman with whom he lived, a certain Maria Tellini. Mother Rosa suffered deeply at her son’s decision. She tried to save the situation by advocating marriage, especially since Alessandro falsely claimed he had fathered a son, born before the above-mentioned marriage, celebrated on 2 June 1879.

The lie, however, perhaps devised to extort money, only gained him a small sum from his mother’s property, since it was declared that he had been left nothing on the death of his father.17

In the meantime, for obvious reasons, he had also been sacked by the bank. He found employment in an oil and lime industry, and then with a paper mill in his own name at Alatri, where he was forced to declare bankruptcy after two years; in the end, reduced to poverty, he was received in Genoa and then in Piacenza.

Another search for a job ~ With the help of relatives he endeavored to start a business in Genoa, where he attempted to open a small grocery shop; but in this venture too he was unlucky. Therefore Mother Rosa had to receive in Piacenza the unhappy young man who was by then seriously ill, and she gave him a job on the property at Gargatano.

However, the sad Odyssey of this son was a real Calvary for the Mother who put up with it all nonetheless, in the hope of saving his soul. In 1887, the sad truth came out: Alessandro confessed to his mother that his wife’s son was not his.18 In fact, he had been born before he had met the woman he married.

Mother Rosa was naturally dismayed; but she forgave him and once again tried to hold out her hand.

In autumn that year, Alessandro lived by himself, only alternating his residence between Gargatano and Via Vescovado in Piacenza. But his health, which had always been precarious, was visibly declining, and finally it became clear that he was consumptive.

Illness and death of Alessandro ~ In summer 1890, the violence of his illness showed the symptoms of an impending catastrophe which by the winter seemed imminent. The Mother was then in Rome, totally absorbed in carrying out her demanding duties when, on 21 November, a telegram from Bishop Scalabrini arrived, summoning her to Piacenza to her son’s bedside.

The illness seemed to be gaining the upper hand, but the young man still had some resources and then appeared to be rallying. In fact, after several days Mother Rosa returned to Rome but in her broken heart she felt that his end was imminent. In January ’91, she was again summoned by the Bishop of Piacenza: she arrived in that city on the morning of the 15th and went straight from the station to her son’s bedside. What a meeting! Pallid and consumptive, Alessandro had eyes only for the mother he had always loved intensely, who “was his all”; for him, “the son, her companion in affliction” who had never known the joy of life. His mother responded in silence to that look; nor could she say a word, gripped by the pangs of a mortal anguish.

Mass was celebrated in the next room by the bishop’s kind concession; the Mother took part in it with several sisters: then she spent the whole day beside her son, almost as if she wanted to prolong his life by offering him that motherly warmth which for so long she had been unable to show him.

So she stayed on in Piacenza, in the meantime fulfilling all her duties in the governance of the Institute with heroic fidelity, sending visitors to the houses, arranging destinations, seeing to her abundant correspondence and bearing the harshest of blows which continued to rain down on her even at that difficult and painful moment.

16 March 1891 was the last day of Alessandro’s life; he had received all the sacraments. Two priests, one of whom was Fr. Tornatore, had been with him continuously, by night and by day, for some time. From 7.00 o’clock that morning until 5.00 o’clock in the afternoon (when he died), Mother Rosa sat motionless beside her dying son; she prayed, in agony, that eternal life would be guaranteed at last to that son of her tears.

When the shadows of the winter evening had already shrouded the misty city and the clock of the cathedral tower was striking five, Alessandro breathed his last.

His broken-hearted mother gave him back to the Father, managing to resist tears to the very end, as she had promised sixteen years before.

She herself recounts in her Memorie: “Oh, how I suffered [from] the violent effort of resisting to the end! Oh, what a struggle! It was atrocious. My heart was breaking and I could not relieve it with tears, no! Oh, what an agony!” (M. 11.3, p. 18).

She then made the arrangements for the body, retired to the house in Via Farnese, extricated herself from the sisters who had accompanied her, locked herself in her cell and gave vent to her grief. Her sisters, outside the door, heard her sobbing for about two hours.

Like St. Monica, it can certainly be affirmed that Rosa Gattorno was doubly a mother to Alessandro, since she had given birth to him on earth and in heaven.

A painful parting: foundation in New York — Mother Rosa’s charity and patience, fortitude and prudence, invested with the great enlightenment she drew from her Crucified Christ, set her above all the rebellions of betrayed or unreciprocated love; nothing had seemed excessive to Rosa, to recover that creature which she had so loved.

God disposed extraordinary things during the Mother’s mourning, to bring her heroic love into the limelight.

Bishop Scalabrini had induced her, in those very days of March, to grant him five religious to open an Italian hospital in New York; this was where his missionaries of the “Cristopher Columbus” Institute for emigrants were working. After hasty negotiations, the sisters departed on 18 March 1891.19

While in the chapel Bishop Scalabrini was celebrating the moving celebration for the departure and blessing the missionaries who were leaving for America, Alessandro’s funeral was going on in the cathedral, widely attended by members of the clergy, the representatives of institutes and the people; the moving tolling of the bells for the funeral could be heard in the chapel of the Daughters of St. Anne, where the Mother among her sisters was giving her last embrace and maternal blessing to those who were leaving for distant parts. Nonetheless, there must have been in her heart a last, agonizing embrace for her son, whom she would not see again on this earth.

The moving coincidence awakened the deepest sympathy in everyone; but the admiration for that truly heroic mother was even greater.

Defections in Tuscany and an injurious letter ~ In that period, another painful event accompanied her mourning for Alessandro’s death.

The prodigal son had thus returned to the Father’s house, and this was enough to give a certain tone of resignation to the heartrending grief of the poor mother, who had known only unhappiness and misfortunes in her son; but at the same time she was the Foundress of a far larger and more complex family than her natural one, and other daughters, attracted by false mirages, were unable to resist the temptation of leaving.

On 4 March she had in fact received the unexpected news that the two superiors of Pistoia and Prato had left the Institute accompanied by several other religious, wishing to found another congregation. Mother Rosa went immediately to the rescue, sending a trusted visitor; but the decision had already been taken and they had fled, after stealing linen, food and money from their respective houses.

The local Ordinaries took it upon themselves to remedy the situation.

What a strong faith the Mother needed to withstand the fury of these violent squalls!

On that 18 March, while the missionary sisters were leaving for America, Alessandro’s body was taken to the cemetery. In the evening, Mother Rosa left for Rome. Here, after two months, she received a nasty letter from a teacher in the Piacenza area who had once been a Daughter of St. Anne but had had to be separated from the Institute for serious reasons; with incredible wickedness that woman had exploded in revenge, even attributing Alessandro’s death to her curses.

Nor was she sparing in her insults and curses to the Mother, who gave the letter to her spiritual director and kept silent, tightly clasping her Crucifix. This evil only became known after her death.20

Carlotta’s marriage ~ Another very sharp thorn in Mother Rosa’s life was her daughter, Carlotta. She had grown up good and affectionate at boarding school in Milan and then in Piacenza with her mother; in fact, although the poor deaf-mute had lacked nothing, she did not have a peaceful life. A Roman patrician, Count Gaspare Barbiellini, fell in love with her and asked for her hand in marriage, perhaps in about 1873. The Mother trembled at the presentiment of so uncertain a future; after saying many prayers she asked the advice of Mgr. Wanstienkist, whom the girl trusted and who was virtually her spiritual director.

The good Prelate advised against any plan of marriage for obvious reasons, given Carlotta’s condition;21 but the real fact which had to be taken into account was that reciprocal love existed between the young man and the girl, as soon as she realized what he felt for her. It was therefore decided that a marriage take place. It was celebrated in spring 1876 in Rosa’s family home in Genoa, which had been inherited by her brother Francesco.22

At first everything seemed to be going well and the Mother was very pleased with her son-in-law, who showed himself to be sensitive, generous and devout. For her part, the Mother had done her best to give her daughter everything fitting, both dowry and gifts, with her brothers’ tender and loving assistance.

Financial claims by her son-in-law ~ The newly married couple settled in Piacenza in a house next door to the Mother House of the Daughters of St. Anne, so that the mother could supervise her daughter closely and continue to be her comfort and guide, given her condition of deafness. Later, when the Generalate was established in Rome, her brother Federico, with Fr. Tornatore’s advice, persuaded her to allow a small house with two floors to be built there on a corner of its land, in which the couple could live so that they would always be close to the Mother.

God blessed the union with several children whose education was partly provided for by the Mother, who assigned several of her religious for the purpose; this was easy, because of the family’s closeness to the Mother House. However, problems soon arose which troubled Mother Rosa for more than twenty years and involved her in a tough struggle to keep a clear conscience in her role as Foundress and in the defense of the Institute’s rights and property against the new couple’s greed.

Her daughter Carlotta, probably ignorant of the wrong she was doing but incited by her husband, began to advance claims for further benefits deriving from the property that her mother, as General of the Institute of the Daughters of St. Anne appeared to possess, almost as if she had a right to them; actually, the Mother owned no real estate.23

Since Mother Rosa had scrupulously given her daughter all she could expect of the family property,24 she was inflexible about not ceding her any property that belonged to the Institute. But the couple, circumventing the obstacle, made overtures to many influential sisters and some superiors, brazenly asking for even valuable gifts. Knowing how upset the Foundress could become, they often condescended to offer them gifts by being economical in the administration of their houses or by drawing on their own personal assets, as Sr. Anna Benedetta Carrega sometimes did. The Mother did not always oppose these gifts which, since they were being made to others, she did not think should be denied outright to those who were so close to her; but she never failed to complain if some superior were excessively lavish.25

Rumors of discontent within the Institute and recourse to the Sacred Congregation — Since this painful situation had lasted for years, in many of the Institute’s houses news of what was happening had spread, that is, of the claims of Carlotta’s family and the gifts she was receiving; as a result, when some house needed to be especially economical because of the scarcity of means or the incapacity of whoever was in charge, voices of discontent were raised as well as complaints that were not exempt from negative judgments of the Mother; some even dared to send accusations to the Holy See saying that she was reducing the religious to hunger in order to enrich her daughter and son-in-law.

Thus, shortly after Alessandro’s death, this unjust and dishonorable series of accusations which had begun in 1889 became more acute. Some people even resorted, as has been said, to provoking the intervention of the Sacred Congregation for Bishops and Regulars which enjoined the Cardinal Protector to appoint a delegate, Mgr. Beniamino Cavicchioni, as secret Visitor.

In the meantime Fr. Francesco Chemin’s petition arrived in Rome from Bassano del Grappa concerning a donation he claimed to have made but which in fact turned out to be a real deed of purchase of property by the Institute. This controversy, like many others, was resolved by Mgr. Beniamino Cavicchioni, who, in his report to the Cardinal Prefect wrote: “The Reverend Chemin’s request does not seem to me at all trustworthy, and I abstain from boring Your Eminence with the tale of the muddles made by the said priest and the upset he caused the Daughters of St. Anne on the occasion of their purchase of the property which he claimed to have given them”.26

These allusions are sufficient to demonstrate the difficulties with which Rosa Gattorno’s governance had to deal in this period, either because of internal reasons of the Institute, or because of the most delicate relationship which bound her to her daughter’s life. With all their maneuvers, her daughter, and perhaps also her son-in-law, were attempting to advance claims, seeking the support of powerful Roman prelates27 to extort all they wanted and, in the meantime, putting the Foundress and her Institute in a bad light.

We therefore have a series of events that document the impropriety and greed of the Mother’s son-in-law.

Barbiellini’s blackmail ~ The marriage between Carlotta and Gaspare seemed happy at the beginning, as has been said, and Barbiellini enjoyed the trust and esteem of his mother-in-law and of all the sisters. In 1877 the Foundress appointed him her procurator general and entrusted many administrative tasks to him. In 1884 she gave him responsibility for overseeing the enlargement of the Mother House; at the same time Barbiellini had renovation work done on his own house, charging the expenses to the Institute. Moreover, many payment receipts were made out in his name, as though he were using his own money and not the Mother’s. In 1889, declaring himself on this account her creditor, he demanded settlement of a debt of 20,000 lire that he had contracted in the past with a certain Marianna Bertola. To spare the Mother distress, her secretary, Sr. Anna Benedetta Carrega, paid off the debt with her own money28.

In 1891, at his insistent request, the administration of the Gargatano estate29 was entrusted to Barbiellini himself; in 1895 he demanded payment of a huge sum (over 250,000 lire) as salary for his post as procurator and for works he had had carried out for the Institute, claiming to have paid for them out of his own pocket. With evident blackmail, he brought Carlotta, then in her last pregnancy, and her children to the Mother House, threatening never to take his family back if his demands were not met. Ten days later Barbiellini, accompanied by his lawyer, came to take back his family, but persisted in his demands30.

The dispute dragged on until 11 May 1896, when an agreement was reached and he was paid a sum of about 13,000 lire31.

One can easily imagine the Mother’s great suffering in these sad events. Her feelings are well expressed by a letter her brother Federico wrote to her on 30 September 1895: “I was sorry at your news, which is never very good; but how can it be otherwise with so many troubles? I take good care not to give advice; it is useless to give it. You are wise enough, but in this case you are also a mother, and motherly compassion and love for one’s descendants cannot give courage for energetic action, even though one knows that the brutish man wants to exploit these natural feelings with usury, feelings that in you are perhaps stronger because of your magnanimous heart. Courage, do what you can…”32.

This Calvary did not last only during the Mother’s lifetime. Examining the chronology of the lawsuits and harassment to which the Institute was subjected after the Foundress’s death, one can only draw a single conclusion, namely that it was a real persecution of the Mother, of her Assistants and of the Institute itself. But in the end truth and justice triumphed completely: every step of the legal proceedings, which dragged on from 1900 to 1912, ended in full victory for the Institute, decreed by the various judgments of the courts. All the claims were rejected and all the accusations were retracted33.

But the most splendid victory was, in its time, that of the Mother’s upright conscience; how many tears she must have shed, clinging to her Crucifix and tasting with him the bitterest chalice! What brings the holocaust to its height is the immolation of love and reputation: in this Mother Rosa was a faithful companion of her Savior, enduring dishonor and hostility not only from her relatives but also from several of her religious Daughters who, as we shall see later, brought about an inquiry by the Church.

In the Apostolic Visitation too, begun in 1898 and concluded in 1903 and undoubtedly occasioned by the deficient religious spirit of some sisters and their lack of a sense of belonging to the Institute, the Visitor, Bishop Domenico Serafini, while making some observations about the government of the Congregation, which during Mother Rosa’s lifetime had in his judgment been “too personal”, recognized that the Mother had had the good of the Institute at heart above all else and that among the Daughters of St. Anne he had generally found a spirit of self-denial and humility, submission to superiors and a will to do good34.

Meanwhile, for the Mother the agony lasted until the end of her life. After so many years the memory of this drama is still alive, and one cannot speak of it without recognizing once again the heroism of this very great woman; it seems impossible that a mother, because she was a mother, should have had to suffer so much, but to have suffered with such humility, firmness and dignity is superhuman.

Mother Rosa was and remains a great witness to human values, to privation, to poverty, and to a most profound interior life that reaches the heights of mysticism.

And her Daughters, while feeling her close and present, sense her greatness, which in a certain sense makes her inaccessible, and the extraordinary quality that makes her so privileged and worthy of boundless admiration.
