Mother Rosa’s open partiality for little ones and the sick — Great lessons in gratuitousness — Mysterious cures — Works of mercy — Special attentions for the sick sisters — The Mother’s extraordinary presence at difficult moments; clairvoyance and the penetration of hearts — The reward for charity.

Mother Rosa’s open partiality for little ones and the sick ~ The exercise of charity is part of the Church’s most firmly established tradition, to the extent that her teaching includes all the works of mercy: seven for relieving the body and another seven for sustaining the spirit. This catechesis was born from the tenderness of Christ’s Heart; indeed all these expressions of love for neighbor are found in the Gospel passages, passed on in the discourses and parables of Jesus or practized by him frequently, in different forms. All his miracles are works of mercy.

He therefore commanded them just as he commanded love, and clearly asserted that in the last judgment they will be the intransgressible condition and measure of the eternal reward.

Christian solidarity and charity in the broadest sense are therefore an imperative, an assumption of responsibility that involves one in the destiny of others. Mother Rosa lived to the full this total uprooting of self, becoming in a certain sense a hostage of the poor and abandoned human beings, in whose suffering faces she saw the unmistakable outline of another face, that of her crucified Love.

Piacenza was the first scene of her great self-giving as we have attempted to say in chapters VI-II and IX.

Before exhorting and sending out her sisters to be “angels of charity” as they were often described, Rosa Gattorno herself wanted to give them an example of the way in which one should love the lowliest; therefore even when her Institute had grown considerably, she took the appropriate opportunities to serve them. Satisfying the hungry and clothing the poor was the continuous work of her life to which she dedicated herself personally. She even made the most of her journeys, during which she would devote herself to knitting or such like for the poor. Since she had been in the world but especially as a religious, she had gone out to collect alms for the poor and did this until her last years, when ill health prevented her. She was also able to organize the work of others for this purpose very wisely, thereby finding greater assistance in alleviating the poverty of society’s outcasts. It is well known in this respect that in the Italo-Abyssinian war of 1896 she obtained effective aid from the National Commmittee of Florence and had a large quantity of clothes made up in Rome which were then distributed by her missionaries in Africa.

Not only was she full of initiative in relieving the misery of the poor, but she arranged that her sisters dedicate themselves to education and to serving the sick, to whom she always gave priority with undeniable, natural joy.

With this unreserved love she devoted herself to the instruction of children in Genoa, Piacenza and Rome, and how zealously she desired all her houses to have good schools for poor children, classes of religious instruction and especially Christian kindness! When she was able to open the Generalate in Rome, she organized meeting places for girls from humble backgrounds there, and gathered many of them every Sunday for catechism.

She often liked to spend time with these little girls and made them happy with the grace of her motherly smile and sometimes, with small presents.

Together with affection for children, Rosa Gattorno had also learned from the Teacher deep compassion for the sick: in the first years of the Institute’s foundation she herself nursed the sick, not only nuns but also the girls she had taken in, spending long hours and sometimes entire nights at the bedside of those innocents.1

With regard to the sick, the way she wanted them treated should be noted in particular. She suggested to the sisters how they should greet them on their visits by drawing near to them: “Since”, she said, “in the sick you are greeting Jesus Christ”.2

Furthermore, when nursing them in their homes, she wanted the sisters to be sure to offer support and comfort to their families as well, so that they would also show heroic patience at the bedside of the suffering and aim for the good of their souls with enlightened wisdom.

Great lessons in gratuitousness ~ It is also known that the Rule established that nothing should ever be accepted in compensation for service to the sick at home, not even a cup of coffee; the Mother only allowed the sisters to accept a glass of water, and only when they really needed one.

On this topic, Sr. Anna Fabiana Orsi tells us how the sealed envelopes containing money received from the families of sick persons were immediately returned to the sender.3

Mother Rosa deeply appreciated the absolute purity and gratuitousness of this self-giving tested in the fire of sacrifice, and she was so avid for it that not even on her deathbed did she consent to mitigate that custom for herself, despite the insistence of Dr. Alessandro Lupi who had been called in for consultation in her last illness.4

The Mother did not only want this austere treatment for herself and her Daughters out of a spirit of penance, but also because she was convinced that respect for the poverty of others is not sincere if one does not participate through love in the privations of others.

The Savior’s examples are so eloquent in this regard! “…he was rich, but he became poor for your sake”(2 Co 8:9); and while he satisfied the crowds with the miracle, he suffered hunger and thirst.

Therefore it was not excessive severity, but illuminated and radical love for perfection that guided Mother Rosa in this; as a result she gave her Daughters, even among the hardships of the distant missions, this precious maxim: “Charity, to be perfect, must not have any compensation on earth”.5

On her journeys, her desire to be close to the sick whom she called “her beloved suffering” showed no signs of abating. The sentiment of love for her sick so dominated her heart that she would go and see them in hospital, even if none of her own religious were there, as she did at Agrigento when she was visiting the house of the Daughters of St. Anne.6

Mysterious cures ~ In lovingly doing her utmost for those tortured bodies, miracles of healing often blossomed under her hands. In the informative processes, all kinds of miracles are recounted. A little girl of about seven who had been taken in with the orphan girls in Piacenza was afflicted with a serious skin infection of the scalp which seemed resistant to any cure, even the treatment she was given in hospital for about three months. One day Mother Rosa, who had gone to the infirmary while the nursing sisters were medicating the poor child, wanted to bandage her tormented little head in her own way and recommended that in future the nurses also do it that way, adding that the doctor would certainly come the following morning.

The doctor was not actually expected since there was no urgent need; but indeed the next morning, without being called, he arrived unexpectedly at the house in Via Farnese. He examined the little girl and to his great amazement found her cured of the stubborn ailment, which he and the hospital doctors had previously diagnosed as resistant to any cure. Knowing that the child had been touched by the Mother the day before, he attested that the cure must have been due to her intervention and not to the medicines which, moreover, had previously had no effect.7

In the Rome novitiate in about 1890, Sr. Anna Candida Quadrana was suffering from a fistula in the leg due to a burst varicose vein. One day the Mother made the sign of a cross with her hand over the sick leg and the sister was instantly healed. Here, Sr. Anna Cunegonda Pacini, who recounts the event, seals her testimony with these crystal-clear words: “I witnessed it personally, since Sr. Anna Candida was my companion in the novitiate”.8

Sr. Anna Bernardina was seriously ill with typhus in the infirmary at Piacenza in 1869 and the doctor considered her in imminent danger of death. In the evening the Mother went to the infirmary with Fr. Tornatore and asked the nurse how Sr. Anna Bernardina was. “Very bad”, she replied, “the doctor thinks she will probably not last the night”. Mother Rosa dismissed Fr. Tornatore and sent the nurse to rest, saying, “In the meantime I will stay and be nurse”.

She was left alone with the sick sister except that in the bed next to her, Sr. Anna Apollonia also lay ill. The Mother stooped over Sr. Anna Bernardina, calling her several times by name, but in vain; then she shook her by the shoulders saying to her: “In the name of obedience, answer me!”. The ill woman opened her eyes and recognized the Mother General, who encouraged her and gave her to drink a spoonful of a liquid which she had brought with her in a little bottle, adding: “Drink! Just think you have to get well and tomorrow morning at six o’clock you will go down to chapel and receive Communion”. The next morning, in fact, the sister, completely cured, was in the chapel at the pre-arranged time and received Communion. Doctor Albertazzi was astonished, recognized a miracle and told Sr. Anna Apollonia that when his time came, he too would seek to be healed by Mother Gattorno’s touch.9

However, these extraordinary events were not always easily achieved. The Teacher bore the burden of our sufferings by teaching us that our love too must truly bear the weight of others’ pain. Mother Rosa had thoroughly understood this message and often asked God to take her Daughter’s sufferings from them and give them to her instead, even if they were very serious troubles of the spirit, as we read in her letters to Sr. Anna Virginia Gaggi.10

Since the very first years of life as a religious she had known these heights of love. Indeed, when one of the first little orphans she had taken in fell ill, she herself took charge of her treatment. The child was afflicted with a form of smallpox so virulent that it seemed like the plague. One evening she appeared in a desperate state and near her end; instead, the following day the sisters found the little girl completely cured, but the Mother herself had contracted the disease. She answered the sisters’ laments saying, “it is nothing, nothing at all, it will pass”. She refused to go to bed, but after three or four days she too was cured11 and her sisters believed she had asked God to give her the ailment so as to deliver the child.

The miraculous cures worked by Mother Rosa are countless and are told by eye witnesses in the processes with unanimous simplicity.

It is therefore not surprising that Rosa Gattorno also wanted her Daughters to be proof of boundless love in caring for the sick, especially if, by their very nature they were repulsive and burdensome. When Sr. Anna Apollonia Marchetti, worn out and exasperated with looking after an old canon in Marcianise, heard that the Mother General had arrived in Naples, she went to see her straight away to ask her to send her to the mission to free her from that harassing patient. But she did not even have time to open her mouth for Mother Rosa, showing that she knew all about it, said to her: “Do you want to be sent to America? Instead go back to your sick old man! He is your America and with him you can exercise your virtue and show your zeal”.

She made the sign of the cross on her forehead and dismissed her.12 The sister left, and all her disgust for her demanding office disappeared.

Works of mercy ~ In the Mother’s heart all the miseries of human life found a compassion so generous that it prompted her to study all possible ways to alleviate it.

Glancing through the list of the 319 houses she had opened, we find all kinds in addition to the hospitals and assistance to the sick in their homes which remained the Institute’s principal work: homes for waifs and strays, premises where babies could be breast-fed, institutes for social assistance, boarding schools, psychiatric hospitals, assistance in prisons. Every age and condition of life are represented, and all these works in Italy and abroad, as well as on the missions, existed under Mother Gattorno’s enthusiastic direction.

It is easy to see that one of the most difficult charitable acts is assistance in prisons; here the detained are not only afflicted by misfortune but the wickedness which warps the human soul is often also present, especially if they are rebellious to justice and hostile to any purifying repentance. Rosa Gattorno wholeheartedly embraced even the work of comforting prisoners. Perhaps she had a first opportunity for it in about 1868, when she went from Piacenza to Alessandria, where some Genoese, including her brother Federico, were being held in the Fortress of Bormida.13 She was admitted to the prisoners as a nurse, but one might presume that she was more specifically involved in consoling and advising her brother.

This event must have awakened in Mother Rosa’s heart the deep desire to concern herself with other such unfortunates; once her Institute had developed, she agreed with the joy of her great heart to provide assistance to the prisons of Bari (1894), Salerno (1895), Genoa (1898), and Santa Maria Capua Vetere (1896). It was precisely at the prison in Genoa that in 1939 a wonderful miracle of healing occurred through Mother Rosa Gattorno’s intercession, almost as if to show her fondness for these poor wretches.

Just as during his public life Jesus aimed to heal minds through physical cures, so Mother Rosa sought with ardent zeal to convert to God those she helped. She encouraged her sisters to do the same whenever she sent them to help these unhappy persons and taught them to show finesse and friendliness in their dealings, combined with a deep spirituality, which for almost all these people, brought close to God if necessary, crowned the humble service of physical healing.

Special attentions for the sick sisters ~ Wishing her sisters to sacrifice themselves entirely to the relief and salvation of others, Mother Rosa looked after their health with motherly care and gave them special support when they were ill, as true charity demands. In Piacenza she once gathered the superiors for spiritual exercises preached by Fr. Manzi, a Vincentian priest; during those days the Mother, as always, treated them with truly exquisite understanding and friendliness; then at the end of the retreat she told all the superiors: “Now we have understood one another: you must treat your sisters as you have been treated here”.14

At this point we must observe that Mother Rosa’s wise provisions were not always obeyed by her superiors, which is why here and there some unjust privation would sometimes be exacted and complaints heard, but when the facts were known, the Mother proceeded to reprimand the superior and even to take rigorous measures to re-establish the proper atmosphere of love.15

For the care of the sick then, in addition to a specific Rule in which her most exquisite religious maternity is vibrant, she founded various houses that were well equipped, obviously in proportion to the means the Institute then had available and according to the area, like that, for example, of Gargatano whose location deep in the countryside was rather inconvenient because of its distance from inhabited centers; here she gathered the religious most in need of attention or seriously ill.

However, no one can deny that the creation of these houses was essential at that time, since the public hospital structures were often in a deplorable condition and there were no other places properly equipped or suitable for this purpose.

It would be superfluous to note here that Mother Rosa’s concern, over and above her solicitude for the health of the body, was to strengthen the spirit; nor was she content with the basic spiritual comforts for her Daughters but wanted a true abundance of these means so that they could enjoy them as befits souls consecrated to God; and woe betide any superior who might be negligent in this!

Once in Naples, while the community was having a small celebration for her, a religious died in the house without Mother Rosa having been informed of her illness or the gravity of her condition. The superior had thought it fitting to be silent in order not to disturb the festivities or perhaps because she did not realize that the sick sister’s death was imminent. Mother Rosa was so indignant with this way of proceeding that she severely reprimanded that superior, as the testimonies reveal.16

The Mother’s extraordinary presence at difficult moments; clairvoyance and the penetration of hearts ~ God sometimes rewarded the Mother’s maternal devotion to her Daughters with extraordinary gifts; so it happened that at the bedside of one who was dying, she was made aware of the restless state of her conscience by a divine revelation; with the most delicate of efforts she induced the patient to reflect, and she confirmed to the Mother that she had been right, asked for the confessor to return and made peace in preparation for her last journey.17

At other times, she was inexplicably informed of the serious condition of some religious in another place; while the Mother was talking to a superior one day, she suddenly said: “Go back to your house, because a sister is dying”.18 And so it was.

Since we are on the subject, several events must be cited here which are certainly extraordinary and which we cannot doubt because of their number and the variety of the circumstances, places and persons who were their object, who attested to them under oath; we are referring to the Mother’s many bilocations or instances of miraculous presence in two places at the same time. One might think that with these inexplicable events, moreover very rare in the history of saints, the Lord wanted to show his assent to Rosa Gattorno’s sincere diligence in the work of her governance, for which a person’s ordinary strength and graces could not have sufficed, given the rapid expansion of the Institute and the many problems which the sisters in the most distant houses were encountering.

Sr. Anna Apollonia Marchetti, as has been said, was helping a sick old man, Canon Benedetto Petrolo, who had bequeathed his possessions to the Daughters of St. Anne; thus the sisters had to put up with much annoyance from his relatives.

One evening, towards 11.00 o’clock, Sr. Anna Apollonia, accompanying some sisters to the station of Marcianise, saw three or four threatening-looking young people. She therefore went to a policemen so as not to be troubled by them. However, returning home alone, she was frightened of meeting them again. In her heart, because she trusted and loved her immensely, she therefore called on Mother Rosa, then far away. All of a sudden she saw the Mother beside her, speaking words of encouragement: “Don’t be afraid, I am with you”. She did indeed meet the same young people again, but they kept their distance. On the other hand, Mother Rosa accompanied her to the door of the house, then vanished.19

As soon as she had entered, with deep wonder she told Sr. Anna Colombana what had occurred; the latter, instead of looking surprised, answered: “I know something about the Mother’s protection too!” and told her of this event: “In our house at Adernò (today Adrano) in Sicily, the local superior, Sr. Anna Pacifica, and another sister had agreed to leave the Institute unbeknown to the Mother who was then living in Piacenza. One evening the Servant of God suddenly appeared in that house, to this local superior’s great surprise. ‘How is it, Mother’, she said, ‘that you come all alone at this hour and without warning?’.

‘As you do, so do I’, replied the Mother. And she desired to receive the sisters of the community immediately. Then, that same night, she had the other sister leave with another companion for a house in North Italy and took the superior with her to Piacenza. They arrived early the next morning. The porter sister was amazed at seeing Sr. Anna Pacifica arrive from Sicily so early and by herself, for she saw no one else; and on being told that she had traveled with the Mother, the porter sister was even more surprised, as she knew that Mother Rosa had been in the house at the time”.20

Sr. Anna Rebecca, in Rome for business and not feeling very well, did not want to return to Santa Maria Capua Vetere where she lived. Mother Rosa encouraged her to go back to her post saying to her: “Go on, don’t be afraid, I will go with you”.

The sister submitted and left, but alone. When she arrived at the station in the evening, a revenue officer was kind and took her home, since he knew her as the superior of the hospital. The following day the same revenue officer, seeing Sr. Anna Rebecca said to her, “Superior, what have you done with the other sister who was with you?”.

“Which one?”, Sr. Anna Rebecca asked, dumbfounded.

“What?”, the exciseman continued, “the one who was with you yesterday evening when you arrived at the station, when I accompanied you; that tall, well-built nun…”. The superior protested, reasserting that she had traveled alone; but remembering what the Mother had said to her the day before, she believed she had accompanied her in an extraordinary way.21

In chapter XV we recounted the Mother’s inexplicable presence in the forest of Jujui, when she presented herself to the Indio who welcomed Sr. Anna Camilla Valentini with her traveling companions, and we have Sr. Anna Giuseppa Troni’s reliable testimony of another event. This sister, who was among Rosa Gattorno’s first companions and had been clothed with her in Piacenza in 1867, was the first superior of the missionaries who went to Bolivia in 1878.

One day, finding herself in serious difficulties and uncertain how to deal with them in such a distant land, she thought of her Mother General and exclaimed: “Ah! If only our Mother were here, how well she would resolve things!” In saying this, she suddenly saw the Mother before her, encouraging her and telling her what to do.

She then made as if to ask the Mother a question, but she vanished. Somewhat scared, she ran to call the other sisters and told them what had happened.22

On 15 December 1891 in the Generalate of Rome, Mother Rosa summoned Sr. Anna Cunegonda Pacini, and invited her to say some prayers with her to the Child Jesus, starting the Novena of Holy Christmas, and said: “I want to show you something…”. So saying she took a figurine of the Child Jesus from a cupboard; it seemed to the sister to be covered in bruises, so she stretched out her hand to touch it, thinking they were dirty marks. The Mother smiled and said: “No, my daughter, Jesus is suffering for our sisters’ sins. Do you want to help me pray to Baby Jesus?”. She answered “yes”. So they both knelt before the figurine which had been put on the Mother’s little desk, and began to pray.

Suddenly the Mother fell silent and stayed motionless gazing upwards, while tears streamed from her eyes and her face looked almost as if she were shuddering with disgust. Sr. Anna Cunegonda, impressed and frightened, shook the Mother several times, but for three quarters of an hour she remained in ecstasy.

At last she came to herself and seeing the sister beside her, said: “I beg you not to tell anyone what you have seen, indeed, you must swear to me that you will not even tell of it after my death, even if our Cardinal Protector were to question you”. The sister swore, and kept the secret until she was interrogated at the informative process in Naples on 9 March 1915. During that Novena of Holy Christmas, she was asked by the Mother herself to do some penance in atonement, and on the 24th, she was again summoned to her study: the Mother showed her the same figurine of the Baby Jesus, which looked luminous and very lovely.

“You see?”, the Servant of God said, “in America some of our sisters were displeasing Jesus, because they wanted to cause a schism […] deserting our Institute for another foundation…”.

“And how did you come to know it, Mother?”.

“Jesus sent me there and everything has been put right; only one had to leave, and it was fitting that she should leave”.

A few months later it became known in the community in Rome that Mother Rosa had been seen in that house in America during the Christmas novena23.

What Sr. Anna Nestore Tagliabue tells of herself is equally surprising. “I was superior for the first time in our house in Crotone, and with regard to some of the sisters my conscience felt a little uneasy. I had not confided this even to my confessor, waiting to see how things would turn out; unexpectedly I received a letter from the Mother giving me instructions about the very matter that was troubling me. I was rather surprised, not only because I had confided in no one, but also because there had been absolutely no time for the Mother to be informed by others”24.

We could go on at length recounting similar facts, since very many wonderful ones are related in the personal experiences of the Daughters of St. Anne and especially in the informative processes held in various dioceses.

The reward of charity ~ This extraordinary light to penetrate the depths of souls, this presence in places so far from where she lived, seem a clear sign of God’s approval of her work, wholly devoted to her neighbor and to the Institute, which she always regarded as solely the work of God. It seems, moreover, that God wished to widen for her, in a wonderful way, the field ordinarily open to a human creature, so that the works of her charity might be greater and more numerous, and so that her charity might shine out as truly heroic, that is, worthy of Christian admiration and a powerful stimulus to imitation.

All this is in keeping with God’s way of acting; indeed, it is part of his promises. There comes to mind the splendid passage of Isaiah: “… the fast that I choose […] is it not to share your bread with the hungry, and bring the homeless poor into your house; when you see the naked, to cover them, and not to hide yourself from your own kin? Then your light shall break forth like the dawn, and your healing shall spring up quickly; your vindicator shall go before you, the glory of the Lord shall be your rear guard. Then you shall call, and the Lord will answer; you shall cry for help, and he will say, ‘Here I am’.

If you remove the yoke from among you, the pointing of the finger, the speaking of evil, if you offer your food to the hungry and satisfy the needs of the afflicted, then your light shall rise in the darkness and your gloom be like the noonday. The Lord will guide you continually, and satisfy your needs in parched places, and make your bones strong; and you shall be like a watered garden, like a spring of water, whose waters never fail” (Is 58:7-11).

This is the sure reward of charity; and for Mother Rosa it meant wonders of interior light, splendid manifestations of God’s inner assistance, extraordinary interventions of the omnipotence and fatherly protection of God, interior riches and mystical unions and, still more, the full abundance of all the supernatural virtues.

The Old and the New Testament agree in saying: “Blessed are the merciful, for they will receive mercy” (Mt 5:7). That is, they will perhaps receive it from men, but certainly and abundantly from God.
